- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2110.14043v2 · version read: v2 · v1: 2021-10-26
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, vol. 49, no. 3, pp. 1086-1101, March 2023 (journal article; early access 2022; also presented in the ICSE 2023 Journal-First Papers track)
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Model-based test generation is proposed as an alternative to costly manual regression test creation for web apps, but existing model inference techniques rely on threshold-based whole-page comparison to decide state equivalence, which cannot reliably identify near-duplicate pages; they therefore infer inadequate models of dynamic web apps and fragile test oracles, making the generated regression suites ineffective. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 61 of the saved text | 61 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The main challenge named is the presence of a large number of near-duplicate web pages that whole-page state abstraction functions (a distance function plus a manually chosen threshold) cannot identify: a high threshold drops distinct states (incomplete model), a low one keeps near-duplicates (imprecise model); near-duplicates cause redundant test cases and wasted exploration effort on already-seen functionality, and whole-page oracles break on minor non-functional changes (false-positive failures). The root cause identified is duplicated functionality within a page (Nd3-struct near-duplicates). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 168 of the saved text | 168 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation objective; evaluation targets are (RQ1) the multi-class classification F1 averaged over clone, near-duplicate and distinct classes plus the number of detected near-duplicates; (RQ2) model quality against a ground-truth model, with Pr = covered ground-truth states / total states in the inferred model and Re = covered ground-truth states / total ground-truth states (and F1); (RQ3) test breakages / successful test actions and mutation-analysis detection of changes. Exploration itself is driven by Eq. 2-3: score(alpha) = -1 if alpha is explored, 0 if an equivalent actionable alpha_eq is explored, otherwise c_0 * size({alpha_eq ...}) with 0 < c_0 <= 1 (default 1); score(S) = sum of score(alpha) over the actionables of state S, and the next state/actionable with the highest score is explored. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 758 of the saved text | 758 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Treat a web page not as a single functional entity but as a hierarchy of fragments (VIPS segmentation); classify state pairs by comparing fragments structurally (APTED on pruned DOM subtrees) and visually (colour histogram) without thresholds, discard clone/Nd2-data states, de-prioritise actionables equivalent to already explored ones so exploration is diversified toward unique fragments, and generate fragment-level assertions with memoised data-fluid fragments so oracles tolerate non-functional changes. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 273 of the saved text | 273 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against whole-page structural and visual state-comparison techniques: on 86,165 labelled state pairs FragGen detects 123% more near-duplicates on average; its crawl models have higher precision and recall (abstract: 62% more precision, 70% more recall; results: 79% precision, 83% recall, F1 0.80 vs 0.47 and 0.46); its test actions succeed nearly 100% on the same app version (introduction: existing techniques' suites have nearly 17% of test actions failing on the same version; results: whole-page techniques' test actions succeed 86.2% on average) and its oracles detect 98.7% of visible changes while ignoring 90.6% of equivalent mutants. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = costly manual test creation and test maintenance cost (motivation; an Accenture study is cited for $120 million per year of test repair), wasted / redundant exploration effort, discover unique states faster, exploration time limit as stopping criterion (maximum exploration time of 1 hour; 60 minute crawls), memoization to improve the performance of the recursive Classify function, costly manual analysis of false-positive test failures (line 262); fewer false positives reduce the manual effort needed to identify app changes (lines 887, 917); agent kind = automated model-based test generation for web apps: a crawler (FragGen, built on Crawljax) that triggers events on actionables to infer a graph-based state-transition model of the web app and derives regression test cases with assertions from its paths; no LLM or learned agent is involved; position = other (state abstraction and exploration strategy inside a web-app crawler that infers an app model for regression test generation). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

The natural-language routines of AWM and ICAL pose challenges for formal verification and precise composition, and both methods rely on test queries (online) or high-quality annotated demonstrations (offline). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 122 of the saved text | 122 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Automated agent design improves agent harnesses through iterative revision, evaluation and feedback summarization, but existing methods are candidate-centric, leaving repair progress implicit; this causes inefficient repair targeting, slow consolidation of partial progress, and propagation of ineffective interventions across rounds. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Organizing cross-round experience around candidates makes repair progress implicit: evidence about each issue is scattered across candidate records, so the optimizer must reconstruct the repair context before each revision; because each candidate is evaluated as a whole, the outcome of a particular intervention is difficult to isolate; and beneficial and harmful changes remain entangled. Realizing issue-centric optimization raises two key challenges: reliable issue-state maintenance (turning heterogeneous trajectories and sparse outcomes into stable, evidence-grounded issue identities and tracking their repair progress) and actionable, attributable revision (turning a multi-issue descriptive state into a focused code modification). Appendix A adds that interactive settings have a larger, task-dependent design space, sparse, delayed and hard-to-attribute feedback, and expensive evaluation, since each candidate needs environment rollouts that may require extensive model calls and interaction steps. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | For a fixed task environment, evaluator and backbone, with an optimization budget of T rounds, the system proposes candidates A_t, evaluates validation performance M_val(A_t), selects the best-validation candidate among A_0..A_T, and 'the objective is to achieve high test performance M_test'. Candidate-centric methods use A_{t+1} = argmax_{A∈Propose(H_t)} J_cand(A), where H_t holds candidates, trajectories, metrics M and diagnostic reports D, and J_cand estimates aggregate candidate quality; ADIAS uses A_{t+1} = argmax_{A∈Propose(H_t,E_t)} J_issue(A;E_t), with E_t the persistent issue state and J_issue the expected repair progress on unresolved issues, and E_{t+1} = UpdateIssueState(E_t, H_{t+1}). Reported: Score (success rate, or mean normalized native score r_i for WebShop/ScienceWorld; Eq. 15), interaction efficiency Eff. = Score / L̄ with L̄ the average number of environment interaction steps (Eq. 16), optimization efficiency as the best-so-far validation score B_t = max_{1≤j≤t} V_j (Eq. 17), and optimization stability as the cumulative average validation score V̄_t (Eq. 18). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Multi-step KL-regularized RL objective E_{pi_theta, env}[ sum_t r(a_t, h_t) ] - beta D_KL[ pi_theta(a_t/h_t) // pi_ref(a_t/h_t) ] (Eq. 3), where pi_theta is the LLM policy, a_t the composite step action (plan/thought/environment/explanation), h_t the agent history (actions so far plus current browser state), r the reward (sparse 1/0 success/failure, discount gamma = 1), env the external environment, pi_ref a reference policy (usually the initial model) and beta the KL weight. It is optimized with step-level DPO (Eq. 5) on preference pairs from MCTS whose action values are Q = alpha * Q_tilde + (1 - alpha) * Q_hat (Eq. 10), Q_tilde being the empirical MCTS value and Q_hat the value from the AI critic's ranking; pairs are kept when /Q(h_t,a_w) - Q(h_t,a_l)/ >= theta_threshold. The DPO loss (Eq. 5) is L_DPO(pi_theta; D) = -E_{(h, a^w, a^l) ~ D}[log sigma(beta log(pi_theta(a^w/h^w)/pi_ref(a^w/h^w)) - beta log(pi_theta(a^l/h^l)/pi_ref(a^l/h^l)))], with a^w preferred over a^l; Theorem 1 states that under preferences p(a^w > a^l / h_t) proportional to sigma(Q(h_t,a^w) - Q(h_t,a^l)) the DPO optimum equals the optimal RL policy pi*(a/h_t) proportional to pi_ref(a/h_t) exp(Q(h_t,a)/beta) (Eq. 9). | 0 | framing_problem | Self-improving agents rely on self-authored tests or metrics to accept their own edits while controlling both the optimised object and its verifier, so self-assigned scores can stay near perfect while real deployment performance degrades or stays low; the paper studies this as the verifier-deployment gap. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 44 of the saved text | 44 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | A structural conflict of interest: the agent can alter both the policy being optimised and the measuring instrument used to judge it, so passing verification may reflect an easier sample distribution, a more local metric or tests sharing the policy's mistaken assumption; formally, no endogenous-only gate can make both false-acceptance and false-rejection small when agent-visible evidence cannot distinguish regressing from non-regressing candidates. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 62 of the saved text | 62 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The primary outcome is deployment truth of the accepted policy after round 10: Y_{D}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{Score}(\mathrm{Rollout}(\pi;D))\right]. Here \pi is a policy, D is the target deployment distribution, Rollout is the task-specific evaluation procedure, and Score is its performance score; in the Atari experiments, one run is measured by mean raw return over five hidden deployment seeds and six complete episodes per seed. Deployment truth is agent-hidden, used only for offline reporting, and does not affect acceptance. With t indexing improvement rounds, the self-report r_{t}=V_{T^{\prime}_{t}}(\pi^{\prime}_{t}) is the scalar score from candidate tests T^{\prime}_{t} on candidate policy \pi^{\prime}_{t}; a verifier–deployment gap occurs when it stays high while Y_{D}(\pi_{t}) for the accepted policy stays low, decreases, or fails to recover. The separate sealed audit is A(\pi)=\frac{1}{/S_{A}/m}\sum_{s\in S_{A}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{Score}\!\left(\mathrm{Rollout}(\pi;D_{A},s,j)\right), where S_{A} is the hidden audit-instance/seed set, D_{A} the audit dynamics/input distribution, m repeats per instance, s an instance and j a repeat. Its non-regression gate uses b_{t}=A(\pi_{t}),c_{t}=A(\pi^{\prime}_{t}),\delta_{t}=\max(\delta_{\min},\rho/b_{t}/), accepting iff c_{t}\geq b_{t}-\delta_{t}, where b_{t} and c_{t} are incumbent and candidate audit scores, \rho is relative slack and \delta_{\min} minimum absolute slack. Secondary outcomes are peak truth, peak-to-final loss, round-level self-report, candidate acceptance rate, rejection precision, and false-rejection rate; multi-seed results use mean plus half-range. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 435 of the saved text | 435 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | SEAL retains self-authored tests but adds a fixed, executable harness-side audit before deployment, using hidden instances disjoint from training, self-tests, and final deployment evaluation. The agent cannot author or inspect the audit and receives only an accept/reject bit. Candidate and incumbent policies are compared with non-regression slack; after a clear audit regression, the whole incumbent policy-test state is retained. The audit is a finite-sample proxy, so SEAL reduces overwrites and large regressions without guaranteeing monotonic deployment improvement. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 47 of the saved text | 47 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Benchmark validation uses the refined forward query \Phi_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{fwd}}\;=\;\widehat{\Phi}^{h}(\mathcal{C}_{\lambda})\;\land\;\widehat{\Phi}_{\mathrm{bg}}^{h}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{S}})\;\land\;\widehat{\Phi}_{\mathrm{post}}^{h}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{S}})\;\land\;\neg\widehat{\Phi}_{\mathrm{pre}}^{h}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{S}}) and backward queries \Phi_{\lambda,j}^{\mathrm{bwd}}\;=\;\widehat{\Phi}^{h}(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{S}})\;\land\;\bigwedge_{k\neq j}\widehat{\Phi}^{h}(c_{\lambda,k})\;\land\;\neg\widehat{\Phi}^{h}(c_{\lambda,j}). Here λ is a scenario, S its sampled document region, the set of checks is \mathcal{C}_{\lambda}, individual checks are c_{\lambda,j}, and \mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{S}} is the independently generated world model; h bounds trace length, and \widehat{\Phi}^{h} denotes bounded SMT encodings. The pre/post parts encode preconditions/postconditions of tools mentioned in the checks, while bg encodes remaining tools. The forward query also includes initial-state values I_{\lambda}; in the backward query j is the check tested for over-restriction and k indexes the remaining checks. Scenarios are validated when both forward conflict search and backward audit pass after the validation loops; unresolved cases go to human review. This is bounded consistency, not formal certification against the original manual. Agent evaluation reports Pass@1 = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tfrac{\alpha_{i}}{n} (single-attempt success), \text{Pass@}k=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\!\left[1-\binom{n-\alpha_{i}}{k}\big/\binom{n}{k}\right] (at least one successful attempt, for n ≥ k), and \mathbf{Pass\text{\textasciicircum}k} =\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\binom{\alpha_{i}}{k}\big/\binom{n}{k} (all k attempts succeed). N is the number of tasks, n the independent runs per task, i the task index, α_i the successful runs on task i, and k the number of attempts considered. | 2 | framing_objective | The survey defines expected improvement in Eq. (6): \Delta J_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[s(\mathcal{A}_{t+1},q;B)-s(\mathcal{A}_{t},q;B)\right]. \mathcal{A}_{t}=(\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t},\theta_{t}), gives the reusable configuration: assets \mathcal{S}_{t}, architecture \mathcal{H}_{t}, and model parameters \theta_{t}, at adaptation round t. \mathcal{D} is an evaluation distribution over tasks or matched continuation states within the intended reuse scope; q is a case, B a common execution budget, and s the performance score (higher is better). The expectation also averages over execution randomness; \Delta J_{t}>0 supports average improvement under that scope and budget (425-435, 465-467, 524-534). The survey supplies additional conceptual objectives and diagnostics below; these are not new empirical gains, and notation is local to each passage. Behavioral change, Eq. (5): \delta_{t}(x)=d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{t+1}}(\cdot\mid x),\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)\right), Here x is a matched decision state, \pi_{\mathcal{A}} the action-selection distribution, and d_{\mathrm{TV}} total variation distance; positive \delta_{t}(x) shows change without establishing benefit (512-523). Skill contribution (1474-1535): G_{t}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}[s(\mathcal{A}_{t}[\mathcal{K}],q;B)]. \mathcal{A}_{t}[\mathcal{K}] replaces only the skill collection with \mathcal{K}; G_{t}(\mathcal{K}) is its expected score at the same distribution/budget, also averaging over execution randomness. For candidate skill k, Eq. (12): \Delta_{t}^{\mathcal{K}}(k\mid\mathcal{K})=G_{t}(\mathcal{K}\cup\{k\})-G_{t}(\mathcal{K}). The survey expresses SkillMOO-style task-success/inference-cost tradeoffs as Eq. (13): \mathfrak{P}_{t}=\operatorname{ParetoMax}_{\mathcal{K}\in\mathfrak{C}_{t}}\bigl(G_{t}(\mathcal{K}),-\operatorname{Cost}_{t}(\mathcal{K})\bigr), \mathfrak{P}_{t} is the nondominated set, \mathfrak{C}_{t} the candidate collections, and \operatorname{Cost}_{t} their average execution cost under cap B. Existing skill removal contribution, Eq. (14): \gamma_{t}(k)=G_{t}(\mathcal{K}_{t})-G_{t}(\mathcal{K}_{t}\setminus\{k\}). Here \mathcal{K}_{t} is the current collection; contribution is conditional on remaining skills and the evaluation distribution. Context token reduction, Eq. (17): \rho_{t}(x)=1-\frac{/c^{\prime}_{t}(x)/_{\mathrm{tok}}}{/c_{t}(x)/_{\mathrm{tok}}}. At state x, c_{t}(x) is the original nonempty context and c^{\prime}_{t}(x) its compressed version; /\cdot/_{\mathrm{tok}} denotes token length. Positive \rho_{t}(x) may coexist with negative task gain, so common-budget downstream performance must also be compared (1640-1651, 1668-1678). Conceptual parent search value, Eq. (20): \Psi_{t}(\mathcal{A};C)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\in\{\mathcal{A}\}\cup\operatorname{Desc}_{C}(\mathcal{A})}u(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\;\middle/\;\mathcal{Z}_{t}\right]. Current performance is u(\mathcal{A})=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}[s(\mathcal{A},q;B)]. \mathcal{Z}_{t} is the current archive, \operatorname{Desc}_{C}(\mathcal{A}) the random descendants of agent \mathcal{A} under a specified search protocol and evolution budget C, and \mathcal{A}^{\prime} a parent/descendant candidate. C pays for construction/assessment; B controls each execution. \Psi_{t} is an idealized value, distinguished from current performance and empirical estimation (1804-1825). Harness regression diagnostics, Eq. (23): F^{+}(\widetilde{h},h)=\frac{1}{/\mathcal{V}/}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{1}[y(h,q)=0,\ y(\widetilde{h},q)=1],\qquad F^{-}(\widetilde{h},h)=\frac{1}{/\mathcal{V}/}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{1}[y(h,q)=1,\ y(\widetilde{h},q)=0]. \mathcal{V} is a fixed nonempty validation set; y(h,q) the binary solve outcome of harness h on q; \widetilde{h} a candidate; \mathbf{1} the indicator. F^{+}, F^{-} are newly solved/failed fractions, whose difference is empirical success-rate change; stochastic outcomes require repeated evaluation (1995-2006). Workflow-stage contribution, Eq. (25): \Gamma(v\mid w)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[s(\mathcal{A}^{w},q;B)-s(\mathcal{A}^{w\setminus v},q;B)\right]. \mathcal{A}^{w} uses workflow w and w\setminus v validly bypasses stage v with other components fixed; \Gamma depends on the workflow/bypass design under matched evaluation (2087-2104). Test diagnostic, Eq. (28): d_{t}(v;q)=\frac{1}{/\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{-}(q)/}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{-}(q)}\mathbf{1}[\text{$v$ rejects $z$}]. For task q, \mathcal{Z}_{t}^{-}(q) is a nonempty set of independently known incorrect programs z and v a test checked against the specification. d_{t}(v;q) is rejection rate for those programs, not coverage of unknown failures (2246-2257). In discussing OPD-Evolver, the survey writes distillation loss Eq. (29): \mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{distill}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{j},u_{j})\sim\mathcal{P}_{t}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\bar{\theta}_{t}}(\cdot\mid x_{j},u_{j})\,\/\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{j})\right). At token position j, x_{j} is student information including its generated prefix, u_{j} additional hindsight information, and \mathcal{P}_{t} student rollouts with hindsight views. \pi_{\bar{\theta}_{t}}, \pi_{\theta} are teacher/student distributions; frozen teacher parameters \bar{\theta}_{t} receive no gradient; D_{\mathrm{KL}} denotes their divergence. Asset/architecture conditioning is implicit (2274-2294). For environment-reward RL, idealized policy objective Eq. (30): \max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{t},\,\tau\sim\operatorname{Execute}(\mathcal{A}_{\theta},q,\mathcal{E}_{q})}[R_{t}(q,\tau)]. \mathcal{A}_{\theta}=(\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t},\theta) holds assets/architecture fixed; q comes from training distribution \mathcal{Q}_{t}, \mathcal{E}_{q} is its environment, \tau the execution trace and R_{t}(q,\tau) the scalar feedback-derived training return. R_{t} and \mathcal{Q}_{t} need not equal evaluation s and \mathcal{D} (2295-2311). In discussing Agent-RLVR, preference loss Eq. (31): \mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{pref}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^{+},y^{-})\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{pref}}}\log\operatorname{sigmoid}\!\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{+}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{+}\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{-}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{-}\mid x)}\right]. In preference data \mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{pref}}, x is the common input, y^{+}, y^{-} preferred/dispreferred continuations; \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is a fixed reference policy, \beta>0 the preference scale, and \pi_{\theta} the learned policy (2313-2329). In describing Harness-R1 editor/target separation, Eq. (32): \widehat{\Delta}_{t}(e)=\frac{1}{/\mathcal{V}_{t}/}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}[s(\mathcal{A}_{t}^{e},q;B)-s(\mathcal{A}_{t},q;B)]. \mathcal{A}_{t}^{e} installs edit e in the target; \mathcal{V}_{t} is a nonempty matched task batch including previous successes. Editor objective Eq. (33): \max_{\omega}\;\mathbb{E}_{e\sim\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid b_{t})}[r_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}}(e)]. \omega denotes editor parameters, b_{t} failure evidence, \pi_{\omega} the edit policy, and r_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}}(e) equals the empirical utility change after valid complete evaluation, zero for invalid/incomplete candidates; expectation also covers training failure bundles (2373-2398). For a,b\in\{0,1\}, j_{ab} is expected score under \mathcal{D}, B with parameters \theta_{t+a} and harness h_{t+b}, compatible interfaces and other components fixed. Positive interaction alone does not imply total improvement, which requires j_{11}>j_{00} (2412-2424). Section 8.3 names pass rate, resolve rate, repair rate, benchmark score and Pass@ k as software-outcome metrics (3629-3631). Matched case change is d_{t}(c)=s(A_{t+1},c;\mathcal{B})-s(A_{t},c;\mathcal{B}). Here c is a case; this passage prints A for agent configuration and \mathcal{B} for the matched budget. For binary outcomes these are newly solved/lost rates; graded metrics also require change magnitudes. | 0 | framing_problem | How to enable an agent to continuously improve its performance after deployment (Runtime Continuous Learning), evolving with continued usage and adapting rapidly to new tasks, without compromising the stability of its pre-trained backbone, which is kept frozen to prevent catastrophic forgetting. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 154 of the saved text | 154 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Fine-tuning internalizes experience by changing weights but is computationally expensive and prone to catastrophic forgetting, while existing memory-based/RAG methods are passive: they retrieve by semantic similarity rather than utility and so often retrieve noise, preventing agents from using runtime feedback to distinguish high-value strategies. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 146 of the saved text | 146 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | MemRL optimizes memory retrieval without updating the frozen LLM: \mu^{*}(m/s,\mathcal{M})=\arg\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}Q(s,m). (Eq. 2). Here s is the User Intent represented by the current query embedding, m is a retrieved memory item, \mathcal{M} is the evolving memory bank, \mu is the retrieval policy, and Q(s,m) is the expected utility of the subsequent action a augmented by m. The agent policy is \pi(a_{t}/s_{t},\mathcal{M}_{t})=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}\mu(m/s_{t},\mathcal{M}_{t})p_{LLM}(a_{t}/s_{t},m). (Eq. 1), where t indexes interaction steps and p_{LLM} is the frozen LLM inference policy. Runtime utility updates use Q_{\text{new}}\leftarrow Q_{\text{old}}+\alpha\big(r-Q_{\text{old}}\big), (Eq. 4), where \alpha is the learning rate, r is environmental feedback, and Q_{\text{old}} and Q_{\text{new}} are utility estimates before and after the update. Appendix A.4 also maximizes the explicit variational objective \mathcal{J}(\mu,Q)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\underbrace{\sum_{m\in\mathcal{S}(s)}\mu(m/s)Q(s,m)}_{\text{Expected Utility }\approx\mathbb{E}[Q_{t}(m)]}-\frac{1}{\beta}\underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\Big(\mu(\cdot/s)\big\/\pi_{\text{sim}}(\cdot/s)\Big)}_{\text{Semantic Trust Region}}\right] (Eq. 20): \mathcal{D} is the state distribution, \mathcal{S}(s) is the semantic support for retrieval, \pi_{\text{sim}} is the fixed semantic prior derived from Phase-A, and D_{\text{KL}} is a KL-divergence regularizer weighted by 1/\beta (this appendix does not separately define \beta). Its value-evaluation step minimizes \min_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mu_{t+1}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(y-Q(s,m)\right)^{2}\right] (Eq. 23), where y=r is the observed reward target, \mu_{t+1} is the fixed updated retrieval policy, and the expectation uses samples \tau drawn under that policy (\tau is not separately defined there). Evaluation metrics are Success Rate (SR), the ratio of tasks completed in an epoch, and Cumulative Success Rate (CSR), the proportion solved at least once across epochs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 200 of the saved text | 200 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Decouple the stable reasoning of the frozen LLM from plastic episodic memory and treat retrieval as a value-based decision: memory is stored as Intent-Experience-Utility triplets; Two-Phase Retrieval recalls candidates by similarity, then selects context with a composite score of normalized similarity and learned Q-values; Utility-Driven Update refines Q-values from environmental feedback with Monte Carlo style updates, so learning happens in memory space without weight updates. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 157 of the saved text | 157 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Over 10 runtime-learning epochs, the paper reports that MemRL surpasses MemP by an average of +3.8% Cumulative Success Rate across BigCodeBench, OS, DB, ALFWorld and HLE (+6.2% on each of ALFWorld and OS, +3.6% on HLE). The benchmark backbones are GPT-4o for BigCodeBench, GPT-4o-mini for OS/DB, GPT-5-mini for ALFWorld, and Gemini-3-pro for HLE. With memory frozen after training, transfer to held-out sets improves average Success Rate over MemP by +2.8% across BigCodeBench, OS, DB and ALFWorld; HLE is runtime-only. Appendix E.3 specifies 7:3 splits with seed 42 for BigCodeBench and OS/DB, and 140 novel instances of seen ALFWorld task types (valid_seen) for transfer. Appendix F reports comparable token consumption to MemP on HLE: approximately 32K total tokens per question averaged across the 10-epoch learning trajectory; runtime per 2,500-question epoch is commensurate with MemP and additional algorithmic overhead is negligible relative to system variance. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 412 of the saved text | 412 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Black-box LLM agents, although often backed by state-of-the-art proprietary models, can only be controlled at test time because API-only access precludes parameter-level optimization, so most RL methods cannot be applied; the paper asks how to perform principled RL-style optimization of such agents. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 71 of the saved text | 71 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | PPO and GRPO assume white-box access to model parameters to compute policy gradients, which API-only models do not allow. Exact sampling from the optimal trajectory posterior is impossible for black-box agents whose full log-probabilities are generally unavailable, and is intractable even for white-box agents because of high-dimensional actions and long horizons. Precisely estimating the soft value function by repeated simulations to the terminal timestep can quickly become computationally prohibitive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The KL-regularized RL objective is \pi_{*}=\argmax_{\pi_{\theta}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(s_{0:T})}\!\left[r(s_{0:T})\right]\!-\!\beta\mathbb{KL}\left[\pi_{\theta}\,\/\,\pi\right], (Eq. 1), with equivalent posterior \pi_{*}(s_{0:T})\propto\pi(s_{0:T})e^{r(s_{0:T})/\beta}. (Eq. 2). Here \pi_{\theta} is the policy being trained (\theta denotes trainable parameters), \pi is the fixed pre-trained reference/prior policy, \pi_{*} is the optimal policy, \beta is a regularization coefficient, \mathbb{KL} is the KL-divergence penalty, s_{0:T} is a trajectory of states over horizon T, and r(s_{0:T})=\sum_{t=0}^{T}r(s_{t}) is cumulative environmental reward without discounting. AMC approximates this posterior using SMC rather than training the black-box policy. Its ideal value-regression objective is \small V{=}\argmin_{V_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{p(t,s_{t})}\!\left\lVert V_{\theta}(s_{t}){-}\log\mathbb{E}_{\pi(s_{t+1:T}\mid s_{t})}\!\!\left[e^{\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{\tau=t}^{T}{r}(s_{\tau})}\right]\!\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\\ (Eq. 5): V is the soft value function, V_{\theta} its learned approximation, p(t,s_{t}) any training-input distribution with full support over timesteps and states, and \tau indexes future rewards. In the experiments, V_{\theta}(s_{t})=f_{\theta}(s_{t})+r(s_{t}), (Eq. 6), where f_{\theta} is a transformer-based regressor predicting future reward and r(s_t) is observed at test time. The practical loss is \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta})\!=\!\frac{1}{P}\sum_{k=1}^{P}\!\left\lVert f_{\theta}(s_{t_{k}}^{(k)})-\sum_{\tau=t_{k}+1}^{T}r(s_{\tau}^{(k)})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\\ (Eq. 7), where P is the number of training state/timestep pairs, k indexes a pair selected from sampled prior trajectories, t_k is its timestep, and the superscript (k) identifies its sampled state/reward sequence. This single-trajectory target accepts bias through the logarithm; training fixes \beta=1 and adjusts sampling temperature afterward. Primary evaluation uses the highest-reward trajectory among N generated trajectories, scored by cumulative environmental reward and reported as means and standard errors over three independent seeded trials. Appendix D.5 also reports mean reward of the top 5 of 15 trajectories, averaged across tasks. Cost is reported in USD (Table 5, average input/output token counts; Table 11, separate training and inference costs). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Using the equivalence between KL-regularized RL and Bayesian inference, AMC treats the fixed LLM policy as the prior and approximates the optimal trajectory posterior with Sequential Monte Carlo: it runs N prior-policy trajectories in parallel, computes importance weights using a separately trained value function, and intermittently resamples with replacement to prune low-weight and proliferate high-weight trajectories. The underlying policy model remains unchanged; the value model is trained separately. Finite-N samples approximate the posterior, with convergence described as N tends to infinity. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 81 of the saved text | 81 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On SciWorld, Figure 3 reports that AMC with GPT-5.1 as policy and a Qwen-2.5-7B value model outperforms the Qwen-2.5-7B GRPO score from Xi et al. (2025b) with N=5 trajectories. When both policies and the AMC value model use Qwen-2.5-3B, AMC outperforms the cited GRPO result at 25 trajectories. In Figure 4, AMC generally reaches parity with Best-of-20 at N=15, described as approximately 25% less test-time compute; this scaling analysis uses Llama-3.2-11B policy/value models for WebShop and TextCraft and Llama-3.1-8B for SciWorld, with TextCraft evaluated at recipe depths 3 and 4. Table 5 compares GPT-4.1-mini AMC with GPT-5.1 Best-of-15: WebShop scores 0.488 versus 0.519 at $0.14 versus $0.39; SciWorld 0.673 versus 0.533 at $0.06 versus $0.18; TextCraft 0.852 versus 0.889 at $0.21 versus $0.45. The paper describes performance as similar with at least 50% lower total cost; these costs are calculated from average input and output token counts across tasks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 330 of the saved text | 330 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Most LLM agents are deployed as frozen models whose parameters stay fixed after pre-training, so the agent is stateless and cannot learn from its own deployment experience; prior approaches rely on human-designed agents rather than letting an agent design task-specific agents end-to-end. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 140 of the saved text | 140 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper argues that achieving practical utility typically requires parameter optimisation via backpropagation, demanding substantial data and computational resources; the cost and complexity of continual parameter updates lead most agents to be deployed frozen, relying on θ and the available context window for novel tasks. It also identifies two skill-specific obstacles: semantic routers capture semantic rather than behavioural similarity, and prior automatic skill-learning approaches produce text-only guides or overfit to single-task trajectories. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 105 of the saved text | 105 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The system is evaluated for its ability to create, refine and reuse skills across reasoning tasks. The SRDP memory-induced policy is Eq. (1): π^µ(a / s, M_t) = Σ_{c∈M_t} µ(c / s, M_t) p_LLM(a / s, c), where a is the action, s the current state, M_t the skill memory, c a retrieved case/skill, p_LLM the frozen LLM decision kernel and µ the retrieval policy. A cited Memento 2 theorem states that KL-regularised soft policy iteration over the Reflected MDP converges to µ* under /r/ ≤ R_max and γ < 1; r is reward, R_max its bound, and γ the SRDP/Reflected-MDP discount parameter. The skill router minimises multi-positive InfoNCE: L_i = −log(Σ_{q∈Q_i^+} exp(s(d_i,q)/τ) / Σ_{q∈Q} exp(s(d_i,q)/τ)), L = (1/B) Σ_{i=1}^B L_i, with Q = ⋃_{k=1}^B (Q_k^+ ∪ Q_k^−), and s(d,q) = e(d)^⊤u(q). B is the minibatch size in skills d_i; q is a routing goal; Q_i^+ and Q_i^− are the positive and hard-negative queries for skill d_i; e(d) = enc_θ(d) and u(q) = enc_θ(q) are embeddings from encoder enc_θ; τ is temperature. The one-step routing reward r(q,d) indicates whether d is the right skill, Q⋆(q,d) = E[r(q,d)], and the learned soft Q-function satisfies Q_θ(q,d) ∝ s(d,q). The routing objective is π*(·/q) = argmax_π {E_{d∼π}[Q_θ(q,d)] − τ KL(π ∥ π_0)}, where π is a distribution over skills for goal q and π_0 is a uniform prior. Router evaluation reports Recall@K (a hit means the ground-truth skill is in the top K) on 140 synthetic queries, route hit rate (an appropriate top-1 skill), and judge success rate (a trajectory that solves the task). End-to-end evaluation reports overall accuracy on held-out GAIA and HLE sets. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 480 of the saved text | 480 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Action-local runtime safeguards do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. PolicyGuard adds procedural remediation to a mutating-call safeguard but remains action-triggered, leaving earlier deviations outside its guarded action class uncovered; workflow-following systems primarily target workflow completion. Domain-specific fine-tuning of the large closed-weight models is often unavailable or impractical. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reliable policy-constrained task outcomes are measured by \text{Pass}^{k}=\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}, averaged across tasks: c is the number of successful trials for a task, n is its total trials (n{=}4 in main cells), and k is the number of trials whose joint success is assessed. Pass1 and Pass4 are reported overall and on PV (prevent a policy-violating mutation) and Mut (complete a permitted mutation under policy prerequisites) slices. Success uses final database state and natural-language assertions, not full temporal conformance. Additional metrics are CRAFT attack-success rate (ASR@ k and per-trial ASR; Airline, 20 attack tasks, GPT 5.4, n{=}4); author-designed Telecom Step-TCR (fraction of applicable checks satisfied) and Trace-TCR (fraction satisfying all checks), both conditional on outcome-passing traces; and process-valid rate (all task-run pairs passing both the Tau2 outcome and rubric, pooled across four runs). Call-NMR is the fraction of successfully executed mutations in passing Mut trajectories lacking at least one earlier read required by the frozen guard; blocked attempts, tool errors and unsuccessful responses are excluded, and Telecom uses an adapted agent-side oracle. Appendix C also reports \mathrm{P}^{4}/\mathrm{P}^{1} (Pass4 divided by Pass1) and pstd (population standard deviation across trial-level Pass1 values). Its paired significance statistic is Z=\frac{\sum_{d}a_{d}-\sum_{d}b_{d}}{\sqrt{\sum_{d}a_{d}+\sum_{d}b_{d}}}, where d indexes domain strata, a_{d} counts PolicyGuide-only Pass4 successes and b_{d} counts the reverse. Guide-side usage and cost, cached input, and mean end-to-end wall-clock time per task are reported separately. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 501 of the saved text | 501 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | PolicyGuide compiles each domain policy offline into a frozen workflow graph. At user-turn boundaries, an external verifier traverses from persisted request positions, reconciles open requests, and returns remediation for the first unmet step. The first unauthorized mutating call in each user-turn region is intercepted and triggers an extra verifier firing; the one-shot gate then permits an immediate retry, and other actions receive advisory remediation. The theorem concerns an ideal binding verifier covering every reachable first deviation; the evaluated advisory runtime does not provide that unconditional guarantee. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The same frozen workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents, with verifiers from the corresponding actor model family. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 97 of the saved text | 97 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The analysis uses \Delta_{\text{aggregate}}\approx p_{\text{fire}}\times\Delta_{\text{fire}}, where \Delta_{\text{aggregate}} is aggregate success lift, p_{\text{fire}} is the share of trials where a gate fires, and \Delta_{\text{fire}} is the conditional effect where firing occurs. It also measures silent wrong-state failures without tool errors and audits gate precision over pooled rejections: a true block rejects a write the ground-truth trajectory also avoids, while a false block rejects one it performs. Gates are pure functions with no LLM calls and no writes. ## f175 — InferCept: Efficient Intercept Support for Augmented Large Language Model Inference

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.01869v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Fri, 2 Feb 2024 19:47:57 UTC

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | LLMs are increasingly integrated with external tools, environments and agents, but today's LLM inference systems are designed for standalone LLMs: they treat each external interaction (an 'interception') as the end of generation and form a new request when it finishes. The paper asks how an LLM inference system should efficiently support interceptions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 55 of the saved text | 55 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Existing inference systems treat an interception as the end of a request, so for each interception the initial prompt and all tokens generated before it are formed as a new request, causing substantial recomputation of the KV cache for all previously processed tokens; this recomputation wastes GPU resources that could serve new requests (37-40% of total model forwarding time with the mixed six-augmentation workload, lines 55, 207). The alternatives have their own costs: Preserve avoids recomputation but occupies GPU memory during the entire interception; Swap avoids recomputation, but with limited GPU-CPU link bandwidth foreground forwarding could be bottlenecked waiting for swapping to finish (lines 75-76). Interception time varies drastically across augmentation types and requests, which complicates request scheduling, and context length and interception time also vary highly across requests (lines 69-70). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Minimize GPU memory waste caused by interceptions ('min-waste interception'; 'minimizing GPU memory waste as a unified objective', line 325). Per-interception waste equations: Eq.1 WasteDiscard_i^j = T_fwd(C_i^j)×C_i^j×M + T_fwd(C_i^j)×C_other×M; Eq.2 WastePreserve_i^j = T_INT^j×C_i×M; Eq.3 WasteSwap_i^j = 2×T_swap(C_i^j)×C_batch×M; Eq.4 WasteChunkD_i^j = T_fwd(C_i^j)×C_i^j×M/2 + n×T_fwd(C_i^j/n)×C_other×M; Eq.5 Waste_i^j = min(WastePreserve_i^j, WasteChunkD_i^j), used to rank intercepted requests. Symbols (from the text): i = request, j = interception; C_i^j = context tokens of request i when interception j occurs; C_i in Eq.2 = the request's context held in GPU memory (line 209); M = KV-cache memory per token; T_fwd = mapping from number of scheduled tokens in a batch to that iteration's execution time; C_other = sum of the contexts of other requests; T_INT^j = duration of interception j (for highly variable or not offline-profiled interceptions estimated as T̂_INT = t_now - t_call, line 282); T_swap = mapping from number of tokens to swap to swapping latency; C_batch appears in Eq.3 without a separate definition; n = number of iterations to finish recomputing the request. Swap limit per iteration: T_swap(N_i) = T_fwd(B_i), where N_i = number of tokens that can be swapped for free (hidden behind forwarding) at iteration i with batch size B_i (line 234); recomputation chunk size = S minus the running group size, S = GPU saturation point in query tokens (lines 247-248). Swap-in/out budgets are set by maximizing inference throughput (tokens added to an iteration) under three memory/bandwidth constraints (lines 238-241). Reported evaluation metrics: normalized latency vs request rate (intercepted time removed from end-to-end latency), completed requests per second, TTFT. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 80 of the saved text | 80 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | InferCept derives waste equations for Discard, Preserve and Swap; reduces the waste of Swap (layer-by-layer swap pipelining overlapped with model forwarding, and swap chunking across iterations so each iteration stays within a swap budget the GPU-CPU link can sustain) and of Discard (recomputation split into chunks small enough to fit the GPU processing capacity left unused by decoding); and sorts intercepted requests in descending order of potential memory waste (Eq. 5), swaps out context from them in that order until the swap-out budget (determined at every iteration, lines 236-241) runs out, and preserves or discards the remaining requests according to the Eq. 5 decision; for resumption, it assigns the swap-in budget to swapped-out requests with the earliest original arrival times and schedules discarded, preserved and non-intercepted waiting requests in FCFS order until the GPU's processing capacity (saturation point) is reached, FCFS ensuring fairness (lines 82-93, 268-278). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 89 of the saved text | 89 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Compared with state-of-the-art LLM inference systems, InferCept improves overall serving throughput by 1.6x-2x and completes 2x more requests per second (abstract, line 57); the introduction states this as 1.6x-2x higher serving load than vLLM while maintaining similar latency per token generation and over 2x more completed requests per second (line 95), evaluated on GPT-J-6B, Vicuna-13B and Llama3-70B on A100 GPUs with a mixed workload of six augmentations. The conclusion states 1.6x-2x higher request arrival rates and 1.3x-12x lower normalized latency compared to state-of-the-art inference systems (line 325); in the 6B technique breakdown at 2 requests/s the full InferCept has 0.69% GPU memory waste (line 322). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 57 of the saved text | 57 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = GPU memory waste / GPU resource wastage (GB*min), recomputation (share of total model forwarding time), serving throughput, serving load / request arrival rate (requests per second), completed requests per second, normalized latency (median end-to-end latency divided by output length), latency per token generation, time-to-first-token (TTFT), swap latency / GPU-CPU link bandwidth (swap budget), GPU processing capacity (GPU saturation point), interception time (tool / human response duration), iteration time (added by recomputation or swapping), GPU core utilization; agent kind = LLM inference (serving) system for 'augmented LLMs': LLMs whose generation is intercepted by external tools, non-LLM models, humans or environments (e.g. ChatGPT plugins, calculators, QA retrieval, ALFWorld virtual environment, chatbot, image generation, TTS); the introduction cites Ng's remark on 'AI agent workflows' (line 65) and views tool use and interaction with humans or environments generally as interceptions (line 66); position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f178 — SPORK: Self-Speculative Forking to Accelerate Agentic LLM Inference

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03333v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Fri, 3 Jul 2026 13:51:32 UTC

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | The agent's Thought-Action-Observation loop is often serial: the model reasons, emits a tool call, then idles the GPU until the result returns, and this tool wait consumes 16-37% of wall time in the authors' workloads (35-61% in prior reports); speculative tool execution can hide it, but existing systems need auxiliary predictors, historical traces or static workflow graphs, leaving a gap for training-free, day-one deployment. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Each tool result conditions all subsequent tokens, so the cycle enforces a strict serial dependency: the tool call cannot be dispatched until decoding completes and the next decode cannot begin until the result arrives; tool wait is bounded by network round-trips, container cold-starts and database I/O, and as model inference gets faster its share of wall time grows. Token-level speculative decoding and serving systems do not dispatch tools earlier, and agents generate tool calls online, so there is no static graph to prefetch. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 240 of the saved text | 240 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Latency ratio (EQ1): Ratio = T_base / (T*_base - α·t_overlap + T_oh); speculation helps when Ratio >= 1, approximately α·t_overlap >= T_oh, with ceiling Ratio = 1/(1 - f_tool) at α = 1, T_oh = 0 (1.58x on BrowseComp, f_tool = 0.366). Symbols (from the text): α = fraction of tool-call turns where speculation is accepted (gate rate, per turn); t_overlap = mean realized time overlap per accepted turn; T*_base = realized main-stream decode cost on the speculative path, equal to T_base unless prefix recovery lowers it; T_oh = per-turn overhead from probe computation and wasted speculative execution on rejected turns; T_base = T_dec + T_tool, the serial baseline per-turn cost (Appendix A), with T_dec main generation wall time and T_tool tool execution wall time; f_tool = T_tool/T_base. Exact form (Appendix A, lines 1199-1223): T_hit = T_base - t_overlap (accepted, p = α); T_miss = T*_base + T_oh (rejected, p = 1-α) with T*_base = T_base - T_D3; S = T_base / (T_base - α·t_overlap + (1-α)(T*_base - T_base + T_oh)); break-even α·t_overlap >= (1-α)(T*_base - T_base + T_oh), reducing without D3 to α·t_overlap >= (1-α)·T_oh; ceiling S_max = (T_dec + T_tool)/T_dec = 1/(1 - f_tool) when α = 1 and t_overlap = T_tool (perfect overlap of all tool time; line 1225). | 0 | framing_problem | Users can query a growing number of LLMs for a fee, the fees are heterogeneous and can differ by two orders of magnitude, and using LLMs on large collections of queries and text can be expensive; the paper asks how to use LLMs affordably and accurately. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 49 of the saved text | 49 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | LLM APIs differ in cost (prompt cost, generation cost and sometimes a fixed per-query cost) and in quality: the largest models are expensive for high-throughput use, cheaper models such as GPT-J can be much worse on difficult tasks, relying on one provider is unreliable, and existing ensemble or cascade methods were built for predictive tasks with a known label set; the strategy search space (prompts, APIs, aggregation) is vast. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 60 of the saved text | 60 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Budget-aware LLM API usage: maximize E_{(q,a)∈Q×A}[r(a, â(s,q))] subject to E_{(q,a)∈Q×A}[c(s,q)] ≤ b, where q is a query from the query distribution Q, a its correct answer, â(s,q) the answer generated by strategy s, c(s,q) the cost of processing q with s, b a user-defined bound on average cost, and r(·,·) a reward measuring how closely the generated answer matches the correct one. Per-API cost: c_i(p) ≜ c̃_{i,2}//f_i(p)// + c̃_{i,1}//p// + c̃_{i,0}, with f_i the i-th of K LLM APIs mapping a prompt p to an answer and c̃_{i,j} constants. For the cascade: max_{L,τ} E[r(a, f_{L_z}(q))] s.t. E[Σ_{i=1}^{z} c̃_{L_i,2}//f_{L_i}(q)// + c̃_{L_i,1}//q// + c̃_{L_i,0}] ≤ b, z = argmin_i g(q, f_{L_i}(q)) ≥ τ_i, where L ∈ [K]^m are the indexes of the m APIs selected by the router, τ the threshold vector, g(·,·): Q×A→[0,1] the generation scoring function giving a reliability score, and z the API at which the router stops and returns the answer. Empirical metrics: accuracy on each dataset and cost in USD (Table 3: 'Cost to reach the same accuracy' of the best individual LLM and its cost savings in %; Figure 5 accuracy-cost trade-off curves). A diagnostic metric, maximum performance improvement (MPI) of LLM A with respect to LLM B, is defined as the probability that A answers correctly while B answers incorrectly (line 219). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 94 of the saved text | 94 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because different LLM APIs have different strengths and even an inexpensive LLM can sometimes correctly answer queries on which a more expensive LLM fails (line 219), an LLM cascade sends each query to a list of LLM APIs sequentially, returns an API's answer as soon as its reliability score from a generation scoring function (e.g. a trained regression model) is higher than that API's threshold, and queries the remaining APIs only if the previous APIs' generations are deemed insufficiently reliable; query cost is reduced when the first APIs are relatively inexpensive and produce reliable generations (line 106). The API list and thresholds are learned as a budget-constrained optimization problem by a specialized optimizer that prunes lists with small answer disagreement and interpolates the objective from a few samples (line 114). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 106 of the saved text | 106 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the best individual LLM API, FrugalGPT matches its performance with up to 98% cost reduction (HEADLINES: 33.1 vs 0.6 to reach GPT-4's accuracy, 98.3%; OVERRULING 73.3%; COQA 59.2% against GPT-3) or improves accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% at the same cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 49 of the saved text | 49 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = cost, inference cost, fee, prompt cost, generation cost, fixed cost per query, budget, cost savings, query costs, computational costs for training, high-throughput, latency improvements (byproduct of fine-tuning; future factor), financial and environmental savings, energy, one-time upfront cost (learning the cascade), cost to reach the same accuracy; agent kind = Not an agent paper: a framework for using fee-charging commercial LLM APIs (the 'LLM marketplace') to answer natural language queries within a budget; the implemented instance is an LLM cascade over APIs such as GPT-J, J1-L, GPT-3, ChatGPT and GPT-4.; position = model inference/serving (choice of which LLM API answers each query; single-turn query answering, not an agent loop). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Tool calls and environment interactions leave the agent idle while waiting for observations; existing works treat this idle time as unavoidable overhead or use restricted solutions that utilize it poorly, so the paper asks how to exploit idle time from agentic interactions robustly and generally to improve agent performance on complex tasks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 105 of the saved text | 105 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Observation uncertainty: during idle periods the observation is not yet available, so plans generated then may become invalid or suboptimal when it arrives; in addition, the reasoning budget available during idle time varies strongly across tool calls, and the prior idle-time method (Sleep-time Compute) ignores this variation (the introduction says it uses only 13.7% of total idle time on GAIA, line 103; Appendix B.1 gives 13.2%, line 832) and assumes predictable future queries. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 114 of the saved text | 114 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | None stated as a formula for the task objective. The stated aim is to improve agent performance while minimizing latency overhead; the reported targets are accuracy (%) on GAIA (Levels 1-3) and FRAMES, and submission, valid-submission, above-median and medal rates (Bronze/Silver/Gold, Any Medal total) on MLE-Bench Lite within a 24-hour wall-clock budget per task. Efficiency metrics: end-to-end latency (Figure 3), per-task wall-clock latency in seconds (Appendix Table 8), idle-time and test-time output tokens (Table 3), and idle-time utilization, Eq. (5): ITU_task = Σ_{k=1}^{K} t^{(k)}_{LLM-on-idle} / Σ_{k=1}^{K} t^{(k)}_{idle} ∈ [0,1], where t^{(k)}_{idle} is the tool execution duration of step k and t^{(k)}_{LLM-on-idle} ≤ t^{(k)}_{idle} the part of it spent on LLM computation, averaged over tasks (and seeds). The method's own equations define the candidate set D_final = D_prog ∪ D_rec (Eq. 1), p = Pr(ℓ = Prog) with p ~ Beta(α,β) (Eqs. 2-3), where ℓ ∈ {Prog, Rec} is the forecast signal and α, β count past Prog and Rec signals (initialized to 1), the posterior update (α,β) ← (α+1,β) if ℓ = Prog, (α,β+1) if ℓ = Rec (Eq. 4), and the sampling rule: draw p̂ ~ Beta(α,β), choose Prog if p̂ > 0.5, else Rec. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | While a tool executes, the agent iteratively drafts plan candidates until the observation arrives, sampling between complementary progressive drafts (assuming a favorable observation) and recovery drafts (assuming no progress) so as to cover plausible future observations; the drafts are then aggregated as non-binding guidance for the next reasoning step, and the strategy distribution is updated from a forecast signal by Thompson sampling. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against a vanilla baseline that does no computation during idle time, IdleSpec raises average accuracy over GAIA Levels 1-3 and FRAMES to 55.6% with Gemini-2.5-Flash (+5.1 from 50.5; +4.6 on Gemma4-E4B, 30.9 to 35.5; +6.8 on Qwen3.5-4B, 33.2 to 40.0) and the MLE-Bench Lite medal rate by 9.1 points (36.4% to 45.5%, Gemini-2.5-Flash, single seed). On latency, the efficiency analysis (Figure 3, vLLM on an NVIDIA A6000) says IdleSpec keeps latency close to vanilla while Sequential Revision and Planning are about 1.30x and 1.33x slower; Appendix Table 8 (full GAIA, Gemini-2.5-Flash, single fixed seed) gives per-task wall-clock latency of 107 vs 99 s (Level 1), 191 vs 196 s (Level 2) and 374 vs 376 s (Level 3) for vanilla vs IdleSpec. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 91 of the saved text | 91 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f183 — Agent-X: Full Pipeline Acceleration of On-device AI Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.10380v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Mon, 11 May 2026 11:23:38 UTC

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents incur high end-to-end latency on edge devices; on-device AI agents still suffer from suboptimal latency even for simple tasks (one TinyAgent task takes 35.4 s on average on a Mac mini M4 Pro), and the paper sets out to systematically characterize and eliminate these latency bottlenecks without accuracy loss. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 61 of the saved text | 61 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Unlike server-based, conversation-oriented LLM workloads whose latency is dominated by decode, on-device agents spend significant time in both prefill and decode: agents process much longer inputs than they generate, and on-device accelerators offer limited compute throughput and memory bandwidth, rendering prefill disproportionately expensive; dynamically retrieved tool descriptions and guidelines inserted early in the Planner prompt limit KV cache reuse by prefix caching; decode output is highly correlated with the provided examples and user prompt (96% of Planner and 87% of Arbiter output tokens overlap with their input prompt), so a large portion of decode time is spent generating straightforward, formulaic sequences that do not require the LLM's reasoning capabilities; and speculative decoding is hindered on-device by draft-LLM latency and the 'multi-token tax' of multi-token verification. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 76 of the saved text | 76 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No overall closed-form objective. The stated objective of PromptWeaver and ExSpec is to speed up their target stages (prefill and decode) without compromising task accuracy or introducing substantial overhead in the resource-constrained on-device environment. Reported targets: end-to-end task latency and speedup, and Planner accuracy (the output plan is turned into a DAG of function calls with dependency edges and compared against the ground-truth DAG; the paper says it translates directly to end-to-end task accuracy). Explicit selection metric in Algorithm 1: under a KV cache budget of N clusters, greedily add the cluster prefix p^ = argmax_{p in options}[coverage(D, C U {p}) - coverage(D, C)], where coverage(D, C) is the sum, over the activated cluster sequences of the Planner training dataset D, of the number of leading clusters whose KV cache is in C (longest cached prefix). Draft token accuracy = fraction of draft tokens ultimately accepted during verification. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 219 of the saved text | 219 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | PromptWeaver reconstructs the input prompt so that most of it forms a cacheable static prefix - all-inclusive static tool descriptions and guidelines, then tool-use examples clustered by tool co-activation in a fixed theme-based order whose KV caches are precomputed offline and stored on SSD, then a few uncacheable dynamic examples - to accelerate prefill; ExSpec uses an n-gram lookup table built on the fly from the few-shot examples and the user query as an LLM-free draft model for speculative decoding, which incurs no draft-token generation overhead, and falls back to standard autoregressive decoding when the table has no entry for the current context, so the multi-token tax is avoided when no speedup is expected. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Average end-to-end task latency improves 1.61x over the baseline TinyAgent pipeline (TinyAgent-7B backend on a Mac mini M4 Pro; the text labels it only 'baseline'), with the prefill and decode stages sped up 1.97x and 1.73x; PromptWeaver alone gives 1.16x and ExSpec alone 1.43x end-to-end; the paper reports no accuracy loss. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | There is a critical gap in understanding how LRMs perform in agentic environments, where models must choose between engaging directly with the environment and relying on internal reasoning about hypothetical actions (the Reasoning-Action Dilemma); the paper introduces and analyzes 'overthinking', the tendency to favor extended internal reasoning chains over environmental interaction, and its effect on task performance. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Balancing reasoning and action is inherently challenging in agentic environments: direct interaction with the environment is time- and space-consuming (in-context memory is limited), while prior research has shown that LRMs are vulnerable to knowledge insufficiency, where gaps in understanding can cascade into compounding errors, so excessive simulation without sufficient external information can ultimately lead to failure, especially where interaction opportunities are limited; the tension is exacerbated by prompt sensitivity, as reasoning steps accumulating in context can overshadow or distort the interpretation of real-world information, and the authors observe that reasoning models consistently resolve this tension by favoring internal simulation over environmental signals (overthinking, whose manifestations are Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions and Premature Disengagement). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 133 of the saved text | 133 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Target performance metric is issue resolution rate on SWE-bench Verified. Overthinking is measured by an Overthinking Score from 0 to 10 assigned by an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 3.5, temperature 0, without access to the resolution outcome; higher = more severe; 0-3 appropriate environment interaction, 4-7 occasional overreliance on internal reasoning, 8-10 complete detachment from environmental feedback). The overthinking-performance relation is fitted per model class by simple linear regression Y^ = beta0 + beta1*X (Appendix C.1: beta1 = -7.894 for reasoning, -15.938 for non-reasoning models; Table 1 R^2 0.892 / 0.839), where a lower beta1 means a larger impact of overthinking on performance. For mitigation: Pass@k = percentage of tasks where at least one successful solution is found among k sampled trajectories; Lowest Overthinking@k = select the trajectory with the lowest overthinking score among k samples and report the percentage of selected trajectories that succeed (Pass@k is its upper bound); confidence intervals by Wilson score. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 241 of the saved text | 241 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Five named challenges for tree-search WebAgents: (i) low-quality action generation (invalid actions that reduce search efficiency and waste computation), (ii) redundant candidate actions, (iii) fragile state reversibility in non-deterministic web environments, (iv) destructive actions that permanently alter the environment and invalidate visited states, and (v) computational overhead of exhaustive search such as MCTS rollouts and costly environment resets. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 100 of the saved text | 100 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Candidate actions are scored before execution by a process reward model v_t = f_v(I, {(o_1,a_1),...,(o_t,a_t)}) in [0,1] that predicts the expected utility of executing a_t (appendix A.2.5); following WebShepherd it is a checklist-based process reward r_k(o,a)=(1/L)Σ_l [P(“Yes”/I,C,o,a,F)+0.5×P(“In Progress”/I,C,o,a,F)] (L = number of checklist items, I = instruction, C = checklist, o = observation, a = candidate action, F = generated feedback), with final reward written r(o,a)=Σ_{k=1}^{K} r_k(o,a) (appendix B.4). - Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2504.13359v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Thu, 17 Apr 2025 21:58:29 UTC

| 0 | framing_problem | The widespread adoption of AI systems in the economy hinges on their generating economic value that outweighs their inference costs (the introduction adds: and on those inference costs being lower than the cost of equivalent human labor); evaluating this trade-off requires metrics that account for both performance and costs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 76 of the saved text | 76 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Standard metrics capture accuracy or other system capabilities but fail to account for cost, and value and cost have been interpreted and reported separately; prior attempts to include cost rely on fixed inference budgets, heuristic performance scores or non-monetary proxies such as conciseness, which tie conclusions to specific constraints or heuristics and limit generality and economic interpretability. LMs act as stochastic producers, and more powerful models, scaffolds or test-time techniques that seek a higher probability of success typically do so at higher computational (and monetary) cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Cost-of-pass v(m,p) = C_m(p) / R_m(p) (Eq. 2): R_m(p) is the probability that model m produces a correct answer on problem p; C_m(p) is the expected cost of one inference attempt by m on p (token counts times per-token prices plus extra charges, instantiating w^T x); 1/R_m(p) is the expected number of attempts to the first correct solution assuming independent trials; R_m(p)=0 gives infinite cost-of-pass. Frontier cost-of-pass V_p(M) = min_{m in M} v(m,p) (Eq. 3) and V_p(M ∪ M_0) = min(V_p(M), v(expert,p)) with v(expert,p) ≈ C_expert(p) (Eqs. 4-5); V_p(M_t) over strategies released up to time t (Eq. 6); gain G_p({m_t}, M_{t-1}) = V_p(M_{t-1}) - V_p(M_{t-1} ∪ {m_t}) (Eq. 7); distribution-level versions are averages over problems p ~ P (Eqs. 8-9). Derived analysis metrics: exponential fit V_p(M_t) ≈ a e^{-bt} + c with halving time of the exponential component T_1/2 = ln(2)/b (Eq. 10); counterfactual essentialness of a model family g = G_{p~D}(M_g, M_T \ M_g) / V_{p~D}(M_T \ M_g) (Eq. 11); relative gain of an inference-time technique = G_{p~D}(M_L*, M_L) / V_{p~D}(M_L) over the lightweight+large model set M_L (Eq. 12). The introduction states the motivating economic goal as minimizing cost per successful output under uncertainty. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 114 of the saved text | 114 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Adapt Farrell's production-frontier theory (and stochastic frontiers of Aigner et al.) to LMs: treat each LM inference pipeline as a stochastic producer whose unit of output is a correct solution, measure the expected monetary cost per correct output, take the minimum across available models plus an estimated human-expert baseline, and track that frontier over model releases and counterfactual removals of model families. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | As an evaluation framework, the headline findings are: frontier cost-of-pass decreased exponentially from May 2024 to February 2025; from a fitted exponential decay (Eq. 10), the exponential component for MATH-500 halved approximately every 2.6 months and for AIME-2024 every 7.1 months. On inference-time techniques applied to lightweight and large models (relative gain over their frontier, Eq. 12, Table 2), majority voting (k=3, 4) gave 0% on every dataset, self-refinement gave 24.9% on GPQA-Diamond and 6.7% on BBQ and 0% elsewhere, and budget-aware TALE-EP gave reductions on more tasks but unevenly; the abstract summarizes that performance-oriented methods with marginal gains rarely justify the costs and that model-level innovations are the primary drivers of cost-efficiency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 285 of the saved text | 285 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Thought generation consumes the majority of inference compute per step, and in reasoning models thinking may continue well beyond the point where the intended action has converged (prior work shows the committed action is encoded in hidden representations well before the trace ends), implying many post-convergence tokens are waste; excessive thinking may also make the edge model increasingly overconfident in a suboptimal action, which complicates cloud-deferral mechanisms that rely on the edge model's internal uncertainty, while early truncation may raise uncertainty above the model's actual confidence and unduly increase deferral. Even a well-reasoned edge action can be wrong and errors compound over the episode. Related work (Section 2) states that thought calibration, early-exit methods and conformal-prediction wrappers do not jointly calibrate a stopping rule with a deferral mechanism under formal statistical guarantees, that model cascades route single-turn queries without multi-step dependencies, and that ReDAct applies PPL-guided deferral inside an agentic loop but chooses its deferral threshold heuristically. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 130 of the saved text | 130 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Eq. (4): min_λ C_L(λ) subject to R(λ) ≥ R^min and C_D(λ) ≤ C_D^max, where λ = (λ_L, λ_D) are the thinking-convergence and deferral thresholds; R(λ) = E[r(λ)] is the expected episode reward (r in [0,1] issued at episode end); C_D(λ) = E[(1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T D_t] is the deferral rate (D_t = 1 if the cloud model is called at step t); C_L(λ) = E[Σ_{t=1}^T L_t] is the thinking cost, L_t being the number of reasoning steps (tokens) before the action at step t, capped at L_max; T is the random number of agent steps. | 3 | framing_solution | A lightweight convergence probe on the edge model's hidden states halts on-device reasoning once the intended action has stabilized, a perplexity-based deferral rule escalates uncertain actions to the cloud model, and the two thresholds are jointly calibrated on end-to-end episode trajectories with multi-objective Learn-Then-Test, giving finite-sample guarantees on expected episode reward and cloud-call rate. The introduction's rationale is that thinking and deferral are intertwined (excessive reasoning can produce overconfident uncertainty signals), so joint calibration has the potential to reduce edge tokens while making cloud deferral more efficient; the conclusion adds, as an insight from the results, that truncated reasoning leads to detecting uncertainty signals at their most meaningful state. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 130 of the saved text | 130 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
