## f189 — Concurrency without Model Changes: Future-based Asynchronous Function Calling for LLMs

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.15077v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Thu, 14 May 2026 17:02:28 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Function calling in LLM agents is typically constrained by synchronous execution semantics: decoding is blocked until each function call completes, which increases end-to-end latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Under the standard synchronous function-calling protocol each call must be immediately followed by its result, and model decoding blocks after each emitted call until the function finishes; this serialization limits concurrency and increases end-to-end latency. Prior approaches that expose in-progress executions to continued generation or shift concurrency management onto the model often alter the function-calling protocol or require model changes. Relaxing strict decode-order execution to gain parallelism introduces correctness risk, since naive parallelization may execute dependent calls prematurely. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 58 of the saved text | 58 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reported target is end-to-end task latency, as speedup of each AsyncFC variant over its corresponding synchronous baseline under the same function-calling API (one-sided paired t-test on per-task log speedups, alternative that the geometric-mean speedup exceeds 1), with accuracy preserved (McNemar test on paired task outcomes). The design-intuition section writes the theoretical maximum speedup ratio R = (T_LLM + T_tool) / max(T_LLM, T_cp) (Eq. 1), where T_tool is the total function execution time summed across all nodes of the task-specific function dependency DAG, T_cp is the sum of function execution times along the critical path, and T_LLM is total decoding time; ideal asynchronous latency is max(T_LLM, T_cp), and large speedups require T_tool >> T_cp and ideally T_LLM ≈ T_cp. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 148 of the saved text | 148 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Offload concurrency management from the model to the runtime: automatically transform function schemas to accept and return symbolic futures and add an await_future function; after each decoded call, dispatch the unmodified synchronous function to a background executor and immediately return a future placeholder so decoding continues; integrate resolved results at turn boundaries; and gate execution with a dependency-aware scheduler that serializes all calls in decode order by default (still overlapping decoding with execution) and runs calls in parallel only when optional developer resource annotations show them to be dependency-safe - all without fine-tuning or changes to the standard function-calling protocol. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f190 — Asynchronous LLM Function Calling

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.07017v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Mon, 9 Dec 2024 21:53:10 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Current LLM function calling is inherently synchronous: each call blocks LLM inference, limiting LLM operation and concurrent function execution, so it is neither resource-efficient nor responsive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Each function call blocks LLM inference, one of the most resource-intensive processes, until the function returns, and the executor must finish calls in the order the LLM initiated them; these inefficiencies grow with the number of functions, and prior optimizations (compiled parallel calls, call fusion, concise syntax, serving optimizations) remain limited by the synchronous LLM-waits-for-executor pattern. Making calls asynchronous raises two further challenges: timing interrupt tokens so they do not disrupt ongoing generation, and getting the LLM to handle interrupts that do not follow its training conversations. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 76 of the saved text | 76 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Fine-tuning trains the LLM to minimize total task completion time (the makespan) while respecting task dependencies and estimated function execution times. Section 6.3 (proofs in Appendix A) models n independent functions F with token generation latency G(f) and execution time E(f) (averages Ḡ, Ē): L_Sync(F) = Σ_f G(f) + Σ_f E(f) = n(Ḡ + Ē); L_Sync-Parallel(F) = Σ_f G(f) + max_f E(f); L_Async(F) = max_f (E(f) + Σ_{g in pred(f,F)} G(g)) with pred(f,F) = {g in F / E(f) ≤ E(g)} under the Longest-Processing-Time-first order. Theorem 6.1: L_Async ≤ L_Sync-Parallel < L_Sync; Theorem 6.2: L_Sync/L_Async ≈ 1 + Ē/Ḡ (error O((Ē/Ḡ)^2), assuming normally distributed E and large /F/); Theorem 6.3: no deviation from LPT order lowers total latency. Evaluation measures end-to-end task completion latency as the time between the first and last token generation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 125 of the saved text | 125 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Make LLM decoding interruptible: function calls are non-blocking, and when one returns the executor injects interrupt tokens into the token stream; a token-efficient DSL (CML) marks call boundaries so interrupts are deferred safely, fine-tuning teaches the LLM to issue asynchronous calls, handle interrupts and signal when it must wait, and calls are prioritized longest-processing-time first to maximize overlap of generation and execution. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | The abstract claims AsyncLM reduces end-to-end task completion latency by 1.6x-5.4x compared with synchronous function calling on BFCL tasks: Section 6.1 reports 1.6x (local Llama) and 2.1x (cloud GPT-4o, emulated at 5 ms per output token) over sequential Sync on parallel tasks, and Section 6.2 up to 5.4x over Sync on the multi-step parallel dataset (Sync-Parallel: 3.2x). The introduction additionally claims up to 2.1x over synchronous parallel function calling, but Section 6.1 reports 2.1x relative to sequential Sync, not Sync-Parallel. Accuracy (Section 6.5, multi-step parallel dataset): the text states that GPT-4o with few-shot prompting and fine-tuned Llama models maintain similar AST-matching accuracy across Sync and Async, while few-shot-prompted Llama models drop significantly; Table 1 gives GPT-4o (ICL) 57.84% Sync vs 59.61% Async, Llama-3B (FT) 57.33% Sync / 66.07% Sync-in-CML vs 65.97% Async, Llama-1B (FT) 6.33% / 12.15% vs 12.06%, GPT-4o-mini (ICL) 55.08% vs 41.44%, Llama-3B (ICL) 16.98% vs 5.46%, and Llama-1B (ICL) 0.49% vs 1.45%. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents face critical deployment challenges due to prohibitive latency and inference costs; existing acceleration methods either fail to preserve performance fidelity, require extensive offline training of router modules, or incur excessive operational costs, and give minimal user control over the trade-off between acceleration and other metrics. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Speculative planning parallelises the inherently autoregressive planning pipeline, but its commonly adopted fixed speculation step k is fundamentally limited: on complex tasks aggressive speculation produces excessive and redundant agent calls (wasted prompt and generation tokens of A, and completed or cancelled T steps after a mismatch), while on simple tasks conservative speculation gives insufficient acceleration; the optimal k is context-dependent, varies even within one task, and is unknown a priori. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 74 of the saved text | 74 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The paper states DSP 'explicitly optimizes a joint objective balancing end-to-end latency against dollar cost', steered by a single user parameter, but writes no single latency-plus-cost formula. The learned component is a state-value predictor of the speculative step: minimise the TD loss L_θ = E_{τ∼π}[(G_t^λ − V_θ(s_t))^2] (Eq. 1), where s_t is the state (a token sequence), V_θ a neural (DistilBERT) approximation of V_π(s) = E_π[G_t / s_t = s], the 'expected speculative step of state s', and G_t^λ the λ-return (Eq. 2) interpolating n-step returns G_{t:t+n} (λ ∈ [0,1], γ = 1). The trade-off is exposed by replacing MSE with the expectile loss L_2^τ(u) = /τ − 1(u<0)/ u^2 (τ > 0.5 over-estimates k: faster, costlier; τ < 0.5 cheaper, slower) or by an offset k = max(1, k̂ + β) with user bias β. Reported metrics: ΔTime = (1/N) Σ_i (1 − T_i^SP / T_i^seq) × 100% (N tasks; total task time under speculative vs sequential planning) and ΔCost = (1/N) Σ_i ((PC_i^SP + GC_i^SP)/(PC_i^seq + GC_i^seq) − 1) × 100% (PC, GC = prompt and generation dollar costs, token counts of approximation and target times their per-token API prices), ΔP and ΔG (Eqs. 3-4) are the analogous relative increases in prompt and generation tokens, where the 'seq' baseline is the sum of target and approximation tokens each run sequentially (line 186), plus ratios T(×), P(×), G(×), Cost(×) against fixed k = 2, average peak concurrency MC̄ = (1/N) Σ_i MC_i (Eq. 10) and average speculative step K̄ = (1/M) Σ_i k_i over M planning episodes (Eq. 11). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A lightweight DistilBERT regressor, trained by asynchronous online reinforcement learning (TD learning on (partial trajectory, k) pairs logged while the system runs, with no offline dataset or pre-deployment phase), predicts per state how many steps A will get right before T must intervene, so speculation is suspended before it wastes calls; T still verifies every step, keeping the output lossless, and biased prediction or a biased offset lets practitioners move along the latency-cost continuum. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On two standard agent benchmarks (OpenAGI, TravelPlanner), DSP 'achieves comparable efficiency to the fastest lossless acceleration method while reducing total cost by 30% and unnecessary cost up to 60%' (abstract); the introduction words it as reducing total cost 'by up to 30%', cutting unnecessary cost by 60% and 'preserving comparable acceleration' (line 78). The reference for both figures is the fastest fixed-k speculative-planning configuration (Fix k = 6), not fixed-k planning in general: e.g. Dyn. (offset = 2) gives time reduction comparable to Fix k = 6 with 60.65% less redundant cost (OpenAGI Setting 1, line 1154), and the high-performance mode (tau = 0.99/0.95) gives over 90% of the fastest setting's time savings while saving 30% total cost (line 1167). Against the cheaper Fix k = 2/4 the cost savings are smaller (e.g. 12% and 23.4%, lines 702-703). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = end-to-end latency, inference costs, dollar cost, total cost, unnecessary cost, operational costs, token consumption, prompt tokens, generation tokens, redundant agent calls, Time Decrease (ΔT), Total Cost Increase (ΔCost), Absolute Time Ratio T(×), Absolute Cost Ratio Cost(×), Average Max Concurrent API Calls (MC), Average Speculative Step (K), Prompt Token Increase (ΔP), Generation Token Increase (ΔG), extra cost brought by parallelizing computations, pre-deployment preparation overhead (router training, prompt engineering), API throttling / concurrency limits; agent kind = LLM-based agents doing multi-step agent planning (evaluated on OpenAGI and TravelPlanner); the method (DSP) is a speculative-planning acceleration framework in which a cheaper approximation agent A drafts steps and the original target agent T verifies them in parallel; position = agent loop (steps, calls, context). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | SE agents powered by LLMs are increasingly adopted in practice but often incur substantial monetary cost; cost efficiency remains a key concern for practical adoption (in a Stack Overflow survey, 53% of software engineers reported agent cost as a barrier), and the monetary cost is also associated with environmental impact through energy consumption. The paper aims to reduce the cost of SE agents while preserving task performance (resolution rate). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper says this cost inefficiency arises largely because SE agents resolve issues through multi-round iterations (e.g. repeated tool invocations) in which the entire conversation history is fed back as context each time, causing computational costs to grow super-linearly ('token snowball'); when stuck on difficult or unsolvable issues, agents often continue consuming iterations that provide little additional benefit (line 84). Existing SE agents typically terminate patch generation and selection only when the backend LLM explicitly signals completion or a predefined iteration budget is exhausted, and the number of generated patches is often fixed by a maximum iteration limit; this coarse-grained control often leads to redundant computation by over-solving simple issues or persisting on difficult ones (lines 114, 122). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation formula. The paper evaluates 'both task performance and cost efficiency': performance = % Resolved (percentage of tasks for which the agent produces a patch that passes all tests); cost efficiency = # API Calls (total LLM API invocations across the benchmark), # Input/Output Tokens (total tokens consumed across the benchmark) and Total Cost (total monetary cost across the benchmark in U.S. dollars). Decision rules: patch generation stops early when the LLM's confidence score after a milestone (code modification or test execution) exceeds τ^gen; patch selection stops generating further patches when the confidence score exceeds τ^sel_upper (patch sufficiently reliable) or falls below τ^sel_lower (issue unlikely to be resolved); only the top-1 retrieved experience with TF-IDF similarity above τ_sim is used. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 271 of the saved text | 271 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Much like an experienced developer, an agent informed by relevant prior experience can navigate directly to a solution, bypassing costly trial-and-error iterations (line 86). EET abstracts successful, validated past issue-resolution runs into structured experience objects (issue abstraction, key-step execution summary, confidence and confidence reason), retrieves for a new issue the top-1 experience whose TF-IDF similarity exceeds a threshold, conditions patch generation on it, and uses it for LLM confidence-based early-termination checks after milestones in patch generation and after each patch in patch selection (lines 100-124). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On SWE-bench Verified, across three SE agents (Agentless, Mini-SWE-Agent, Trae Agent) and two LLM backends (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2), compared with the same agents without EET, total cost falls by 19.3%-55.1% (31.8% on average) with at most 0.2 percentage points loss in resolution rate (Trae Agent with DeepSeek-V3.2; % Resolved changes are absolute differences, Table 1), via early termination on 8.6%-14.0% of issues (11.3% on average) and average reductions of 20.8% in API calls, 29.9% in input tokens and 25.1% in output tokens. Total cost is the per-benchmark inference cost; the one-time, offline experience-generation cost is excluded from it and reported separately (Appendix J, line 1054). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper attributes the loss of time efficiency to three main reasons: (1) the backbone LLM can be inefficient because of its increasingly large size and high request volume, (2) complex agent structures such as tree-of-thought and ReAct generate prolonged thought before the final answer, extending waiting time and token generation costs, and (3) action steps in a plan are sequential, one must finish before the next can begin; yet not all planning steps need computationally intensive thought, so applying complex agents or advanced backbones to every step is inefficient. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 81 of the saved text | 81 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | GUI agents face an inefficiency challenge: processing long sequences of high-resolution screenshots and solving long-horizon tasks makes inference slow, costly and memory-bound; storing the full KV cache is prohibitive for image-heavy contexts, and existing cache-compression methods are sub-optimal for GUIs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Caching all KV states can require extensive GPU memory (UI-TARS-1.5-7B can consume over 80GB GPU memory on a single inference with 5 screenshots and a maximum of 50 steps, which can easily trigger out-of-memory errors on most consumer GPUs), while token-merging or higher-layer pruning alternatives require re-training GUI agents (line 58). The abstract says existing cache-compression methods are sub-optimal because they do not account for the spatial and temporal redundancy of GUIs (line 54); the introduction describes spatial redundancy (large uniform backgrounds, repeated UI elements, static components) and temporal redundancy (consecutive screenshots often share significant visual overlap) and says approaches developed primarily for natural images and documents 'may not be optimal' for GUIs (line 59). In addition, measured on ScreenSpotV2 trajectories with UI-TARS-1.5-7B, GUI attention sparsity averages above 0.99 across all layers (lowest around 0.98, versus natural images averaging 0.92 with minimums around 0.88), so per-layer budget schedules that normalize sparsity (e.g. PyramidKV, VL-Cache) over-amplify tiny differences and misallocate cache (lines 60, 67, 96-97). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single objective; KV cache selection under a budget γ ∈ (0,1] (fraction of KV states kept, applied uniformly across layers and heads): keep C^h = {i ∈ C : /{j ∈ C : ψ̂_i^h > ψ̂_j^h}/ < ⌈n·γ⌉} (Eq. 10 as printed; the text 'select the top-scoring tokens' (line 145) and Algorithm 1 (line 979) keep the top-⌈n·γ⌉ tokens by ψ̂^h, whereas the printed inequality literally counts lower-scored tokens), where C = {1,...,n} indexes the n input prompt tokens and ψ̂_i^h (Eq. 9) = A_i^h + αS_i for current-frame visual tokens, (A_i^h + αS_i)·1[ρ_i^h ≥ ρ̃^h] for previous-frame visual tokens, and A_i^h for text tokens; A_i^h is the attention a token receives from the last ω observation tokens in head h, S_i the softmax of standardized L2 norms of residual-stream hidden states (temperature τ, Eq. 4), α > 0 balances the two, ρ_i^h = //k_i^h (I − P_t^h)//_2 is the residual of a previous-frame key outside the rank-r QR subspace P_t^h of the current screenshot's keys (Eq. 7), and ρ̃^h the (1−γ) percentile threshold (Eq. 8). Reported targets: click accuracy, step accuracy and success rate at each budget vs full cache, and MFLOPs per token for pre-filling and decoding. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 150 of the saved text | 150 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because GUI attention sparsity is uniformly high across layers, GUI-KV assigns a uniform budget to each layer and ranks tokens by attention augmented with a softmax-normalised residual-stream L2-norm saliency (spatial saliency guidance), while zeroing the scores of previous-frame visual tokens whose keys lie largely in the rank-r QR subspace of the current frame's keys, i.e. whose residual falls below the per-head (1-γ) percentile (temporal redundancy scoring); it thus retains tokens that are both intrinsically important and temporally unique, plug-and-play without retraining. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 151 of the saved text | 151 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | The abstract claims that across standard GUI agent benchmarks and models GUI-KV outperforms competitive KV compression baselines and closely matches full-cache accuracy at modest budgets (line 54). The results section (six benchmarks, UI-TARS-1.5-7B and OpenCUA-7B, baselines SnapKV, PyramidKV, VL-Cache) words it as 'consistently matches or surpasses the best competing compression schemes' across budgets 1%-80%, with positive average absolute gains over the best baseline on four of six benchmarks (+0.7 to +3.6) and a baseline sometimes ahead at 1-3% budgets (lines 685, 688); the introduction's 'typically 10-20%' budget for near-full-cache accuracy is qualified to UI-TARS-1.5-7B (lines 63, 688, 736). | 0 | framing_problem | A major bottleneck in current LLM agent frameworks is the high inference cost of tool selection, especially in ReAct-style agents that repeatedly invoke the LLM to decide which tool to use at each step, which limits use in resource-constrained or real-time scenarios. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Agents repeatedly infer the next tool (and its parameters) with a complete LLM inference at every step, even though not all decision steps are equally complex: many tool invocations occur in highly patterned or repetitive contexts that do not need the LLM's full reasoning, so universal use of the LLM over-utilises it and creates unnecessary computational overhead. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Given historical trajectories D_hist = {tau_1, ..., tau_N}, each tau_i = (o_0, a_0, o_1, a_1, ...) of observations o and actions a, where an action a_t = (tool_{t+1}, params_{t+1}) is chosen at timestep t from observation o_t, task goal G and tool set T (ReAct infers a_t ~ p_LLM(a / o_t, G, T) via a complete LLM inference), construct M_AutoTool, a training-free decision-making algorithm based on the Tool Inertia Graph that selectively bypasses the LLM for predictable actions to improve efficiency. Tool choice uses CIPS = (1 - alpha) * Score_freq + alpha * Score_ctx (Score_freq from Tool Inertia Graph edge weights; Score_ctx the semantic alignment of the agent's current intuition with the candidate tool's description); the highest-CIPS tool v* goes to parameter filling only if CIPS(v*) > theta_inertial, and the inertial call is executed only if all required parameters are filled, otherwise the LLM is called (experiments: theta_inertial = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, inertial calls capped at 30% of operations, line 408-409). Evaluation target: reduce computational overhead measured by number of LLM calls and token consumption while maintaining comparable task performance measured by AgentBoard progress rate (line 406). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 253 of the saved text | 253 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Exploiting 'tool usage inertia' (tool invocations follow predictable sequential patterns), AutoTool builds a directed graph from agent trajectories, with tools as nodes, edges capturing transition probabilities, and parameter-dependency edges; before each LLM call it attempts an 'inertial' call: choose the next tool by a score combining historical frequency and contextual relevance (CIPS), then fill its parameters non-LLM (dependency backtracking, then environmental state matching, then heuristic filling), falling back to the LLM whenever either stage fails. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the plain ReAct and Reflexion baselines, AutoTool reduces LLM call count by 15-25% and total token consumption by 10-40% on average across three datasets while maintaining comparable progress rate (abstract: inference costs reduced by up to 30%). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 542 of the saved text | 542 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The scheduling target is to minimise Cost_recompute, Cost_unused and Cost_caching, thereby maximising throughput, subject to GPU memory capacity (line 147). ## f205 — Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2511.02230v7 · version read: v7 · v1: Tue, 4 Nov 2025 03:43:05 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Inference engines evict a finished request's KV cache when new requests are waiting (end-of-turn eviction); this breaks for agentic workloads that interleave LLM calls with tools, because the tool calls introduce pauses that prevent effective KV reuse across turns, and the paper aims to optimize job completion time for multi-turn agent workloads. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | After eviction the engine must recompute the prefix (prefill) or reload the KV cache from CPU when the tool returns, and, even with CPU offloading, the returning request suffers a per-turn queueing delay waiting for GPU memory, which accumulates over turns and is not measurable by offline profiling; at the same time tool-call durations are variable (some extremely long-tailed), so a retention time must be bounded, since a pinned KV cache can occupy GPU memory for a long time and even cause deadlocks, yet a TTL that expires just before the tool returns wastes the waiting time. Prior work falls short: InferCept decides only on reload cost and does not model per-turn queueing delay or handle variable tool durations, Autellix uses end-of-turn eviction, Pie provides no retention policy, and Ayo/Alto/Parrot assume static workflows. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 98 of the saved text | 98 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | TTL choice maximizes expected net benefit in units of time (total job completion latency): τ* = argmax_τ P(τ,f) × Benefit(r) − Cost(τ,r) (Eq. 1), with Cost(τ,r) = MemUsage(r)/M × τ; Benefit(r) = CacheMissCost(r) + OutofOrderCost(r); CacheMissCost(r) = MemUsage(r) × Prefill-Reload(r) / M; OutofOrderCost(r) = T/M × MemUsage(r) × η; η = −Corr(k, N−k); P(τ,f) = (1//S[f]/) Σ_{t∈S[f]} I[t ≤ τ]; after cancelling MemUsage(r)/M this becomes argmax_τ P(τ,f) × (T·η + Prefill-Reload(r)) − τ (Eq. 2). Symbols: r a request that generates tool call f; τ the TTL (seconds); MemUsage(r) GPU memory of r's KV cache; M average GPU memory footprint of active requests; Prefill-Reload(r) time to reconstruct the KV cache by prefill or CPU reload (from offline profiling); T average queueing delay of evicted requests (sliding-window average); η memoryfulness factor of the workload, with N the total requests in a program and k those already served; S[f] historical durations of tool f; I the indicator function. Reported end-to-end targets are average job completion time / delay and throughput. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 479 of the saved text | 479 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | For requests that generate tool calls, Continnum pins the KV cache in GPU memory for a time-to-live set by weighing reload/prefill cost and the queueing delay that eviction would cause against the memory it occupies, using the empirical distribution of that tool's durations; when the TTL expires the cache is evicted automatically, which keeps it robust to unexpectedly long tool calls, and a TTL-aware program-level first-come-first-serve priority preserves multi-turn continuity. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 103 of the saved text | 103 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Delay (job completion time) and throughput on multi-turn agentic workloads: across three hardware and model setups Continnum reduces delay by 1.12x to 3.66x and improves throughput by 1.10x to 3.22x (the sentence does not name the baseline; the evaluated baselines are vanilla vLLM, vLLM+LMCache CPU offloading, Autellix/Autellix+ and InferCept); on Company A's internal H100 testbed it reduces delay for real SWE-agent workloads by up to 8.18x, where the comparison is against distributed inference solutions (SGLang, Dynamo); the abstract states 'improves the average job completion times by over 8x while improving throughput'. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 166 of the saved text | 166 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-brained web agents face a critical cost-performance trade-off: upgrading to a more powerful model often yields only marginal accuracy gains while substantially increasing operational costs, e.g., price, which makes it impractical to use a single 'best model' in real-world web agents; the paper therefore argues it is important to develop a dynamic router that matches each web query to the most cost-effective LLM capable of resolving it. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 40 of the saved text | 40 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Web-agent prompts are verbose and complex, concatenating user goals, action histories (memory) and detailed environmental states (perception); the paper says this informational redundancy can degrade the performance of conventional routing mechanisms such as ZOOTER and RouterDC (line 60). As a task progresses the growing action history makes prompts increasingly verbose and noisy, with a significant portion of queries exceeding thousands of tokens (Fig. 3), and the paper posits that this noise challenges traditional routers that rely on direct semantic embeddings (lines 101-103); the abstract states that the complex prompts lead to degraded LLM ensemble performance (line 41). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 60 of the saved text | 60 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Learn a router psi that takes a query q_i and outputs a probability distribution p_i = psi(q_i) in R^T over T candidate LLMs (line 83), by minimising the cost-aware VIB loss (Eq. 6): L_ca-VIB = (1/N) sum_{i=1..N} ( E_{p_theta(z_i/q_i)}[-log p_phi(y_i/z_i)] + beta * KL[p_theta(m_i/q_i) // r(m_i)] + lambda * E_{p_theta(z_i/q_i)}[ sum_{t=1..T} p_phi(y_t/z_i) * C(M_t) ] ). N = training samples; q_i = query (user's high-level goal, agent's action history, current web representation); z_i = m (.) h_q, the input feature representation h_q masked element-wise by a stochastic binary mask m; p_theta = stochastic encoder; p_phi = decoder predicting the target model distribution; r = the reference distribution in the KL (compression) term, not defined further in the text; y_i = the ground-truth outcome in the problem formulation (line 83); in the prediction term the cross-entropy target is a distribution derived from a softmax over the score vector s_i (line 135); beta = weight of the compression term; lambda = hyperparameter controlling cost-sensitivity; C(M_t) = pre-defined, query-agnostic unit cost of invoking model M_t (e.g. c_p^(t)+c_c^(t) for a single token). | 1 | framing_challenge | Each agent step incurs latency from both LLM inference and action execution, and in interactive settings (customer service, web navigation, embodied control) this sequential latency accumulates and directly affects user experience; speculation hides latency only when the prediction is correct, yet most speculative execution methods for LLM agents are stateless, treating every task independently, and no existing method retrieves contextually similar past trajectories or adapts to its own prediction failures during deployment, even though agent tasks exhibit strong regularity (the same action sequences recur across episodes). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reported target is speculation accuracy (aggregate accuracy): 'total correct steps divided by total steps, pooled across all tasks' (Type 1 action prediction: read-only action full match; Type 2 observation prediction: observation exact match; Type 3 chained prediction: action full match; tau^2-bench excludes turn 0), with best-of-k counted as a hit if any of k parallel speculators matches (main table uses k=1). Latency saved per hit (Sec. 2.1): Type 1 min(l_env, l_LLM - l_spec); Type 2 min(l_LLM, l_env - l_spec); Type 3 up to l_LLM + l_env, where l_LLM = the actor's LLM-call latency, l_env = environment latency (API responses, user input, state computation), l_spec = speculator inference latency. Estimated latency reduction per 100 agent steps (Appendix A.4, Table 6): acc x l_hit x 100, against baseline latency T_100, with l_hit = l_env (Type 1), min(l_LLM, l_env - l_spec) (Type 2), l_LLM - l_spec (Type 3). Net expected additional cost for Types 2 and 3: k*C_S + (1 - acc)*C_act (k = number of speculators; C_S = speculator cost without memory context; C_act = actor LLM cost; Table 6 gives both per 100 steps). No single optimisation objective is stated. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 205 of the saved text | 205 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Give the speculator three online memory systems built from past agent trajectories (a contrastive transition table of action-sequence statistics, an episodic memory retrieving contextually similar segments, and a confusion tracker suppressing recurring errors) so its hit rate rises with experience; only side-effect-free work is pre-launched during idle time and misses are discarded, so the actor's trajectory is identical to non-speculative execution (lossless). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 91 of the saved text | 91 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Compared with the stateless speculator, memory-augmented speculation gives a 19-39% relative accuracy improvement on action prediction and up to a 2.5x increase on observation prediction tasks with repetitive action spaces; on ALFWorld the estimated latency reduction (counting each correct speculation as hiding one actor LLM call) grows from about 28% with the stateless speculator to over 50% with memory. | 1 | framing_challenge | Because the service does not understand how requests are correlated, it cannot exploit three opportunities: dependent consecutive requests go back and forth to the client, adding network latency and queuing delays; scheduling optimizes per-request latency rather than end-to-end latency; and common prompt prefixes (e.g. long system prompts, over 94% of tokens repeated in a production search engine) are provided repeatedly in each request, wasting storage, computation and memory bandwidth. The paper adds that without knowledge of the prompt structure, token-by-token matching of every request is expensive at the cluster level, so a public service can hardly detect and co-locate prompt-sharing requests and engine-level redundancy avoidance is hard to bring into effect (line 146). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 90 of the saved text | 90 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The scheduler's primary goal is to meet the varied performance goals of LLM applications while optimizing GPU cluster utilization (line 208): applications annotate final output Semantic Variables with a performance criterion, end-to-end latency or throughput (line 183), e.g. minimise the end-to-end time to receive the final summary (line 140) or to deliver the final code (line 341). Requests generating a throughput-annotated variable are marked throughput-preferred when scheduling (line 200); for latency-critical outputs, parallel requests at the same stage form a task group whose latency as a whole the scheduler should minimise, often with a higher batch capacity (line 201); to meet latency targets an engine must keep its token count below a threshold set by the request with the strictest latency constraint (line 208). No formula is given; the scheduling policy is Algorithm 1. Evaluation reports mean and P90 end-to-end latency, latency per output token (TPOT), normalized latency (request latency per number of output tokens), token generation speed, sustainable request rate and GPU memory of KV cache. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 208 of the saved text | 208 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Expose application-level knowledge to the service through Semantic Variables (annotated input/output regions of prompts that also form the data pipeline between requests), so the service can run conventional data-flow analysis to recover the dependencies between LLM requests and use the declared prompt structure (prefix hashes at Semantic Variable positions) to detect commonality; it then executes dependent requests server-side, deduces request-level scheduling preferences from the end-to-end performance criterion, shares prompt prefixes, and schedules requests application-centrically. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 76 of the saved text | 76 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Parrot achieves up to 11.7x speedup or 12x higher throughput compared with state-of-the-art solutions (baselines: LangChain applications calling FastChat with vLLM or HuggingFace engines). The 11.7x is end-to-end latency for multi-agent MetaGPT programming against the latency-centric baseline (one A100, LLaMA 13B); against the throughput-centric baseline the gain is up to 2.45x. The 12x is the sustainable request rate when serving multiple GPTs applications on four A6000 GPUs against the baseline without prompt sharing. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 92 of the saved text | 92 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The formal definitions are the traces tau_seq = <X, (R_1,A_1,O_1), ..., (R_{T-1},A_{T-1},O_{T-1}), (R_T, Y_hat)> and tau_par, in which each A_t becomes a set A_t^par = {A_t^(1), ..., A_t^(m)} with observations O_t^par; X = user query (system prompt and question), R_t = reasoning thought, A_t = tool call, O_t = observation, T = final step, Y_hat = final answer, m = number of concurrent tool calls, f_theta = the LLM producing R_t, A_t; U_t = inserted user message fixing the number of calls. | 3 | framing_solution | The paper hypothesizes that providing explicit budget signals enables the model to internalize resource constraints and adapt its strategy without additional training (line 173). | 1 | framing_challenge | Standard prefix-caching techniques work only when the KV cache is reused by the same LLM, and naively sharing the KV cache across different LLMs causes generation quality to drop greatly (reusing the whole KV cache loses more than 50% of accuracy points on HotpotQA for most model pairs); the challenge is to figure out which part to re-compute or re-use without incurring much delay overhead or degradation of quality. Recomputing only the scattered critical layers is inefficient, because every transition layer from reuse to recompute needs the sender model's E cache (up to 2x the KV cache size for Mistral-7B/Llama-3-8B, up to 4x for Llama-3.1-70B) stored in GPU memory and loaded from remote nodes, and inaccurate, because the E-cache deviation at each transition layer propagates to later layers. As background motivation, lengthy prefill reduces goodput because TTFT grows super-linearly with input length. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 100 of the saved text | 100 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No explicit formula. The central design question is how to determine the layers to re-compute to reduce latency while keeping the quality loss minimal. Offline profiling on a held-out 'training' set (50 HotpotQA contexts) builds a Pareto frontier of quality (F1) versus number of re-computed contiguous layers; the configuration chosen keeps the F1 drop within 5% of the receiver model's original quality while minimizing the number of re-computed layers (lines 344, 417-418). Online, the point on the frontier is chosen based on the latency SLO (line 355); Appendix B (line 945) gives the rule: if requests are queuing, choose the configuration with the lowest number of re-computed layers above an accuracy target; otherwise estimate prefill latency from the request's token count and select the highest recomputation ratio that satisfies the latency SLO, to maximize accuracy. Evaluation reports quality (F1, Rouge-L, code similarity) and system metrics TTFT, TBT, E2E, prefill latency (GPU prefill time plus KV/E-cache loading delay over InfiniBand, line 422) and throughput; goodput is defined as the number of queries processed per second within a latency SLO (line 190); Appendix B reports SLO violation rate (line 944). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 306 of the saved text | 306 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because only a small subset (often around 10%) of layers are sensitive to KV cache differences and these are largely consistent across inputs for a model pair, DroidSpeak recomputes a contiguous group of critical layers identified by offline profiling and reuses the other model's KV cache for the remaining layers, and pipelines layer-wise recomputation with loading of reused KV cache from remote nodes to hide the loading delay. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Up to 4x throughput improvement and about 3.1x faster prefill (time to first token), with negligible quality loss in F1, Rouge-L or code similarity, compared with a baseline that allows no KV cache sharing across models (prefill speedup 1.7-3.1x, average 2.1x). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action-observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition and observation can delay subsequent decisions; the central question is whether recurring action patterns can reduce agent latency without requiring the model to choose new meta tools. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 40 of the saved text | 40 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The main constraint is sequential dependence: the next prompt usually cannot be built until the previous action returns its observation. Token-level speculative decoding works inside one model call and cannot remove this cross-step dependency; Speculative Actions only accepts progress at the granularity of adjacent action steps; and exposing mined action sequences as callable meta-tools is unreliable because open models rarely select them. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 57 of the saved text | 57 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No explicit optimisation objective; average per-task wall time (seconds per task) is the latency metric, reported with binary task accuracy on tau^2-Bench Telecom and task-goal completion (TGC) on AppWorld; Delta is relative to the sequential baseline within each benchmark (Table 1, line 230). The only formula is the macro-filtering reliability estimate (Eq. 1): p_m (underlined) = F^{-1}_{Beta(k_m+1, n_m-k_m+1)}(delta), the lower delta-quantile of a Beta posterior, where n_m is the number of labeled opportunities and k_m the number of correct drafter proposals for candidate macro m; m is retained only when n_m >= n_min and p_m >= tau, with n_min and tau selected on held-out tasks. At runtime a macro commit skips l-1 actor decisions (l = remaining draft actions aligned to the macro) and requires l-1 >= L_min. Diagnostic metric: skip density = skipped steps / (tasks x max_steps) (Table 2 caption, line 272); commit precision is audited stage-by-stage on 100 held-out tau^2 Telecom tasks (Table 5, lines 339-366). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 222 of the saved text | 222 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | SMC shifts mined recurring action patterns from model-side macro selection to executor-side validation: the drafter pre-executes future action chains on an isolated state, and when a mined macro aligns with the draft chain and the actor's next call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining matched draft steps and their observations to the official trajectory, skipping the corresponding large-model calls and environment delays. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 72 of the saved text | 72 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The sequential baseline runs only the actor on one GPU, while SA and SMC use three GPUs (actor, actor-class replica for speculative requests, drafter), so only the SA comparison is equal-hardware. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 44 of the saved text | 44 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents in complex embodied environments often suffer from inefficiencies in multi-turn interactions, frequently trapped in repetitive loops or issuing ineffective commands, leading to redundant computational overhead (abstract, line 110); the paper explores early-exit behavior so that an agent can terminate its interaction when appropriate (lines 110, 140). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 110 of the saved text | 110 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | A key underexplored limitation is that agents often fail to recognize when a goal is too difficult or when they are stuck; prior work shows they may repeat the same errors in unproductive loops without meaningful actions or self-correction, leading to unnecessary computational overhead, and in real-world settings repeated mistakes can waste energy, cause wear-and-tear or damage objects (line 116). Without early exit, an agent keeps exploring until the task is completed or a predefined maximum number of steps is reached (line 138; 'continue until the step limit, often wasting valuable interactions', line 769). Existing trajectory-training and prompt-design methods 'often neglect efficiency, especially in failure cases', and post-hoc strategies (self-reflection, trajectory revision, experience extraction) help only after trials conclude (Related Work, line 814). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

PR at step t is r_t = max_{0<=i<=t} (1/K) sum_{k=1..K} f(s_i, g_k), with subgoals g_1..g_K and f a binary indicator that state s_i satisfies subgoal g_k. A practical variant hands control after exit to a stronger agent within the remaining step budget. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 117 of the saved text | 117 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Although major LLM providers offer prompt caching to reduce cost and latency, its benefits for agentic workloads remain underexplored in the research literature; to the authors' knowledge, no prior work quantifies these cost savings or compares caching strategies for multi-turn agentic tasks (abstract, line 70; intro, line 81). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | As agentic workloads grow in complexity, conversations can span dozens of API calls with context windows accumulating tens of thousands of tokens, leading to significant costs and latency overhead (line 75). For caching, agentic workloads feature dynamic, session-specific content that accumulates unpredictably; tool results often contain user-specific data that will not benefit other sessions, and the interleaving of static system prompts with dynamic tool outputs complicates cache reuse (line 97). Naive full-context caching can paradoxically increase latency because dynamic tool calls and results may trigger cache writes for content that will not be reused across sessions (line 86). The Discussion adds that dynamic values in the system prompt (timestamps, session identifiers, user information) and changing tool definitions break the cached prefix (lines 217-218). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Two primary metrics measured against a no-cache baseline: API cost per session, computed from token counts in API responses (standard input tokens, cached input tokens, cache creation tokens) each multiplied by the provider's price and summed over all API calls in the session; and TTFT, the time from request initiation to receipt of the first streamed response chunk. Reported as percentage improvement over the baseline with independent-samples t-tests (alpha = 0.05, n = 40 per condition). No optimization formula. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 115 of the saved text | 115 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Prompt caching reuses previously computed KV tensors to avoid redundant computation on repeated prompt prefixes (line 75); the paper compares full-context, system-prompt-only and exclude-tool-results caching against a no-cache baseline, forcing cache boundaries with UUIDs (lines 109-113), and concludes that strategic control of cache boundaries - such as caching only the system prompt or explicitly excluding tool results, so that only stable, reusable content is cached - beats naive full-context caching, with system-prompt-only caching giving the most consistent benefits across cost and latency (line 86). The abstract's guidance also names placing dynamic content at the end of the system prompt and avoiding dynamic traditional function calling (line 70). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f218 — Autellix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.13965v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Wed, 19 Feb 2025 18:59:30 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): 23rd USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 26)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Agentic programs scale LLM calls and output tokens, but existing LLM serving systems ignore dependencies between programs and calls, missing significant opportunities for optimization (abstract, line 53); because they optimize individual LLM calls without program-level context, they often suffer from suboptimal end-to-end performance for complex programs, in particular programs' end-to-end latencies (line 90). The authors' analysis shows programs submitted to LLM serving engines experience long cumulative wait times, primarily due to head-of-line blocking (line 54). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 53 of the saved text | 53 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Head-of-line blocking at two levels: call-level, where LLM calls with long decodes delay shorter ones (line 132), and program-level, where program-agnostic schedulers let longer programs with many LLM requests delay shorter programs - without program-level context even preemptive MLFQ blindly prioritizes new LLM requests, leading to starvation of shorter programs when long programs' new calls are prioritized (lines 134-135). LLM calls within a program often share common prefixes and cumulative conversation states, while calls across programs typically share only the system prompt (line 96); within a program cache-hit rates remain above 90% across all input lengths, whereas across programs the cache-hit rate decays exponentially with input length, so serving systems across engines should consider a program's data locality to avoid recomputing its KV cache (lines 96, 141). The authors assume a program's LLM invocation pattern emerges only at runtime, making it difficult to fully know or predict the entire graph in advance (line 88). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Minimize programs' end-to-end latency (response time), which for a single-threaded program comprises (1) waiting time (total queuing time of its LLM calls on the engine), (2) execution time (cumulative feedforward time of its LLM calls) and (3) interceptions (time waiting for external interrupts such as tool calls or human input); Autellix targets (1) and (2) because (3) is unrelated to LLM serving (line 124). Priority formulas: PLAS, Eq. 1, p(c_j) = sum of runtimes t_k of all prior LLM calls k<j with the same program ID (larger value = lower priority, lines 254-260); ATLAS, Eq. 2, p(c_j) = 0 if c_j is a root, otherwise max over parents c_k of (p(c_k) + t_k), an estimate of the critical path (lines 262-268). Anti-starvation promotes a call to Q_1 when W_total / T_total >= beta (line 276-278). Stated system objectives: (1) program end-to-end latency for users, (2) maximizing GPU utilization for providers, (3) mitigating starvation / fairness measured via P95 and P99 latencies (line 147). Evaluation metric: program-level token latency = total program response time / number of tokens generated (critical-path response time / total tokens across threads for multi-threaded programs), with throughput compared at equal latency (lines 353-355). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 124 of the saved text | 124 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Treat programs as first-class citizens: intercept LLM calls through a stateful session API, keep a global process table, and, inspired by OS schedulers, prioritize LLM calls by program-level attained service with preemption into discretized queues and anti-starvation - PLAS for single-threaded programs uses the total execution time of the program's previously completed calls (lines 93-94, 254-260), and ATLAS for multi-threaded DAG programs uses the maximum cumulative service time across threads, i.e. an estimate of the program's critical path (lines 95, 262-269) - so LLM calls from long programs, which are unlikely to complete soon, are deprioritized, allowing shorter programs to complete first; a data-locality-aware load balancer routes long calls to their programs' engines and load-balances shorter calls to other engines to avoid recomputing the programs' KV cache (line 96). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Across diverse LLMs and agentic workloads, Autellix improves throughput of programs by 4-15x at the same latency compared to state-of-the-art systems such as vLLM (abstract, line 55); across engines, up to 1.5x over standard load balancers (intro, line 97). Per-workload single-engine results (Sec. 6.3, lines 365-367): ShareGPT/BFCL up to 8x vLLM, 2x vLLM-opt and 1.5x MLFQ; LATS up to 5x vLLM, 2x vLLM-opt and 2.5x MLFQ; Mixed up to 15x vLLM, 4x vLLM-opt and 5.5x MLFQ. Sec. 6.4 reports up to 1.4x higher throughput than round-robin and least-used load balancers (line 377). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 55 of the saved text | 55 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = end-to-end latency, waiting time, execution time, throughput of programs, program-level token latency, P95/P99 tail latency, makespan, GPU utilization, prefix cache hit rate / KV-cache recomputation, number of LLM calls and output tokens, KV-cache swap overhead (GPU-CPU swaps); agent kind = LLM serving system (serving engine) for agentic programs: dynamic, non-deterministic DAGs of LLM calls from one or more agents plus external interrupts (tool calls, code execution, human input), e.g. chatbots, ReAct agents, Map-Reduce and MCTS programs; position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Common orchestrators treat tool return as the settlement trigger, so faults, speculation and concurrent agents can leave partial effects, losing-branch residue, stale writes or irreversible sends; the paper frames this as the question of when a tool effect may become permanent. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 127 of the saved text | 127 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Correct settlement needs two facts that retries, checkpoint replay, locks and compensation each conflate: which effects must settle together, and when earlier conflicting work is exhausted; current orchestrator mechanisms (checkpointing, retries, timeouts, idempotency keys, Saga-style compensation) recover after a tool effect has externalized or after the workflow restores its own state, checkpoint rollback restores agent memory but not an email, booking or remote API update, Saga compensation cannot prevent an irreversible send, and locks either miss the read-plan-write gap (per-call) or serialize unrelated work (workflow-wide). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 127 of the saved text | 127 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation objective; the primary metrics are clean task success (RQ1, final state checked for residue, duplicate effects and unresolved compensation), conflict-serializability violations (RQ2) and classified-before-externalization leak rate (RQ3) (line 198); the combined-stress 'joint surface' uses run-clean rate (zero invariant violations, stale commits, confirmation leaks and duplicates, line 396) with wait, rejected commits and adapter LOC as the secondary axes on which tied baselines pay (line 398); RQ5 reports runtime cost (per-step wrapper overhead, line 1533). The commit rule is written as: a sealed transaction T commits only when \mathit{frontier}(r)\geq e(T) for every r\in\mathcal{R}(T), where \mathcal{R}(T) is the set of read and effect scopes recorded in its sealed footprint and e(T) the maximum epoch of those recorded reads and effects; the orchestrator advances \mathit{frontier}(r) to e only after every transaction with \mathit{commit\_epoch}<e that touches r has finalized (line 184). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 198 of the saved text | 198 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Progress-aware transactions separate execution, sealing, frontier checks and settlement: the runtime records reads and effects during execution, seals a transaction when its footprint is complete, and commits only after per-resource frontiers show no earlier conflicting work can still arrive; commit releases bufferable effects, accepts reversible external effects as final and lets irreversible effects leave the gate, while abort suppresses unreleased effects and compensates externalized reversible ones. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 127 of the saved text | 127 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f221 — Optimizing Agentic Language Model Inference via Speculative Tool Calls

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.15834v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Wed, 17 Dec 2025 18:22:44 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Tools improve LM capabilities but introduce performance bottlenecks during inference: the model alternates between generation and tool invocation, leaving gaps while waiting on tool completion, and the overhead of tool-centric agents is increasingly dominated by the time spent waiting on tools. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Each tool call forces generation to stop and return to the user, an interrupt-driven process with a strict sequential dependency in which tool latencies accumulate; evicted sequences and tool output must be rescheduled back into the engine (and the history prefilled again), and prefix caching does not remove the overheads of removing, processing and rescheduling sequences, which worsen in multi-tenant settings; breaking this is non-trivial because tool latencies span orders of magnitude and are hard to predict or bound, long tools dominate end-to-end latency while for short tools eviction and re-entry overheads can outweigh latency hiding, running tools early or out of order risks wasted computation or outputs inconsistent with the model's eventual decisions, and existing in-engine optimizations (speculative decoding, KV-cache management) treat tools as opaque interruptions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reported metrics: Time Saved = 100\times\frac{T_{\text{base}}-T_{\text{spec}}}{T_{\text{base}}}\,\%, where T_base and T_spec are the agent's start-to-finish times without and with speculation for the same prompt(s) (mean over async agents), and throughput = tokens generated per second averaged per agent; for commercial models, the additional cost of speculation per 100 agent turns. Walltime is deliberately not used because response lengths vary. Analytic model (client side): S_{\mathrm{spec}}(\alpha)=\frac{G+T}{\alpha\,\max\{G,\,g+T\}+(1-\alpha)(G+T)}, where alpha is the acceptance rate of the speculative model S, G and g the generation times of the main and speculative models, and T the tool call time, with S_max < 2. Engine side: T^{\ast}_{\textrm{spec}}=(1-\alpha)2Ko+\varphi(X_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{K}(t_{i}+t_{o,i}))+\delta(\alpha K+\sum_{i=1}^{K}R_{i}+(1-\alpha)\sum_{i=1}^{K}t_{i})+(1-\alpha)\sum_{i=1}^{K}T_{i} over K consecutive agent turns, where X_i are prefilled tokens, R_i reasoning tokens decoded, t_i tool-call tokens decoded, t_{o,i} tool-output tokens, T_i tool seconds and o the HTTP/batch-loading overhead per pass; varphi and delta multiply prefill and decode token counts but are not defined in the readable prose of the saved text. Prefix-cached baseline (Eq. 5, line 1762): T_{\textrm{cached}}=2Ko+\varphi(X_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{K}(t_{i}+t_{o,i}))+\delta\sum_{i=1}^{K}(R_{i}+t_{i})+\sum_{i=1}^{K}T_{i}; Eq. 6 equals T_cached at alpha=0, and at alpha=1 saves 2Ko+\delta(\sum t_{i}-K)+\sum T_{i} over prefix-cached inference (line 1779). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1839 of the saved text | 1839 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Speculative tool execution: a client-side strategy sends the prompt to a small speculative model alongside the main model, launches its predicted (stateless, cheap) tool calls asynchronously and reuses the cached result if the main model emits the same call, breaking the sequential dependency without engine changes; an engine-side variant posts speculated tool outputs to a tool cache in the inference engine, validates tool-call tokens by speculative sampling and ingests tool outputs directly so the sequence stays resident and avoids eviction and re-prefill. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 97 of the saved text | 97 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against non-speculative tool calling, client-side speculation (1x speculation, gpt-oss-120b on BFCL prompts with configured tool latencies) can save between 6-21% end-to-end time per agent at average tool latencies of 0.5-3 s (up to 6% for ~0.5 s tools, up to 21% for ~2.0-2.5 s tools); engine-side speculation gives 2-3% better time savings than client-side when tools finish before the main model is done reasoning (tool latencies ~0-1 s, one async agent only); Figure 1 reports up to 196 tokens/s throughput improvement with 32 agents (the abstract says 'several hundred tokens per second'); and with gpt-5 plus one gpt-5-nano speculation nearly 10% time is saved per agent turn for about a 4% price increase (cost shown per 100 agent turns), while nine speculations add only marginal time saving at around 25-30% of the main generation's cost (Figure 7, lines 1867-1872). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1861 of the saved text | 1861 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = throughput (tokens generated per second), percent time saved, end-to-end time, total generation time, tool latency, eviction and rescheduling overhead, prefill time, decode time, inference time, speedup, walltime, cost per 100 agent turns (additional cost of speculation), performance bottlenecks during the inference process, economically viable and efficient; agent kind = LM-based agents / tool-calling agents (e.g. SWE agents, reasoning models using web search and code execution) and the inference engine that hosts them (OpenAI-API client and a modified vLLM server); position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper calls optimal routing (maximizing quality within a cost constraint or minimizing cost for a target quality) challenging and lists what an ideal router must do: (1) optimize response quality while invoking a single LLM per query, minimizing cost and latency compared with multi-LLM approaches; (2) generalize to out-of-domain queries without separate per-domain routers; (3) work across a broad range of LLMs without retraining. Routing rule R^{\alpha}(q) = M_weak if P(win_s/q) < alpha, M_strong if P(win_s/q) >= alpha, where P_theta(win_s/q) is the learned probability that the strong model beats the weak model on query q (trained by \max_{\theta}\sum\log P_{\theta}(l_{s,w}\mid q) over preference data with labels l_{s,w} in {win_s, tie, win_w}) and alpha in [0,1] is the cost threshold. | 0 | framing_problem | Agentic workflows incur high inference latency because LLMs are invoked repeatedly for each agent; prefix caching of the agents' fixed prompts reduces this, but prefix caching alone is insufficient under limited GPU memory, where the LRU eviction of existing serving systems leads to suboptimal performance in agentic workflows. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | LRU eviction fails to anticipate future agent usage and often discards KV caches shortly before their reuse (an agent about to run may have been idle a long time), causing frequent cache misses and recomputation or swapping overhead; memory runs out with many concurrent workflows or very large agent prompts on limited hardware, and reactive CPU-to-GPU loading of offloaded prefixes still adds noticeable transfer latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No formal objective function. The evaluation asks (1) whether KVFlow reduces end-to-end latency for individual workflows with large prompt prefixes and limited GPU memory and (2) how it performs under high concurrency with multiple parallel workflows. Single-workflow latency is measured at batch size 1 for a 10-agent sequential workflow executed ten times (latency averaged over all runs) and reported as speedup over SGLang (GPU-only radix cache), with SGLang w/ HiCache also compared; the high-concurrency results are reported as speedup / 'performance' over SGLang and HiCache without a further metric definition in the saved text. The paper states the evaluation focuses exclusively on system performance metrics like latency because output semantics are unchanged. The design quantity is each agent's steps-to-execution (how soon the agent is expected to run), computed on the Agent Step Graph by step aggregation functions, e.g. \max(E1,E2)+1 when an agent needs both upstream executors E1 and E2 to finish and \min(E1,E2)+1 when either suffices. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 149 of the saved text | 149 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because the workflow structure predicts which agents run next, KVFlow replaces LRU with a workflow-aware eviction policy that evicts KV cache nodes of agents with large steps-to-execution first (priorities set per cache-tree node so shared prefixes are kept, varying suffixes evicted first), and prefetches the KV tensors of next-scheduled agents from CPU to GPU in background threads with status-aware scheduling so transfers overlap with computation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
