| 0 | framing_problem | Current test-time scaling makes agents 'think' longer before acting, which does not allow them to acquire new information from the environment or adapt their behavior over time; post-trained agents are reactive and often suboptimal in partially observable or non-stationary settings where information-seeking behavior is needed. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Teaching agents to scale interaction autonomously presents key challenges: without appropriate training signals agents may overfit to exploratory behaviors like blindly clicking links without progress toward the task, wasting the additional steps; prompting alone ('check-again') only lets the agent revisit its behavior upon task completion and cannot produce mid-rollout switching between exploration and exploitation; and RL with a fixed horizon either overfits and terminates prematurely (short h) or learns slowly because of higher loss variance and noisy credit assignment (long h). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Task success rate: each task is a finite-horizon sequential decision process with maximum h interaction steps, and the agent receives reward 1 for task success and 0 otherwise. Training objective (Eq. 5.1, online filtered BC): \argmax_{\theta} E_{\mathcal{T}~tasks}[ E_{o_{0:h},a_{0:h-1}~\pi(./\mathcal{T})}[ (\sum_{t=0}^{h-1} \log \pi_{\theta}(a_t / o_{\leq t}, \mathcal{T})) · 1[R(o_{0:h},\mathcal{T})=1] ] ], where \theta are the policy parameters, \mathcal{T} a task, o_t the observation and a_t the action at step t, h the maximum interaction horizon, and R the binary task reward, so only successful trajectories are imitated. TTI sets the horizon per iteration i by a curriculum: additive h_i := clip(h_min + i, h_max) or multiplicative h_i := clip(h_min · i, h_max) (default, h_min = 10, h_max = 30). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 160 of the saved text | 160 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Scale test-time interaction (more interaction steps within one rollout) as an axis complementary to per-step reasoning, because each extra step of interaction provides new information from the environment whereas thinking longer only reorganizes information the agent already has; to learn this, combine online RL with a curriculum over the interaction horizon that trains on short trajectories first and gradually exposes the agent to longer ones, so it learns effective exploitation before extending its horizon to explore. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Within lossless KV cache management under GPU memory pressure (long contexts, concurrent sessions, multi-turn workloads), decide which KV cache blocks should remain resident in GPU memory, with the goal of improving serving efficiency without sacrificing output correctness. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 112 of the saved text | 112 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Existing lossless systems base eviction decisions on access frequency or positional heuristics without considering how different KV cache blocks affect the execution efficiency of GPU attention kernels; their policies do not explicitly model each block's future reuse likelihood and marginal impact on attention-kernel latency, although recomputation cost is asymmetric (later positions cost more because attention is quadratic) while shared prefixes carry hit rate. Supporting non-contiguous cached segments needs an attention kernel that handles disjoint KV regions, and dispatching each segment to a separate kernel call adds kernel launch and host synchronization overheads; and the straightforward frequency-value definitions of existing cost-aware policies cause linear-time eviction, which is highly inefficient compared to LRU's O(1). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 92 of the saved text | 92 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Eviction criterion (Eq. 3): block_id <- \argmin_{B} E(B,t) = \argmin_{B} f_{B}(t) · \Delta T_{B}, i.e. evict the block with the lowest expected recomputation cost. f_B(t) is the frequency value of KV block B at time t (historical access frequency with decay, taken as a proxy for reuse probability), defined in Eq. 9 as f_B(t) := min(exp(-\tau_B(t)/\alpha), exp(-(\tau_B(t)-\tau_0)/\beta)), where \alpha and \beta set the decay rates of the two exponential pieces and \tau_0 shifts the second piece (\tau_B(t) itself is not defined in words in the saved text). \Delta T_B is the block's cost, the additional prefilling time if it is evicted, approximated from a fitted linear latency model T(l_1,q_1,l_2,q_2) as \Delta T_B = 2k_5·(l_1+q_1)+(k_2-k_3+k_5), where (l_1+q_1) is the block's positional index (number of preceding blocks) and the k's are coefficients fitted on about 1.1K profiling instances (l_1,q_1,l_2,q_2 refer to Figure 6 and are not defined in words in the text). In the implementation (Algorithm 1) the two exponential pieces are kept in two balanced trees and the evicted block is \argmin\{B_1.w_1, \lambda × B_2.w_2\}, where \lambda (initially 1) is adjusted online from the average lifespan \tau of cache blocks in a sliding window as \lambda_{new} <- \exp((\tau-\tau_0)/\beta - \tau/\alpha) (Eq. 10). Reported metrics are average TTFT and TPOT plus request- and block-level hit rates; for agent workloads, average and P90 job latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 202 of the saved text | 202 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | AsymCache aligns KV cache residency decisions with GPU attention-kernel performance: the evictor ranks blocks by frequency times position-dependent recomputation cost (keeping both shared prefixes and costly later blocks, dropping less useful middle segments) with a piecewise exponential frequency function that allows logarithmic-time eviction; a Multi-Segment Attention kernel computes attention over non-contiguous cached segments in one kernel call; and a chunking scheduler adapts prefill chunk sizes. For agent workloads it uses a shorter lifespan turning point and a tool-call correction factor to keep the current turn's cache. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 120 of the saved text | 120 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Serving latency: TTFT reduced by up to 1.90–2.03x and TPOT by 1.62–1.71x over the latest baselines (the evaluated baselines are vLLM-LRU, Max-score and Pensieve+MSA), and, when integrated into the agent serving system Continuum, average job latency further reduced by up to 18.1% relative to Continuum alone. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = time-to-first-token (TTFT), time-per-output-token (TPOT), average job latency / P90 tail job latency (agent workloads), prefill latency / additional prefilling time, recomputation cost, expected (attention) latency, cache hit rate, GPU memory / memory footprint, throughput / GPU utilization, kernel launch and host synchronization overheads, eviction time complexity (O(1), logarithmic, linear), control-plane (eviction) overhead per request (~200 ms for O(n) vs ~2 ms for O(log n)), head-of-line blocking / tail latency (chunked prefill); agent kind = LLM serving system (lossless KV cache management for LLM inference, system named AsymCache); agentic workloads (tool-calling agent sessions) are one application, evaluated by integrating into the agent serving system Continuum; position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00023v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Wed, 8 May 2024 06:30:58 UTC

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Prompts are long and partially shared across requests, and existing KV-cache reuse is confined to a single-GPU optimization, while production LLM serving systems are distributed; current distributed serving systems are not prompt-cache-aware and distribute computation load equally across GPUs, which could send requests with shared prefixes to different GPUs, causing KV computation at all of them that could otherwise be avoided if prefixes were cached and reused on the same GPU. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 64 of the saved text | 64 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Load balancing and prefix reuse conflict: equal load distribution could send shared-prefix requests to different GPUs and cause avoidable KV computation there (line 64), while a naive solution that always sends shared-prefix requests to the same GPU would result in imbalanced loads and low overall GPU utilization, because the GPU first serving a popular prefix accumulates a huge load of new requests (line 65); in addition, the variations in prompt-sharing features and request arrival patterns make it challenging to build an efficient distributed serving system (line 95), and the Azure trace shows requests arriving at varying speeds over time and across LLM usages (line 68). Prompts are 37x to 2494x longer than generated sequences in the five studied workloads (line 67), and long prompts with short generations imply that the prefill phase significantly outweighs decoding (line 60). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 65 of the saved text | 65 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The system aims at high serving throughput and low average and tail request latency (line 78). The E2 scheduler, when exploring and all GPUs have relatively balanced prefill-decoding loads, assigns request R_k to the GPU with the lowest total cost L_{i}+M_{i}+P_{i}, all expressed as GPU computation time: L_{i}=\sum_{r\in W}(PT_{r}+DT_{r}) is GPU_i's load over the requests W in a recent window H (default 3 minutes), with PT_r the prefill time estimated by regression from the tokens of R_r not matching prefixes on GPU_i and DT_r the decoding time estimated from the average output length in H; M_{i}=\sum_{j\in E}PT_{j}\times N_{j} is the eviction cost, with E the set of tree nodes to evict, PT_j the prefill time for node j's length and N_j the number of requests sharing node j in H over the total requests on GPU_i in H; P_i is the prefill time of the missed tokens of R_k. E2 exploits (sends to the GPU caching the longest matched prefix, with ties broken by the lightest load) when matched prefix tokens exceed the remaining tokens (lines 115-116). Before the load-cost comparison, a request to be explored is sent to a GPU heavily loaded with decoding-phase units (requests whose prompts are fully cached); this prefill-decoding balancing rule is prioritised over the load-cost comparison (line 144). Post-assignment rules: if the most heavily loaded GPU's load exceeds Th_{bal} times the lightest GPU's load, requests that would exploit the heavy GPU are redirected to the light one until the difference is below Th_{bal} (lines 139-140); a prefix is autoscaled (replicated, subtree split by load) when its average queueing time doubles over H after rebalancing (line 141). Local wait queue: P priority groups by cached-token percentage, with more requests selected per batch from higher-priority groups (lines 155-156). Evaluation metrics: requests per second (serving capacity), average end-to-end request latency (scheduling, queueing, prefill and decoding time) and p99 request latency (line 173). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 134 of the saved text | 134 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A distributed scheduling algorithm, E2 (Exploitation + Exploration), co-designs computation load-balancing and prefix-cache sharing: requests reuse cached prefixes on the same GPU when the saved recomputation exceeds the new computation, and otherwise explore the GPU with the lowest prompt-aware load; this is complemented by load rebalancing and prefix autoscaling, prefill-decoding mixing based on cache hits, and fairness-aware local scheduling. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Preble reports 1.5x to 14.5x lower average latency and 2x to 10x lower p99 latency than the SOTA serving systems (abstract, line 56); in the body the ranges are over data-parallel (round-robin) SGLang on the five workloads with Poisson arrivals, Mistral 7B on two/four A6000 GPUs and Llama-3 70B on eight H100 GPUs (Figure 3; lines 165, 176, 181, 188). The introduction says results are similar against vLLM (line 85), while Appendix C reports less relative improvement with vLLM as the backend (line 611). The Azure-trace experiment (mixed tool-use and video QA on four A6000 GPUs) is described only as significant improvements in average and p99 latency, TTFT and TPOT, with no range (lines 189-193). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 56 of the saved text | 56 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Three limitations of prior approaches: a static tool set of primitive actions (the minimum spanning set to reach any browser state) that costs longer execution times and higher error rates; sequential execution that does not explore the space of schedules such as task parallelism and request hedging; and non-determinism post-plan, where the standard agent loop calls the LM at each step even when no LM call is needed between tool calls; in addition, prior code-action work ignores that many valid code plans exist with different latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Two argmin objectives. Planner (Algorithm 1): among k = 32 valid candidate plans, return argmin over (pi, c) of c, where c is a unitless weighted call count that accumulates C_tool * gamma^d for each tool call and C_eval * gamma^d for each ai_eval (LLM) call at CFG depth d (base weights C_tool = 0.1, C_eval = 10.0; gamma = 10 is a loop-nesting penalty), and a plan is invalid if the tracked state s does not contain a tool's precondition (s is updated with the tool's postconditions); the paper states this cost only ranks plans by expected latency (by number of LLM calls and nesting depth) and does not predict absolute latency. Scheduler (Algorithm 2): minimizes estimated latency. Scheduler (Algorithm 2): return argmin over sigma in {Ser, Par, Hed} of mean latency L-bar_sigma over N_MC Monte Carlo trials, with serial latency S(U_sigma), hedge latency min_{w=1..n} S(U_sigma) + delta_h, and parallel latency S(U_sigma^seq) + max_{w=1..n} S_w(U_sigma,w) + delta_p, where S(U) = sum_{e in U} sum_{i=1}^{count(e)} sample(D_e), U_sigma is the LLM-predicted element usage, count(e) the predicted number of interactions with element e, D_e its learned latency distribution, n the workers (vCPU budget, n = 4 in experiments), N_MC = 1000, and delta_h (5-15 s), delta_p (20-30 s) overheads. | 0 | framing_problem | As AI agents move toward persistent, stateful execution, checkpoint and rollback are becoming essential for recovery, yet their security implications remain largely unexplored: correct rollback does not imply secure recovery, since a faithfully restored checkpoint may resume an execution whose states, assumptions and external effects never coexisted in any valid history. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 65 of the saved text | 65 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Recovery carries forward security-relevant facts (an artifact validated, an operation authorized, an external effect not yet occurred) whose validity depends on state spread across framework components, files and runtimes, nondeterministic decisions and external services, which do not necessarily share the same recovery scope, so a checkpoint's recovery boundary may not cover the full set of security dependencies on which the restored state relies. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 99 of the saved text | 99 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Prevalence of each of five security failures (SF1-SF5) at the execution level: for each task execution, whether a given SF is observed at least once during its execution and rollback, validated by restoring a random checkpoint with the framework's native mechanism and re-executing (for SF4 candidates the post-checkpoint execution is re-executed independently three times, and SF4 is validated when the replay produces a different security-relevant execution path). The formal model writes the recovered configuration as X̂ = ((s_i^{k_i})_{P_i∈K} ⊕ (ρ_j)_{P_j∉K}, W^{t_r}), where P_i are logical processes, s_i^{k_i} their checkpointed local states, K the set of processes covered by checkpoint C_K (its recovery boundary), ρ_j the recovered state of an uncovered process, and W^{t_r} the outside world at rollback time t_r; execution continuity requires security-relevant states, decisions, assumptions and effects to stay jointly consistent with a valid continuous execution history. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1041 of the saved text | 1041 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Characterize existing C/R designs by recovery boundary (framework, workspace, OS/VM state), build a general execution model with partial recovery boundaries and a non-rolling-back outside world, derive five failure modes from it, and detect them with a multi-agent pipeline (collector, analyzer, checker, validator) that reconstructs execution semantics from traces and validates candidates through actual rollback. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | No efficiency gain is claimed; the paper reports that failures are common across 1,735 framework-task executions (347 TerminalBench and AgentBench traces, five frameworks), with SF1 and SF4 in 67.2% and 67.7% of executions and SF5 in 2.3%, and demonstrates three end-to-end attacks (malware-verification bypass, unauthorized mail forwarding, double payment); the detection pipeline reaches 98.7% precision and 99.9% recall under manual validation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1141 of the saved text | 1141 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f238 — Reducing Cost of LLM Agents with Trajectory Reduction

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.23586v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Sun, 28 Sep 2025 02:43:41 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering, 3

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM agents show promising effectiveness on software engineering tasks, but the high computational cost of input tokens caused by ever-growing trajectories is a significant efficiency concern that existing studies and agent products have largely overlooked. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The root cause is the ever-growing trajectory: once the LLM calls a tool, the call and its result stay in the trajectory until the task ends and are included in every subsequent input, so verbose outputs snowball in cost (the paper cites that in September 2025, 99% of Claude 4 Sonnet's daily tokens on OpenRouter were input tokens accumulated in the trajectory); trajectories contain useless, redundant and expired information. Existing token-reduction work targets single-turn tasks, reducing all input tokens at once (so the timing of reduction is an open question for agents), working on natural language rather than structured code, or requiring changes to LLM inference or the model; agent products compact only when the context window is full or the user asks, aiming at robustness rather than efficiency. KV Cache does not remove the need and makes reduction harder, since modifying a token invalidates the cache for all later tokens, and LLM agents given an erase tool often did not reduce their own trajectories despite explicit prompts. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 94 of the saved text | 94 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Efficiency metrics: Keep% = Σ l_reduced / Σ l_orig * 100, the average percentage of trajectory tokens retained by the reflection LLM (l_orig, l_reduced = step lengths before and after reduction in Algorithm 1); I and O, accumulated input and output tokens normalized so the Original baseline has I=1; $ and $+, LLM cost of agent steps and of reflection steps from provider pricing (input tokens with KV Cache discount plus output tokens), normalized so Original has $=1. Performance metrics: Pass% (resolved instances) and Step/PStep (average agent steps over all / resolved instances). Efficiency improves if Keep% is low and I/O/$ fall; performance is unharmed if Pass% does not decrease and Step/PStep does not increase. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 302 of the saved text | 302 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | AgentDiet removes useless, redundant and expired information during execution with a separate LLM-based reflection module called by the outer system rather than by the agent. To control overhead it uses a cost-efficient LLM (GPT-5 mini) and a sliding window: at step s the module may reduce only step s-a, given context from step s-a-b to s; reflection is skipped when step s-a is within a token threshold θ, and a reduction is applied only if it removes more than θ tokens. Because only a fixed recent step is modified, KV Cache entries for earlier steps are preserved. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 87 of the saved text | 87 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the Original Trae Agent without reflection, on two LLMs (Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro) and two benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, Multi-SWE-bench Flash), AgentDiet reduces input tokens by 39.9%-59.7% and total computational cost by 21.1%-35.9% (including reflection overhead) while keeping Pass% comparable (-1.0% to +2.0%). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 87 of the saved text | 87 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = computational cost, input tokens (accumulated input / prompt tokens), output (completion) tokens, LLM cost for agent steps ($) and reflection steps ($+) from pricing, with KV Cache discount, average US$ cost per instance, Keep% (trajectory tokens retained), KV Cache, VRAM and I/O bandwidth, steps (Step, PStep; used as performance-impact metrics), latency (discussed as future work, not measured), trajectory length and accumulated token usage per issue (48.4K tokens in 40 steps; 1.0M accumulated tokens); agent kind = multi-turn LLM agents for software engineering tasks (coding agents), implemented on Trae Agent; position = agent loop (steps, calls, context). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Eq. (1): max over M of [ sum_{m in C'} U^(m / C') ] / K(C'), where M is a context management framework, C the raw session history (instructions, reasoning traces, tool calls, responses), C' = M(C) the optimized runtime context, U^(m / C') the estimated marginal contribution of message m to subsequent agent actions (context utility), and K(C') the serving cost. Eq. (2): K(C') = alpha * /C'_hit/ + /C'_miss/, where C'_hit are tokens served from the prompt cache at discounted rate alpha << 1 and C'_miss tokens incur full pre-fill cost, subject to /C'/ = /C'_hit/ + /C'_miss/. (10): Score = s_safe x (0.80 s_comp + 0.20 s_rob) (safety as a multiplicative gate); PinchBench aggregates task-specific verification checks on deliverables. ## f247 — CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2405.16444v3 · version read: v3 · v1: Sun, 26 May 2024 06:00:17 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the Twentieth European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys 2025)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Context text chunks prepended to a query (e.g. retrieved chunks in RAG) significantly slow down LLM inference because prefill must process the whole input before the first token; the paper tackles one challenge: when an LLM input contains multiple text chunks, how to quickly combine their individually pre-computed KV caches while achieving the same generation quality as the expensive full prefill. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The delay and computation of prefill grow super-linearly with input length. Existing KV-cache reuse does not cover the multi-chunk case: prefix caching only reuses the KV cache of the input prefix (the first chunk), and full KV reuse of non-prefix chunks ignores the cross-attention between a chunk and its preceding chunks, which cannot be precomputed because the preceding chunks are not known in advance, so quality drops. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Goal (Sec. 4, Goal 0, line 230; formalized in Sec. 4.1, line 290): quickly update the precomputed KV cache KV^pre to the new KV cache KV^new such that the attention deviation Δ_attn(A^new_i, A^full_i) on any layer i is minimized. Symbols from the text: i is the layer index and j the token index; KV^full is the KV cache from full KV recompute, KV^pre the pre-computed KV cache, KV^new the CacheBlend-updated KV cache; A_i is the forward attention matrix on layer i (A^full_i for full KV recompute, A^pre_i for full KV reuse, A^new_i with CacheBlend); Δ_attn is the L-2 norm of the difference between A_i and A^full_i; the KV deviation Δ_kv(KV_i, KV^full_i)[j] is the absolute difference between KV_i[j] and KV^full_i[j]. Goal 0 states the speed side only as 'quickly'; the delay side is written as explicit formulas for the loading controller (Sec. 5.1, footnotes 5-6, lines 385-398): T_recompute(r%, LLM, L) = r% × Prefill(LLM, L), with Prefill(LLM, L) profiled offline and L the length of context to be loaded, and T_load(LLM, L, storage_device) = PerTokenKVSize(LLM) × L / Throughput(storage_device); the controller picks r% so that T_recompute equals T_load and then takes the max of r% and r*%, where r*% (15% in practice) is the minimal recompute ratio with negligible quality drop; for storage it uses a storage-cost estimator C_store(LLM, L, T, storage_device) (T = time the KV must be stored) and picks the cheapest device with T_recompute ≥ T_load at a fixed 15% ratio. Recomputing r% of tokens per layer costs r% of full-prefill compute (line 309). Results are reported as TTFT, throughput and quality (F1, Rouge-L). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 290 of the saved text | 290 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | CacheBlend reuses the pre-computed KV caches of all chunks, prefix or not, and in each layer selectively recomputes the KV of only a small fraction of tokens (the high-KV-deviation tokens, chosen by gradual filtering from layer to layer) based on the preceding texts in the specific input, which suffices because attention matrices are sparse. The partial KV update on one layer is pipelined with fetching the next layer's KV cache into GPU memory; the introduction states this adds no inference latency and lets KV caches be stored on slower non-volatile devices (lines 128-130), while Sec. 5 makes this conditional on loading one layer's KV being at least as slow as selective recompute of one layer (line 369) — for Llama-70B on NVMe SSD the loading does not completely hide the recompute delay (lines 373-374) — so a loading controller picks the recompute ratio and storage device. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 118 of the saved text | 118 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | CacheBlend reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 2.2–3.3x and increases inference throughput by 2.8–5x 'without compromising generation quality'. The baseline differs by location: the abstract (line 84) and the evaluation (Fig. 12 caption line 432; takeaways lines 437-438) state the TTFT reduction against full KV recompute, and the evaluation gives throughput 'at the same TTFT' as up to 5x vs full KV recompute and 3.3x vs prefix caching (line 442), while the introduction (line 134) attributes both ranges to a comparison with prefix caching. Against full KV reuse, the introduction reports almost the same TTFT with 0.1–0.2 higher absolute F1 on QA and 0.03–0.25 higher absolute Rouge-L on summarization (line 136); the evaluation instead states a 0.15–0.35 quality improvement over full KV reuse and no more than 0.01–0.03 quality drop vs full KV recompute and prefix caching (line 440). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = prefill delay, time-to-first-token (TTFT), inference throughput, inference delay / inference latency, delay and computation of prefill, prefill overhead, speed, compute overhead (r% of full prefill), KV loading delay, storage cost, recompute ratio / update fraction of tokens; agent kind = LLM serving system (KV-cache reuse inside the LLM inference engine, implemented on vLLM) for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) inputs made of multiple text chunks; not an agent paper; position = model inference/serving (prefill / KV-cache reuse in the LLM serving engine). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f248 — KVCOMM: Online Cross-context KV-cache Communication for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.12872v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Tue, 14 Oct 2025 18:00:01 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Multi-agent LLM systems often suffer substantial overhead from repeated reprocessing of overlapping contexts across agents: every message must be prefilled with the full conversation history, and agents sharing overlapping context (retrieved passages, peer outputs) redundantly recompute KV caches for all input tokens, which the paper defines as the multi-context redundancy issue; with M agents each receiving all peers' messages, prefill complexity scales as O(M^2). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | KV caching is effective for avoiding redundant computation in single-agent settings where prefixes remain unchanged, but it cannot be directly reused in multi-agent scenarios because agent-specific context extensions create diverging prefixes; the paper identifies the core challenge as the offset variance of KV caches across agents — the same shared text incurs vastly different KV deviations under different prefix contexts (line 96). Existing methods (prompt-level reuse, selective recomputation, cache compression, kernel-level optimizations) share a fixed acceleration policy crafted for a particular workload; when the policy fails to model offset variance, cache reuse becomes misaligned, causing either large accuracy drops or a fallback to full recomputation that erodes the speed benefits (line 96; line 148: none of the existing static policies can predict the positional and contextual shifts). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No explicit optimisation objective or loss is written. The stated target is to reduce prefilling latency without sacrificing task performance (line 149); the conclusion calls it a trade-off between prefilling efficiency and system accuracy (line 735). Reported metrics: accuracy (MMLU, GSM8K), Pass@1 (HumanEval), Reuse Rate and TTFT (individual agent TTFT and average TTFT across agents, TTFT speedup). Reuse Rate is defined twice for KVComm: 'the proportion of agents employing the cache reuse scheme' (Sec. 4.1, line 481) and 'the frequency of agents reusing all KV-caches in the whole serving procedure' (Table 1 caption, line 232); for CacheBlend it is the proportion of tokens reusing KV caches (line 232). Eq. (5) is an anchor-prediction criterion (with entropy threshold γ and anchor-pool size V as hyperparameters) and Eqs. (6)-(7) are the offset approximation, not objectives. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 149 of the saved text | 149 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | KVComm treats every reuse attempt as an approximate translation problem: the KV cache of overlapping text becomes reusable under a new prefix once the positional shift and the cache offsets observed for similar samples are known. It keeps an online anchor pool of previously shared samples with their measured offsets under different prefixes, matches the nearest anchors by token-embedding similarity, and adds the interpolated offsets to the base cache (after RoPE re-positioning of keys), so agents skip redundant prefilling; unshareable segments become new anchors. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 98 of the saved text | 98 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Abstract (line 88): KVComm achieves over 70% reuse rate across RAG, math reasoning and collaborative coding workloads 'all without quality degradation', and, when each fully-connected agent receives 1K input tokens with 512 prefix and 512 output tokens in a five-agent setting, up to 7.8x speedup compared to the standard prefill pipeline, reducing TTFT from ~430 ms to ~55 ms; in Table 2 the 7.82x is Agent 5's TTFT speedup while Agent 1 gets 1.11x (lines 515-520, 564-565). Introduction (line 106): ~6.7x average prefill speed-up (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, one H100) and less than 2.5% accuracy drop at 95% reuse rate on 1,319 GSM8K samples with four agents. In the body, 6.72x is the mean TTFT speedup of three agents in the longest setting (1024 prefix, 1024 output tokens), ranging down to 2.24x in the shortest (Table 3, lines 552-553, 567); the ~95% reuse corresponds to the hyperparameter study with γ=0.5 (94.9% reuse, 80.0% vs 82.1% accuracy, Table 6), not the default γ=0.3 (73.4% reuse). Table 1 lists KVComm reuse rates of 69.9% and 67.6% on MMLU with three and five agents, below the abstract's 'over 70%'. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Model- and system-level acceleration (quantization, pruning, distillation) lowers per-call latency but leaves the serial loop untouched (line 106). Parallel execution in turn faces three challenges: the instruction does not specify dependencies between steps, so the system must identify which sub-tasks can run concurrently; concurrent workers may conflict when modifying shared artifacts; and local completion by a worker does not guarantee that the combined result satisfies the original instruction (line 112). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 104 of the saved text | 104 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Prior work sped up tool-calling with parallel and asynchronous execution, but redundant or repeated tool-calling requests remain largely unaddressed; repeated invocations prolong response time and amplify the financial and resource costs of API usage, and conventional cache policies do not work for LLM tool-calling. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 63 of the saved text | 63 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Tool calls sit between two stages of LLM inference and their execution time can be a dominant contributor to end-to-end latency, particularly for remote APIs; tool-calling workloads show substantial redundancy (over 40% of invocations repeated in a movie recommendation dataset); but caching them is hard because cacheability is uncertain (information retrieval vs. state-changing commands), freshness requirements vary widely (a single TTL is unsafe or inefficient), workloads shift rapidly, and LRU/LFU rely on recency or frequency without accounting for the high and uneven cost of tool execution. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Caching value of request r_i (Eq. 2): v_i = λ1·NormLatency_i + λ2·NormCost_i/NormSize_i − λ3·e^(−TTL_i/τ), where each feature is min-max normalised (Eq. 1: NormFeature_i^(j) = (Feature_i^(j) − Feature_min^(j)) / (Feature_max^(j) − Feature_min^(j))), λ1, λ2, λ3 are tunable weights for latency, cost-to-size ratio and TTL-based staleness risk (set to 0.8, 0.2, 0.2), and τ is a smoothing parameter equal to the average lifetime of cached entries. Admission is cast as a multi-armed bandit over feature groups g_i with reward F_i = log(H_i+δ1)·log(L_i+δ2)·log(V_i+δ3) / log(C_i+δ4) (H_i group hit ratio, L_i node level, V_i average caching value, C_i number of times the group was admitted, δ small constants), solved with UCB1 to maximise cumulative reward, selecting the group with the highest UCB_i = F_i + c·sqrt(ln t / N_i) (Eq. 6, Appendix B.2; N_i times group i was selected, t the current round, c an exploration parameter); eviction removes, among the 10% least recently used entries, the one with lowest e_i = log(v_i + h_i + δ5) (h_i hit ratio). Reported metrics are cache hit ratio, total/end-to-end latency, result size and resource cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 175 of the saved text | 175 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | ToolCaching intercepts tool-call requests and serves repeated ones from a cache: an LLM prompt extracts semantic features (request type, parameter category, TTL) that feed rule-based cacheability checks (no COMMAND requests, no TTL <= 60 s); for cacheable requests, system features (result size, system latency, resource cost) and TTL give a caching value, while access count, associated users and hit ratio drive grouping, admission and eviction; the VAAC algorithm combines bandit-based admission over feature groups (v-CACA) with value-aware LRU eviction (v-LRU). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 63 of the saved text | 63 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Cache hit ratio up to 11% higher than CACA and LRU across most cache sizes and synthetic workloads; end-to-end latency up to 34% lower than the LLM Compiler framework without caching on Movie Recommendation (Table 4: 16.2 s to 10.7 s at a cache size of 100% of calls, labelled 1.34x in the table) and up to 23% lower on ParallelQA (15.9 s to 12.18 s). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f253 — Budget-Aware Agentic Routing via Boundary-Guided Training

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21227v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Wed, 4 Feb 2026 07:39:27 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | As LLMs become agents executing long-horizon workflows, invoking a high-capability model at every step becomes economically unsustainable, while using a cheap model everywhere can fail on the few critical steps where advanced reasoning is necessary; the paper studies Budget-Aware Agentic Routing, choosing between a cheap and an expensive model at each step to maximise task success under compute costs, both as a soft cost-success trade-off and under strict per-task budgets. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Unlike single-turn routing, agentic routing is sequential and path-dependent: early mistakes compound, feedback is often only at the end of the episode so credit assignment over long horizons is hard, and deployments often demand strict per-task spending limits; directly training for hard budgets with RL is unstable (discontinuous objective, high-variance gradients), and vanilla GRPO under sparse terminal rewards may reinforce the cheapest failure mode and drift toward a degenerate 'always-small' policy. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Soft-budget routing (Eq. 1): J_soft(θ) = E_{τ~π_θ}[ I(success(τ)) − λ Σ_{t=0}^{/τ/−1} c(a_t) ], where I(success(τ)) ∈ {0,1} is a sparse terminal indicator of task success, λ >= 0 is a Lagrange multiplier whose variation traces the efficiency frontier, a_t ∈ {M_small, M_large} is the model chosen at step t from history state s_t, and c(a_t) > 0 is its scalar cost. Hard-budget routing (Eq. 2, a CMDP): max_π E_{τ~π}[I(success(τ))] s.t. Σ_{t} c(a_t) <= B_max, with B_max the maximum allowable per-task budget (e.g. API cost limit or number of large-model calls). The RL training reward (Eq. 5) is R(τ,x) = (r_success + r_hard) − λ·C_norm(τ,x), with r_hard a bonus only for Hard tasks and C_norm = clip((C(τ) − C_min(x)) / (C_max(x) − C_min(x) + ε), 0, 1), where C(τ) = Σ_t c(a_t) and C_min, C_max are the min and max of the always-small and always-large trajectory costs. Hard-task SFT expert (Eqs. 3-4): sample N trajectories with P(a_t = M_large) = p_k = k/N and take τ* = argmin over successful trajectories of Σ_t c(a_t). BoPO advantage (Eq. 7): A(τ_g) = (R(τ_g,x) − max(μ_group, R(τ*,x))) / (σ_group + ε); policy objective (Eq. 8): J_BoPO(θ) = E[(1/G) Σ_g (π_θ(τ_g)/π_old(τ_g)·A(τ_g) − β_KL·D_KL(π_θ // π_ref))], π_ref the SFT model (G = 8, β = 0.04, r_success = 1.0, r_hard = 0.5, λ ∈ {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}; Appendix D). Budget-Constrained Decoding (Eq. 9): with residual budget b_t = B_max − Σ_{i<t} c(a_i), force M_small if c(M_large) >= b_t, else follow π_θ; in experiments B_max is the number K ∈ {5,10,15} of large-model calls. Reported metrics: Success Rate (average episode score 0-100 on SciWorld, binary success on ALFWorld, Task Goal Completion on AppWorld; Appendix D) and Average Cost E_τ[Σ_t c(a_t)] in dollars; hard-budget runs also report Use% = Avg.#LargeCalls/K. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Boundary-Guided Training anchors learning to two boundary policies (always-small and always-large): tasks are profiled as Easy/Hard/Intractable, SFT data use the small-model trajectory for Easy and Intractable tasks and the cheapest successful stratified-sampling trajectory for Hard ones (BoSFT), and BoPO adds a boundary-relative reward and a reference-guided advantage so the router pays for the large model only when it is likely to change the outcome; strict budgets are enforced at inference by Budget-Constrained Decoding. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 71 of the saved text | 71 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | BoPO pushes the success-rate vs. average-cost frontier beyond single-turn, cascading, zero-shot GPT-5 and vanilla RL routers on all three benchmarks, matching always-large success at a fraction of the cost (e.g. >63% success on ALFWorld at $0.125 per task). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = cost / computational cost, cost-success frontier / efficiency frontier (Pareto curve of success rate vs. average cost), Average Cost: expected monetary cost per task in dollars (OpenAI list prices per 1M input/output tokens), per-task budget, spending limits, budget caps, number of large-model calls per task (hard budget K; Use% = Avg.#LargeCalls/K), compute, estimated end-to-end latency of the router (tokens/s throughput model); agent kind = LLM agents running long-horizon multi-step workflows (ReAct-style agents on SciWorld, ALFWorld and AppWorld); the paper trains a step-wise model router (Qwen2.5-1.5B) that chooses between a cheap model (GPT-4.1 mini) and an expensive model (GPT-4.1) at each step; position = agent loop (steps, calls, context): which LLM serves each step, with the router trained by SFT and RL. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | No overall task objective formula. Training: RFT of the Planner with GRPO uses a per-step binary reward R_total = R_format + R_filtering + R_grounding, where R_format checks that the generated low-level sub-task has the correct format, R_filtering checks that the filter's scoring program keeps the ground-truth element in the pruned list, and R_grounding checks final sub-task success of the Action Grounder's output (1 success, 0 failure). Appendix D.2 writes it as R_t = R_fmt + α·R_filtering_success + β·R_grounding_success with α = β = 1, gated step-wise (failure at one stage gives zero for all later stages; filtering success = ground-truth element in the top-20 list; grounding success = exact match of action type, element and parameters), and uses the GRPO advantage A_i = (r_i − mean(r)) / (std(r) + ε_std). | 3 | framing_solution | Because the Plan stage incurs the majority of LLM compute cost and is often repeated (within or across workflows), APC, after a cache-miss execution completes successfully with correct outputs, extracts a structured plan template from the execution log (rule-based filter plus lightweight-LLM filter that removes context-specific elements), matches new requests to cached plans via keyword extraction and exact keyword match, and on a hit uses a small planner LM to adapt the template with task-specific context instead of calling the expensive large planner LM. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 100 of the saved text | 100 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

On GAIA with the Open Deep Research agent, cost falls from $69.02 to $16.27 (76.42%) with accuracy 37.58% to 36.97%. | 1 | framing_challenge | Two challenges: programming LM programs is tedious and difficult due to LLM non-determinism; and executing LM programs is inefficient due to redundant computation and memory usage, because inference engines are optimised without knowledge of the workload: the KV cache of a request is discarded after it completes, so it cannot be reused across calls sharing a common prefix, and constrained decoding only decodes one token at a time. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The runtime's cache-aware scheduling targets the cache hit rate, defined as number of cached prompt tokens / number of prompt tokens (line 187); Theorem 3.1 states that visiting the radix tree of a batch of requests in depth-first search order (equivalently longest-shared-prefix-first) achieves an optimal cache hit rate when cache size is at least the maximum request length. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 249 of the saved text | 249 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | The core idea is to systematically exploit the multi-call structure in LM programs: a frontend with generation and parallelism primitives, and a runtime with RadixAttention (keeping the KV cache of all requests in a radix tree with LRU eviction and cache-aware scheduling so it is reused across calls), a compressed finite state machine that decodes multiple tokens at once for constrained outputs, and API speculative execution for API-only models. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 89 of the saved text | 89 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Compared with Guidance, vLLM and LMQL, SGLang improves throughput by up to 6.4x and reduces latency by up to 3.7x on open-weight models (results in Figs. 5-6, captioned as Llama-7B; 7B models run on a single A10G GPU; lines 226, 250-253), across workloads including agent control (ReAct and generative-agent traces replayed), logical reasoning, few-shot benchmarks, JSON decoding, RAG and multi-turn chat; Guidance and LMQL are excluded from some benchmarks (line 260). Throughput is maximum programs per second with a large batch and latency is average single-program latency without batching (line 249). API speculative execution reduces input-token cost by about threefold on one GPT-3.5 prompt that extracts three fields (line 281). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 253 of the saved text | 253 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Recent GUI agents replicate the R1-Zero paradigm (online RL with explicit chain-of-thought before object grounding); the paper analyses the three components of that training pipeline (input design, output evaluation, policy update) and finds that each reveals distinct challenges arising from blindly applying general-purpose RL without adapting to GUI grounding tasks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Three named challenges: grounding is harmed by longer reasoning due to grounding's reliance on image tokens (longer chains lower grounding accuracy); Hit-based and IoU-based rewards induce opposite, box-size-sensitive reward hacking (Hit favours smaller boxes, IoU larger boxes); and the GRPO objective biases the policy toward simpler examples: a response-level length bias from dividing by /o_i/ (longer incorrect and shorter correct responses) and a question-level difficulty bias (described as treating all samples equally in line 71; Sec. 3.3 notes, citing [25], that dividing by the reward std can make the model focus disproportionately on harder or easier samples), so online RL overfits easy examples and under-optimises harder cases (abstract). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Training objective: the GRPO objective J_GRPO(pi_theta) (Eq. 2: expectation over queries q ~ p_Q and N responses o_i sampled from pi_theta_old, of (1/N) sum_i (1//o_i/) sum_t min[ratio * A_hat_{i,t}, clip(ratio, 1-epsilon, 1+epsilon) * A_hat_{i,t}], where ratio = pi_theta(o_{i,t}/q, o_{i,<t}) / pi_theta_old(o_{i,t}/q, o_{i,<t}), t is the token index and epsilon bounds deviation from the old policy), with the advantage A_i = (r_i - mean(r_1..r_N)) / std(r_1..r_N) (Eq. 1). GUI-G1 replaces /o_i/ with a constant Max_Tokens and multiplies the objective by a difficulty coefficient w_q = 0.5 + (1/lambda_q - min_i 1/lambda_i) / (max_i 1/lambda_i - min_i 1/lambda_i), where lambda_q in (0,1] is the sample's relative box size (Sec. 3.3 uses the relative box size of the target as the difficulty proxy; the only written formula, Appendix C.2, defines relative box size for the predicted box as (y2_hat + x2_hat - y1_hat - x1_hat) / (IMAGE_WIDTH + IMAGE_HEIGHT)); the reward is R_Hit + alpha R_IoU + beta R_Box, with R_Hit = 1((x_p, y_p) in B_gt) (predicted box centre inside the ground-truth box), R_IoU = IoU(B_pred, B_gt), R_Box = 4 / (x_p1 + x_p2 + y_p1 + y_p2) with x_p1 = 1 / (1 - /x1_hat - x1/ / image width) and similar terms, and alpha, beta tunable hyperparameters set to alpha = 0.25 and beta = 0.125 (line 427); no KL-divergence regularization is applied in training (line 427). Evaluation target: grounding accuracy on ScreenSpot and ScreenSpot-Pro. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 205 of the saved text | 205 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Each diagnosed issue gets a targeted fix: a Fast Thinking Template that makes the policy answer directly (no intermediate reasoning) during training; a box-size-based reward R_Box added to the Hit and IoU rewards to counter size-driven reward hacking; and a revised GRPO objective without length normalization plus a per-sample difficulty coefficient from relative box size so harder samples receive larger gradients. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 72 of the saved text | 72 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | GUI-G1-3B, trained on about 17K public grounding samples, reaches 90.3% accuracy on ScreenSpot and 37.1% on ScreenSpot-Pro; the paper claims it surpasses all prior models of similar size and the previous best R1-style agent InfiGUI-R1-3B (87.5% on ScreenSpot, 35.7% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 32K samples), and outperforms the larger UI-TARS-7B on ScreenSpot-Pro (35.7%; UI-TARS-7B is not in the ScreenSpot table), while requiring less data, fewer output tokens (about one-third of InfiGUI-R1-3B's average per example on ScreenSpot: 37-39 vs 107-114, Appendix D.2 Table 7) and fewer training stages. | 0 | framing_problem | Coding agents are rapidly becoming a major application of agentic LLMs, but serving them efficiently remains challenging; progress requires understanding real workload patterns, yet the data needed for such analysis is largely absent: existing public traces and benchmarks do not capture real, day-to-day coding-agent usage across multiple agents and model families for serving-system analysis. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 80 of the saved text | 80 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | From a systems perspective, contexts grow over sessions, SLOs are tight, and repeated tool calling pressures both the tool-serving infrastructure and the LLM-serving engines; understanding these workload characteristics is a prerequisite for efficient serving, but serving traces (Mooncake, Splitwise) lack multi-step tool-call behavior and capability benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench) capture isolated, narrowly scoped tasks rather than long sessions with accumulated context and human-paced gaps. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 85 of the saved text | 85 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | none stated as an optimisation objective (the paper characterizes a workload and does not optimise a target). It defines measurement metrics with formulas: per-step input I is decomposed into prefix tokens P (history read from the prefix cache) and append tokens A (user messages, tool results and tokens introduced by prefix-cache misses), mapped from provider fields (Claude: P = cache_read_input_tokens, A = input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens; Codex: P = cached_input_tokens, A = input_tokens_total - cached_input_tokens), with O = provider-reported output tokens including reasoning (Section 3.2, lines 287-313). Normalized decode speed s_norm = O / (t_last - t_input), where t_input = latest input-event timestamp (user_message or tool_result) before the first model output and t_last = last model-output timestamp (reasoning, text or tool_call); this is an end-to-end trace speed that includes TTFT, reasoning, visible output emission and trace logging effects (lines 886-890). For Codex steps: s_pure_decode = O_visible / (t_visible - t_reason), l-hat_pure_decode = sum(t_visible - t_reason) / sum(O_visible), and residual TTFT-hat = (t_reason - t_input) - O_reason * l-hat_pure_decode, with O_reason = reasoning tokens, O_visible = O - O_reason (lines 891-902). Codex tool-call overhead R = max(0, T_e2e - T_int), trace-observed end-to-end tool span minus runner-reported internal execution time (line 933). Prefix cache hit rate is token-weighted (Table 11). Prefill amplification factor = total prefilled (append) tokens / irreducible fresh tokens, equivalently 1/(fresh % of append), where fresh tokens = per-step context growth minus prior output tokens (lines 1012, 1078-1079). KV storage ratio of suspended to active-decoding requests R = (T-hat_human + T-hat_tool) / T_generation, with human and tool times capped by the eviction time (lines 1081-1083). The consumer-side upper-bound saving caps a user-initiated step's append tokens at max(0, L_S - L_P), L = prefix + append tokens (line 1089). Costs are computed from published API pricing per token category (append, prefix, output; Table 6). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 886 of the saved text | 886 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Fixed prompts predefine what to extract and how to update memory instead of adapting to the downstream agent, and in software-engineering agents long-horizon, tool-driven trajectories contain dense and heterogeneous feedback, making it difficult to separate reusable procedural knowledge from task-specific or accidental details. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The downstream objective is \displaystyle\max_{\theta} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau,x^{\prime}}\!\left[R_{\mathrm{task}}\!\left(\pi(x^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{B}^{\prime})\right)\right], with \displaystyle u=M_{\theta}(\tau,\mathcal{C}),\quad\mathcal{B}^{\prime}=\mathrm{Update}(\mathcal{B},u). Here \theta parameterizes the skill-management policy M_{\theta}, \pi is the frozen coding policy, \tau=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T},y) is a trajectory of observations o, actions a and outcome y over T steps, x^{\prime} is a future task, R_{\mathrm{task}} its downstream task performance, \mathcal{B}=\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} is a bank of N skills, \mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{B} its relevant context, and u=(a,z) an operation type and its content. Supervised warmup minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(q,u^{\ast})}\log M_{\theta}(u^{\ast}\mid q). Here q=(\tau,\tilde{s},\mathcal{C}) contains evidence, an optional candidate/existing skill and retrieved similar skills; u^{\ast} is the teacher operation target. For skill-output operations the RL reward is R(u;q)=\lambda R_{Q}(u;q)+R_{A}(u;\tau^{u}_{\pi})R_{E}(u;x_{u},\pi). R_{Q}\in[0,1] is rubric-based quality, \lambda is its weight, R_{A}\in[0,1] measures whether the rollout follows the skill, and R_{E}(u;x_{u},\pi)=V(\tau^{u}_{\pi})-b_{\pi}(x_{u}). The baseline is b_{\pi}(x_{u})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}V(\tau_{\pi,i}^{0}),\quad\tau_{\pi,i}^{0}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{u}). Here x_{u} is a reverse-retrieved training task, V\in[0,1] is the verifier score, \tau^{u}_{\pi} is the skill-conditioned rollout, and \tau_{\pi,i}^{0} is the i-th of n no-skill rollouts. Skip/add/drop operations use only quality reward at a higher weight. Policy optimization minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\left[\min(\rho_{j}\hat{A}_{j},\bar{\rho}_{j}\hat{A}_{j})-\beta D_{j}\right]. G is the number of sampled operations u_{j} for prompt q; \rho_{j}=M_{\theta}(u_{j}\mid q)/M_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(u_{j}\mid q) compares current and old policy probabilities, \bar{\rho}_{j}=\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{j},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon), and \hat{A}_{j}=(R_{j}-\mu_{R})/(\sigma_{R}+\epsilon_{A}) is the group-normalized advantage. R_{j} is the operation reward; \mu_{R} and \sigma_{R} are its group mean and standard deviation; \epsilon defines the clipping interval and \epsilon_{A} is the denominator offset; D_{j} is the KL penalty to the reference model, weighted by \beta. Evaluation reports task pass rate, average issue count for EnvBench, and average reasoning steps on the common subset solved by all methods within each benchmark and downstream-policy setting, with macro-average success/steps across benchmarks; skill-bank size is also reported. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 106 of the saved text | 106 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Node-prompt optimization is complicated by prompts affecting how prompts on connected nodes operate. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 184 of the saved text | 184 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Edge optimization solves \max_{\mathcal{E}}u_{\tau}(G_{\mathcal{E}}), where \tau is the task, u_{\tau} maps a candidate graph to a real-valued task utility, \mathcal{E} selects additional inter-agent edges from d potential edges, and G_{\mathcal{E}} is the resulting composite graph, restricted to a DAG. Equation (1) reformulates this as \argmax_{\theta\in\Theta}\E_{G^{\prime}\sim D_{\theta}}[u_{\tau}(G^{\prime})], with D_{\theta} a distribution over feasible DAGs, \Theta the feasible real-valued parameter set, and \theta_i the inclusion probability for potential edge e_i when it does not create a cycle; REINFORCE optimizes the distribution. Node optimization applies I(h_n,p_n,d_n) to history h_n, current prompt p_n and function description d_n. For HumanEval, the explicit prompt-selection rule is i=\argmax_{i\in\{1,2\}}\sum_{z\in Z}\mathbbm{1}_{z}(f_{n}^{p_{n}^{i}}(z,q_{z})): Z is the last ten inputs of node n on first-seen problems, q_z the original graph input associated with z, f_n the program-generating routine, p_n^1 the retained demonstrations and p_n^2 a sampled augmented set, and \mathbbm{1}_z tests whether the generated program passes the unit tests stated in z. | 1 | framing_challenge | Three deployment dimensions that static evaluation misses: (D1) unbounded streams, where accumulating history must be compressed by a single-agent evolver into a finite context window; (D2) task heterogeneity, where a static dense harness is deployed with no solve-time adaptation; (D3) distributional non-stationarity, where the harness drifts out of fit for new tasks. | 2 | framing_objective | Harness construction minimizes regret against an oracle: V(C,x_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{t},C)}[r(a_{t},y(x_{t}))], V(\mathcal{H}_{t},x_{t})\,:=\,\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\,:\,/C/\leq K\end{subarray}}V(C,x_{t}), and \text{Regret}(\varphi,x_{t})=V(\mathcal{H}_{t},x_{t})-V(\varphi(\mathcal{H}_{t}),x_{t})\geq 0. Here x_{t} is the incoming task, y(x_{t}) its fixed ground truth, a_{t} the solver action, \pi the harness-conditioned LLM policy, r its reward, C the harness, K its capacity budget, \mathcal{H}_{t}=\{(x_{i},r_{i},\tau_{i})\}_{i=1}^{t-1} the prior tasks, optionally realized rewards and solving trajectories, and \varphi the evolver. The decomposition is \mathbb{E}_{x_{t}}[\text{Regret}(\varphi,x_{t})]=L_{\text{evo}}(\Phi)+L_{\text{adapt}}(\varphi), where \Phi is the evolver class, L_{\text{evo}} is its capability gap to the full-history ceiling, and L_{\text{adapt}} is the gap between the task-conditioned optimal harness C^{*}_{\Phi}(x_{t}) and the harness committed before observing x_{t}. PolyBench metrics are \mathrm{Coverage}=\tfrac{/\mathcal{T}/}{N}, \mathrm{Acc}=100\cdot\tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}s_{i}, \mathrm{CWR}=100\cdot\tfrac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}g_{i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}b_{i}}, and \mathrm{Return}=\mathrm{Coverage}\cdot\mathrm{CWR}; N is all markets, \mathcal{T} executed trades excluding gated, empty and Skip decisions, s_{i} trade correctness, b_{i} confidence-weighted investment, and g_{i} realized profit. | 1 | framing_challenge | Dependence on a fixed evaluator constrains self-improvement when the target task has no direct benchmark (paper writing, proof writing), when evaluation is slow or weakly informative, and when static benchmarks saturate or become vulnerable to reward hacking; changing the utility during search would otherwise break the fixed-criterion assumption behind prior self-improvement guarantees. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 58 of the saved text | 58 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Self-improvement searches an archive T𝑡 until the search evaluation budget 𝐵 is exhausted. Node outcomes 𝑜 ∈ {0, 1} accumulate successes 𝑆 𝑎 and failures 𝐹𝑎. The search utility is clade metaproductivity (CMP), the pooled success fraction over the subtree 𝐶 (𝑎): 𝑛𝐶 success (𝑎) / (𝑛𝐶 success (𝑎) + 𝑛𝐶 failure (𝑎)), where these counts pool all successes/failures in the clade; Thompson sampling selects nodes. Final selection uses 𝐵𝐵 𝜖 (𝑎) = 𝐼 𝜖−1 (1 + 𝑆 𝑎 , 1 + 𝐹𝑎 ) ∈ [0, 1], where 𝜖 ∈ (0, 1) is a confidence level and 𝐼 𝜖−1 is the inverse regularized incomplete Beta function (the posterior 𝜖-quantile). Agent utility 𝑈 𝒋 (𝑎) averages 𝑝 𝑟 , 𝒋 (𝑎) uniformly over roles R, and each role rate averages 𝑝 𝑟 ,𝑑, 𝒋 (𝑎) uniformly over its task set D𝑟; the latter is the expected binary success rate of node 𝑎 on task 𝑑 for role 𝑟 under evaluator-epoch vector 𝒋. Thus both averages are normalized by their respective set sizes; the saved PDF text splits/corrupts their fraction and summation layout. Evaluation reports held-out Polyglot pass rate; writer acceptance averaged over a fixed four-reviewer panel; prover mean Score (0–7), Pass@6 (at least 6 of 7) and Pass@7 (full credit); and grader exact-match accuracy and normalized mean absolute error on IMO-GradingBench. Search cost is blended tokens (input plus output weighted at 5× input cost), counting generation and evaluation calls, measured when the selected agent first attains its highest best-belief score. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 212 of the saved text | 212 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Controlled utility evolution freezes each evaluator slot within an epoch, allowing stationary within-epoch search; task agents and challenger evaluators share an evolvable workspace. At a replacement checkpoint, a slot compares challengers and incumbent by the ground-truth-anchor 𝜖-best-belief score and freezes the largest score for the next epoch, with ties favoring the incumbent. It then selectively erases utility records dependent on the displaced evaluator. This preserves the conditions for per-epoch self-improvement guarantees while allowing the objective to change across epochs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 17 of the saved text | 17 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The three \lambda coefficients are loss hyperparameters. \mathcal{L}_{\text{MLE}}=-\log P(X_{j}^{t+1}/Pa_{\mathcal{G}_{u}}(X_{j})) is the negative log-likelihood of next-state variable X_{j}^{t+1} conditional on its parent set Pa_{\mathcal{G}_{u}}(X_{j}) in the subgraph for meta state u. \mathcal{L}_{\text{sparse}}=\/\hat{M}_{\theta}\/_{1} is the L1 norm of the causal skeleton probability matrix. The codebook loss is \mathcal{L}_{\text{quantization}}=\/\text{sg}(E_{\phi}(X))-z_{u}\/_{2}^{2}+\beta\/\text{sg}(z_{u})-E_{\phi}(X))\/_{2}^{2} (copied as printed, including its unmatched parenthesis); E_{\phi} encodes observed state X, z_{u} is the prototype for meta state u, \text{sg} is stop-gradient, and \beta weights the commitment term. ## f315 — Planning to Explore: Curiosity-Driven Planning for LLM Test Generation

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.05159v1 · version read: arXiv 2604.05159v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2026-04-06
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Current LLM-based test generation maximizes immediate coverage gain (greedy), which plateaus on code where reaching deep branches requires setup steps that individually yield zero new coverage. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 83 of the saved text | 83 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Deep branches sit behind 'corridors' (import chains, class initialization, validation gates) that yield zero immediate coverage; greedy methods generate tests independently without learning from previous executions or reasoning about what remains unexplored, so they ignore corridors; the exact curiosity Q-value is intractable (exponential in the planning horizon). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 92 of the saved text | 92 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The goal is to choose tests so cumulative branch coverage grows as quickly as possible. The Bayesian exploration objective selects the action maximizing q(h,a)=\tilde{g}(a\mid h)+\gamma\cdot\mathbb{E}_{o\mid h,a}[v(hao)], with \tilde{g}(a\mid h)=I(O;\Theta\mid h,a) and v(h)=\max_{a}q(h,a). Here h is the history of test/coverage-result pairs, a is a test plan, o is its observed branch coverage, hao is the history after a and o, \Theta is the unknown program branch-reachability structure, I is mutual information between observation O and \Theta conditional on h and a, v is the curiosity value, and \gamma is a discount factor. The practical heuristic is Q=\hat{g}+\gamma\cdot\hat{v}: \hat{g} predicts new branches and \hat{v} additional branches made reachable for future tests, both on a 0–50 scale; experiments use \gamma{=}0.5. The main metric is branch coverage, the cumulative number of unique branches executed across all test scripts, under an equal number of executions N{=}24. Additional metrics are line coverage and pass rate (the fraction of generated scripts executing without error). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 111 of the saved text | 111 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Feed an evolving coverage map (proxy posterior of what has been discovered) back to the LLM, generate K diverse candidate multi-step test plans, and select the plan with the highest LLM-estimated curiosity Q-value, so that plans that invest in setup with high future reachability are chosen over surface-level ones. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 83 of the saved text | 83 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the Greedy selection baseline at the same 24 test-script executions, the abstract and introduction report that CovQValue achieves 51–77% higher branch coverage on TestGenEval Lite (140 files, excluding scikit-learn), winning on 77–84% of targets, and 40-74% higher branch coverage on RepoExploreBench (93 modules from 9 Python packages). The ranges span Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.4 Mini, and Mistral Large 3; the execution budget is equalized, but total LLM calls are not. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 83 of the saved text | 83 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = execution budget, number of test script executions, Q-value scoring calls per round, total LLM calls, feedback frequency, scoring cost, planning horizon, execution steps, plan length; agent kind = LLM-based iterative test-generation agent (coding agent that generates and executes test scripts against a program); position = improvement loop (learning, search, memory). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | The assistant aims to maximize task reward R_{t} for the user's task \mathcal{T}_{U}, iterating until checker validation or limit N. Section 3.1.3 gives the explicit evolutionary objective \mathcal{G}^{t+1}=(\mathcal{A}^{t+1},\mathcal{D}^{t+1}),\quad\mathcal{D}^{t+1}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{D}_{t}\in\Delta}\sum_{i\in I_{t}}L_{D}\left(\mathcal{D}_{t};f_{t}^{i},\pi_{\theta}^{t}\right). Here t indexes iterations, \mathcal{G}^{t+1} combines updated memory-optimization mechanisms \mathcal{A}^{t+1} and model self-adjustments \mathcal{D}^{t+1}; L_{D} is a self-adjustment MSE loss, f_{t}^{i} checker feedback in iteration i, and \pi_{\theta}^{t} the assistant policy with parameters \theta. The minimization domain \Delta and feedback-sum index set I_{t} are not further defined in that passage. The printed policy update is \theta^{t+1}=\phi\bigl(\theta^{t},\mathcal{G}^{t+1}\bigr)=\theta^{t}+\alpha\nabla_{\theta}\Bigl[\lambda_{A}L_{A}\bigl(\theta^{t},\mathcal{A}^{t+1}\bigr)+\lambda_{D}L_{D}\bigl(\theta^{t},\mathcal{D}^{t+1}\bigr)\Bigr]. Here \phi denotes the update, \alpha scales the gradient \nabla_{\theta}, L_{A} is the memory-optimization MSE loss, and \lambda_{A},\lambda_{D}\geq 0 weight the two losses; the paper prints a plus sign. Appendix A.1 gives the separate memory objective \max\sum_{t}M_{t}\cdot S(I_{t}),\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{t}M_{t}\leq C, with S(I_{t})=\frac{H(I_{t})}{f(t)}. In this memory formulation, I_{t} is information received at time t, H(I_{t}) its information entropy, f(t) the forgetting curve, S(I_{t}) its retention strength, M_{t}\in\{0,1\} whether it is retained, and C the total memory capacity. Evaluation uses AgentBench task scores; Precision, Recall, and F1 for LCC and RepoBench-P; answer F1 for HotpotQA and TriviaQA long-text tasks; and QA accuracy, latency (ms), and memory usage (MB) for the RAG-agent comparison.
