| 1 | framing_challenge | Prevailing search methods such as MCTS treat trajectories as independent entities, ignoring interdependence among trajectories, and lack search-space diversity: even with varied temperatures or prompts, probabilistic language models gravitate to high-probability patterns and converge on structurally similar trajectories, which leads to redundant reasoning and suboptimal, homogeneous outcomes. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 36 of the saved text | 36 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Find an optimal policy π ∗ = arg maxπ Et∼T [R(τ π (t), t)], where t is a task from task space T, τ π (t) is the trajectory (s0, a0, ..., sn) generated by policy π : S × T → A, S is the state space, A is the action space, s0 and sn are the initial and final states, ai is the action at step i, and R(τ, t) = R(sn, t) is the final-state reward for task t. Within a task, Reward(τ, t) = w1 · TaskCompletion(τ, t) + w2 · ReasoningQuality(τ ) + w3 · Efficiency(τ ) (Eq. 8). TaskCompletion(τ, t) = AutoEval(τ, t) + λ · ExpertEval(τ, t) (Eq. 9): AutoEval uses rule-based structural validation, ExpertEval is LLM-based solution-quality evaluation, and λ weights ExpertEval. ReasoningQuality evaluates logical coherence, depth and robustness; Efficiency quantifies computational efficiency in reasoning steps and resource utilization; w1, w2 and w3 control the relative importance of these dimensions. The final output is τ ∗ = arg max Reward(τ, t) over τ ∈ΓK (Eq. 11), where ΓK is the final trajectory pool after all evolution cycles. On the 500-issue SWE-bench Verified set, Pass@1 is the percentage resolved on the first attempt, and Pass@5 is the percentage with a correct solution within five attempts. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 156 of the saved text | 156 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Manual harness tuning is time-consuming and hard to scale: the design space is large, evaluating each candidate harness is costly because the agent may need to execute many steps before success or failure becomes clear, and analysing the resulting long-horizon trajectories requires substantial manual effort (existing trace-diagnosis methods also often assume a trace fits in the LLM context window, line 151). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 126 of the saved text | 126 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^{\ast})\sim\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}_{(\tau,\hat{y})\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[\mu(\hat{y},y^{\ast})],\qquad\theta^{\ast}=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}J(\theta): maximize expected task performance. Here x is a task description sampled from task distribution \mathcal{T}, y^{\ast} the gold answer, \tau the execution trace, \hat{y} the final output, P_{\theta} the stochastic execution distribution induced by harness H_{\theta}, and \mu a task-level metric such as accuracy or pass/fail success. The harness parameters are \theta=(\theta_{\text{prompt}},\theta_{\text{tool}},\theta_{\text{middleware}})\in\Theta: instructions/system prompts, tools/interfaces, and runtime control logic. Each execution consumes a rollout; budget K limits explored candidates to \mathcal{V}_{K}\subset\Theta. For finite dataset D, \widehat{J}_{D}(\theta)=\frac{1}{/D/}\sum_{(x_{i},y_{i}^{\ast})\in D}\frac{1}{R_{i}}\sum_{r=1}^{R_{i}}\mu(\hat{y}_{i,r},y_{i}^{\ast}),\qquad(\tau_{i,r},\hat{y}_{i,r})\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i}), where R_{i} is the number of repeated executions of task i. It returns \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{AS}}=\arg\max_{\theta\in\mathcal{V}_{K,\mathrm{dev}}}\widehat{J}_{D_{\mathrm{dev}}}(\theta), where \mathcal{V}_{K,\mathrm{dev}} contains candidates evaluated on development data within budget, then reports \widehat{J}_{D_{\mathrm{test}}}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{AS}}) on held-out test data. | 0 | framing_problem | Deployed LLM agents accumulate interaction trajectories but their behavior typically remains fixed; the paper asks whether a dedicated harness engineer can be post-trained with online reinforcement learning so that improving an existing executable runtime harness from observed target-agent failures becomes a learned capability, instead of relying on fixed prompted editors. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 144 of the saved text | 144 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Prompting strong but fixed models to edit the harness is not reliable (a fixed Self-Refine rule lowers reward on all three benchmarks; frontier editors give unstable or limited gains), and existing harness-optimization pipelines keep the proposer fixed. Training an engineer is hard because the editable runtime spans interdependent execution stages, so unrestricted code edits can break interfaces or produce non-executable behavior, and patch quality can only be judged from the target agent's behavior after the patch is applied (the reward is non-differentiable and observable only after a rerun). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 146 of the saved text | 146 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The engineer reward is \Delta_{B}(P)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(R_{i}^{P}-R_{i}^{0}) and r(B,P)=\Delta_{B}(P) if valid and complete, 0 otherwise (Eq. 1). A is the frozen target agent; B=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} is a batch of n tasks in environment E; R_{i}^{0} and R_{i}^{P} are rewards before and after installing executable overlay P, generated by engineer H_{\theta} from failure packet s_{B}. Every task in the same batch, including prior successes, is rerun, defining a transductive objective. Cold-start SFT minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}/y_{j}^{T}/}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{t=1}^{/y_{j}^{T}/}\log H_{\theta}(y_{j,t}^{T}\mid s_{j},y_{j,<t}^{T}) (Eq. 2): M retained examples pair packet s_{j} with teacher response y_{j}^{T}, t indexes response tokens, and /y_{j}^{T}/ is response length. Online GRPO samples K=8 candidate patches per packet; r_{k}=r(B,P_{k}), \mu_{B} and \sigma_{B} are their reward mean and standard deviation, and \widehat{A}_{k}=\frac{r_{k}-\mu_{B}}{\sigma_{B}} (Eq. 3). It maximizes \mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{T_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{k}}w_{k,t}g_{k,t}(\theta)], where g_{k,t}(\theta)=\min\{\rho_{k,t}\widehat{A}_{k},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{k,t},1-\epsilon_{\ell},1+\epsilon_{h})\widehat{A}_{k}\} (Eq. 4). Here y_{k} is the engineer response parsed into P_{k}, T_{k} its token length, \rho_{k,t}(\theta)=H_{\theta}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,<t})/H_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,<t}) is the current/old policy ratio, and \epsilon_{\ell},\epsilon_{h} are clipping bounds. The truncated importance weight is w_{k,t}=\operatorname{clip}(\exp(\ell^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,t}-\ell^{\mathrm{ro}}_{k,t}),0,2); the two log probabilities are recomputed by the training engine and recorded by the rollout engine, respectively. Only engineer parameters \theta are updated. WebShop supplies shaped reward; ALFWorld and DBBench supply binary success. Evaluation reports task success over 500 WebShop, 500 ALFWorld, and 300 DBBench tasks, shaped score on WebShop, ALFWorld task-level micro-average, and an equal-weight average of the three benchmark success rates. Harness-R1 and all non-Reflection rows use \mathrm{success@1}; Reflection separately uses two-episode \mathrm{success@2}. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 202 of the saved text | 202 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f338 — Training-Free Group Relative Policy Optimization

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | LLM agents often underperform in specialized real-world domains that require external tools and domain-specific prompting strategies. Agentic RL methods typically improve adaptation through costly parameter updates, such as SFT followed by GRPO. The paper asks whether agent performance can instead be improved without changing parameters and with lower data and computational costs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Reliance on tuning LLM parameters brings four practical problems. (1) Computational cost: prohibitive for large models, and fine-tuned models need dedicated deployment. (2) Poor cross-domain generalization, so several specialist models must be deployed. (3) Data scarcity plus overfitting on few samples. (4) Diminishing returns, because cost forces fine-tuning of models below 32B, which creates a cost-performance dilemma against larger general-purpose models. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 57 of the saved text | 57 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No separate scalar objective formula is given for Training-Free GRPO. Vanilla GRPO maximizes a PPO-clipped objective \mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta), with a KL penalty against a reference model, using the group-relative advantage \hat{A}_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\text{mean}(\mathbf{r})}{\text{std}(\mathbf{r})}. Here \theta denotes policy-model parameters, G is the number of outputs for query q, o_{i} is output i, \mathbf{r}=\{r_{1},\dots,r_{G}\} is the reward group, and r_{i}=\mathcal{R}(q,o_{i}) is its reward-model score. Training-Free GRPO freezes \theta and conditions its policy on the external experience library \mathcal{E}, written \pi_{\theta}(o_{i}/q,\mathcal{E}). It updates \mathcal{E} using semantic advantages from the current batch: A_{\text{text}}=\mathcal{M}({p_{\text{extract}}},q,s_{i},\mathcal{E}), where \mathcal{M} is the same LLM, p_{\text{extract}} is the experience-extraction prompt template, and s_{i}=\mathcal{M}(p_{\text{summary}},q,o_{i}) is the output summary generated with the summarization prompt template p_{\text{summary}}. This context update steers the policy toward higher-reward outputs. Main evaluation metrics are Mean@32 (average Pass@1 over 32 independent runs per problem) on AIME24/AIME25 and pass@1 on WebWalkerQA, with learning cost in dollars. Learning dynamics also report Mean@5 on the training set; WebWalkerQA ablations report pass@1 and pass@3 on a difficulty-stratified sample of 51 test instances after two optimization epochs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 108 of the saved text | 108 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | The method moves policy optimization from parameter space to context space. For each query it generates a group of rollouts conditioned on an external experience library and scores them with a reward model. For groups with clear winners and losers, the same LLM summarizes each rollout and distils a natural-language semantic advantage. The library is then updated through Add/Delete/Modify/Keep operations. The library acts as a learned token prior in later API calls and shifts the output distribution the way a GRPO update would. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | With DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus plus ReAct and a code interpreter, Mean@32 rises from 80.0% to 82.7% on AIME24 and from 67.9% to 73.3% on AIME25 after learning from DAPO-100 (100 sampled DAPO-Math-17K problems) for three epochs at about $18 learning cost. The text contrasts this with 32B RL methods such as ReTool and AFM, which typically require thousands of examples and costs exceeding $10,000. On WebWalkerQA, the same base model improves from the static ReAct baseline's 63.2% pass@1 to 67.8% after three epochs on AFM-100 (100 web-interaction queries). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 185 of the saved text | 185 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | There is a disconnect between the model's apparent understanding of a game and its ability to follow the rules (the 'action applicability' problem of knowing which actions are valid in a state); the traditional remedies fall short: fine-tuning flagship-scale LLMs is neither fast nor cost effective and can degrade other tasks, while hand-designed harnesses are brittle and labor-intensive, needing extra work for every new game. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 97 of the saved text | 97 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Harness synthesis is a tree search over programs with Thompson sampling; each node's heuristic value is the average legal move accuracy (legal action success rate), and verifier training ends when this reaches 1.0 or times out. ## f372 — RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.24972v2 · version read: v2 · v1: 2026-09-21
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Recent methods automate harness improvement by iteratively proposing and selecting component-wise harness edits, a form of recursive self-improvement at the agent-system level, but such recursive evolution may overfit by memorizing the training tasks, giving large in-distribution gains that shrink or vanish out of distribution; the paper studies this generalization problem (the evolved harness transferring to unseen benchmarks with different task descriptions, tool interfaces or verifiers). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Harness evolution reuses a finite evolve set adaptively (candidates at round t depend on measurements of the same tasks in earlier rounds), creating an adaptive overfitting risk; the search may encode benchmark-specific patterns, promote candidates favored by evaluation noise, or accumulate complexity that raises evolve-set scores without improving the agent mechanism, and apparent gains can come from increased test-time computation rather than reusable mechanisms. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | For agent A=(\pi,H), S(H;\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim A(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,\tau)],\qquad C(H;\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim A(\cdot\mid x)}[c(\tau)]. Here \pi is the fixed backbone policy, H the harness, \mathcal{D} a task set, x a task, \tau an agent trajectory, r(x,\tau)\in[0,1] its verifier score, and c(\tau) its number of policy tokens. With k stochastic trials per task, the empirical measures are \hat{S}(H)=\frac{1}{k/\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}/}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}r(x,\tau_{x}^{(j)}),\qquad\hat{C}(H)=\frac{1}{k/\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}/}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}c(\tau_{x}^{(j)}), where \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}} is the evolve set and \tau_{x}^{(j)} is trial j on task x. RRSI selects H_{t+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}_{t}\cap\mathcal{A}_{t}}\hat{S}(H^{\prime}), where \mathcal{H}_{t} contains round-t candidates, \mathcal{A}_{t} the candidates admissible to replace current harness H_{t}, and \hat{S} the empirical score; H_{t+1}=H_{t} if no candidate is admissible. Admissibility requires leakage screening, the stability floor \hat{S}(H^{\prime})\geq S^{\star}-\delta, and the appropriate cost branch. S^{\star} is the best evolve-set score so far and \delta the empirical noise tolerance estimated by repeated evaluations of the unchanged base harness. Relative changes are \Delta S=\hat{S}(H^{\prime})-\hat{S}(H_{t}),\qquad\Delta C=\frac{\hat{C}(H^{\prime})-\hat{C}(H_{t})}{\hat{C}(H_{t})}. For \Delta S>\delta require \Delta C\leq\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}\Delta S, with \beta_{0} the cost increase tolerated for negligible gain and \beta_{1} the allowance as gain grows. For \Delta S\leq\delta require w_{s}\Delta S-w_{c}\Delta C+w_{n}\nu_{t}(H^{\prime})>0, where nonnegative w_{s},w_{c},w_{n} weight score change, relative cost change and novelty; \nu_{t}(H^{\prime}) counts structural component types touched by the candidate that never appeared in a previously accepted edit (client_tool, skill, memory or subagent). The coding instance uses w_{s}=0. The engineering instance additionally rejects a valid-output-rate fall greater than 0.03 or no-submission-rate rise greater than 0.02 relative to the incumbent. Proposal sparsity uses b_{t}=\Big\lceil b_{\min}+(b_{\max}-b_{\min})\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1+\cos(\pi t/T)\big)\Big\rceil, where t is the round, T the number of rounds, and b_{\max},b_{\min} the initial and final edit budgets. Reported evaluation metrics are Terminal-Bench accuracy (fraction of 89 tasks passing their tests); SWE-bench resolve rate (fraction satisfying both fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests); Harvey LAB fraction of rubric criteria passed over all tasks; JobBench weighted rubric score; GDPval win rate against human expert deliverables over 185 tasks; APEX-Agents pass@1 over all 480 tasks with missing rollouts counted as failures; EngDesign simulator-verified pass rate on 61 tasks; and Frontier-Eng Medal Score, mean credit over 47 tasks reported as a percentage, awarding 1, 0.67 or 0.33 for reaching the frozen gold, silver or bronze thresholds. OOD Avg. in the workspace experiments is the mean over JobBench, GDPval and APEX-Agents; resource metrics are policy tokens and steps per trial. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Translate machine-learning regularization into the harness search while leaving the edit space open: on the proposal side, an annealed edit budget (L0-style sparsity), evidence-aware credit assignment over the evolution history and structured exploration; on the selection side, a leakage-screening critic, stability-aware acceptance against a noise band, cost-aware (Ridge/L2-style) acceptance and pruning of unproductive components (Lasso/L1-style), so that reusable mechanisms rather than benchmark-specific fits survive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 111 of the saved text | 111 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Relative to the unevolved base harness H_{0}, RRSI gains 14.1 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with Gemini 3.5 Flash (64.6 to 78.7); the Claude Opus 4.8 coding run gains 6.0 points (74.2 to 80.2). In the main Claude Opus 4.8 experiments every held-out split improves, with the largest OOD gain of 4.7 points on JobBench (36.0 to 40.7). The abstract claims 30% fewer policy tokens than unregularized evolution; the agentic-workspace ablation instead reports 2.42 million tokens/trial for RRSI versus 3.80 million for unregularized evolution. These printed values are reported separately because they do not imply the stated 30% reduction. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 104 of the saved text | 104 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = policy-token cost, policy tokens, Tokens/trial (m), inference cost, test-time compute, test-time computation, steps per trial, trajectory length, aggregate resource footprint, candidate budget, edit budget, search budget, relative inference-cost change; agent kind = LLM agents A=(pi,H) built from a frozen backbone policy and a harness (prompts, control flow, tooling, memory, context management), on coding, agentic workspace and engineering design benchmarks; the method is an automated harness-evolution (recursive self-improvement) loop; position = improvement loop (learning, search, memory): regularized proposal and selection in iterative harness evolution with a frozen backbone; the token-cost constraint acts on the deployed agent loop. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The Gödel machine requires formal proofs that self-modifications are beneficial, which the paper says is impossible in practice without restrictive assumptions about the system; for example, whether another tool helps depends on the model's training and task context. Empirical search can instead get stuck in a local optimum in the space of possible systems, while meta-learning is limited by first-order improvements and human-designed search spaces. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 85 of the saved text | 85 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The main evaluation metric is percentage of solved coding tasks: SWE-bench Verified uses staged subsets (10 tasks, 50 additional tasks, and 200 total for qualifying top agents), while Polyglot uses staged subsets and a full-benchmark comparison, reported as pass@1 without ground-truth test feedback (rather than the leaderboard's pass@2). Benchmark performance is an empirical proxy for coding and self-improvement ability. The separate parent-selection rule is \displaystyle p_{i}\;=\;\frac{w_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}}, with \displaystyle w_{i}\;=\;s_{i}\,h_{i}, \displaystyle s_{i}\;=\;\frac{1}{1+\exp\!\bigl(-\lambda\,(\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{0})\bigr)}, and \displaystyle h_{i}\;=\;\frac{1}{1+n_{i}}. At iteration t, a_{i}^{t} is candidate agent i in the N-agent archive; \alpha_{i}=\mathrm{performance}(a_{i}^{t}) is its performance, n_{i} counts its children with codebase-editing functionality, s_{i} is sigmoid-scaled performance, h_{i} is the novelty bonus, and w_{i} is the unnormalized weight. The sigmoid sharpness is \lambda=10 and midpoint accuracy is \alpha_{0}=0.5. Only agents with \alpha_{i}<1 are eligible; k parents are drawn with replacement, with k=2 for SWE-bench and k=4 for Polyglot. Appendix H additionally evaluates a solve hallucination score averaged over three SWE-bench tasks: its stated components are 0 - 1 according to whether hallucination occurs in logs and 1 - 2, counted only after hallucinations cease, if tools were used in all Claude calls. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 113 of the saved text | 113 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Current LLM agents either follow fixed, hand-coded workflows that are static after deployment and do not adapt to novel situations, or update the LLM through supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, which is computationally costly and impractical for continuous online adaptation; the paper asks how to build LLM agents that learn continuously from a changing environment without the prohibitive cost of fine-tuning the underlying LLMs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Fixed workflows and hard-coded reasoning lack flexibility and neither incorporate online information nor adapt after deployment, while parameter tuning of the underlying LLM gives flexibility but comes at a high computational cost, making it inefficient for continuous adaptation and online learning; in the method, directly learning the Q function for case selection is further described as hard because states and cases are natural-language descriptions (line 154). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 85 of the saved text | 85 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Learn the case retrieval policy \mu with the LLM component p_{\text{LLM}} fixed, maximizing the maximum-entropy RL objective J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\left[\mathcal{R}(s_{t},a_{t})+\alpha\mathcal{H}\left(\mu\left(\cdot/s_{t},M_{t}\right)\right)\right]\right] (Eq. 3). The overall CBR policy is \pi(a/s,M)=\sum_{c\in M}\mu(c/s,M)p_{\text{LLM}}(a/s,c) (Eq. 1). Here s_t is the state and a_t the action (finite-length token sequences); M_t is the case bank of cases c=(s,a,r); \mu(c/s,M) is the case retrieval policy; p_{\text{LLM}}(a/s,c) is the LLM action likelihood given the state and case; \mathcal{R} is the reward function; \mathcal{H} is entropy; \alpha is its weight; T is the maximum trajectory length; and \tau is a trajectory sampled according to p, the trajectory distribution. The expected value form is \displaystyle J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,M)\sim d^{\pi}}\left[V^{\pi}(s,M)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{(s,M)\sim d^{\pi}}\left[\sum_{c\in M}\mu(c/s,M)\left[Q^{\pi}(s,M,c)-\alpha\log\mu(c/s,M)\right]\right] (Eq. 6), where d^{\pi} is the discounted visitation frequency, V^{\pi} the value function and Q^{\pi} the case-selection action-value function. For kernel-based episodic control, minimize \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,c,r,s^{\prime},M,M^{\prime})}\left[\left(Q_{\text{EC}}(s,M,c;\theta)-[r+\gamma\alpha\log\sum_{c^{\prime}\in M^{\prime}}\exp(Q_{\text{EC}}(s^{\prime},M^{\prime},c^{\prime};\bar{\theta}))]\right)^{2}\right] (Eq. 10). Q_{\text{EC}} is the Q estimate formed from past interactions with the same retrieved case using a learned state-similarity kernel k_{\theta}; \theta parameterizes that kernel, \bar{\theta} is its target network, \gamma is the discount factor, r is the observed reward, s^{\prime} is the next state, M^{\prime} is the updated case bank, and c^{\prime} ranges over its cases. In the implemented single-step CBR planner, this reduces to \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,c,r)}\left[\left(Q(s,c;\theta)-r\right)^{2}\right] (Eq. 14), where Q(s,c;\theta) is a neural Q-function with parameters \theta and (s,c,r) comes from replay buffer \mathcal{B}. Because r\in\{0,1\}, the paper replaces that MSE with \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,c,r)}\left[-\,r\log Q(s,c;\theta)-(1-r)\log\big(1-Q(s,c;\theta)\big)\right] (Eq. 15), with Q interpreted as the probability p(r=1/s,c;\theta) that case c is a useful reference for state s. Appendix A expresses the same entropy objective with a normalization constraint as \mathcal{J}(\{\mu_{c}\},\lambda)=\sum_{c}\mu_{c}Q_{c}-\alpha\sum_{c}\mu_{c}\log\mu_{c}-\lambda(\sum_{c}\mu_{c}-1) (Eq. 20), where \mu_c=\mu(c/s,M), Q_c=Q^{\pi}(s,M,c), and \lambda enforces \sum_c\mu_c=1. Appendix B also gives the direct neural-Q TD loss \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\left(s,c,r,s^{\prime},M,M^{\prime}\right)}\left[\left(Q(s,M,c;\theta)-\left[r+\gamma\alpha\log\sum_{c^{\prime}\in M^{\prime}}\exp\left(Q\left(s^{\prime},M^{\prime},c^{\prime};\bar{\theta}\right)\right)\right]\right)^{2}\right] (Eq. 24), where \bar{\theta} is the target Q network, as an alternative to the kernel-based loss. ## f385 — Online Skill Learning for Web Agents via State-Grounded Dynamic Retrieval

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.04391v1 · version read: v1 · v1: 2026-06-03
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Existing online skill learning methods largely reuse skills at the task level: a fixed set of skills is retrieved from the initial task instruction and held fixed during execution, which is misaligned with web execution where the appropriate next action also depends on the current webpage state; the paper asks how an online agent can retrieve the right reusable skill dynamically according to both the task goal and the current execution state. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 103 of the saved text | 103 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Skill retrieval operates at the task level rather than at the intermediate execution states where skills actually need to be invoked; dynamic retrieval is further hard because of a granularity challenge: full-trajectory skills may fail to apply at arbitrary intermediate states, while single-action skills are too primitive to give meaningful procedural abstraction (line 107). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 102 of the saved text | 102 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | \max_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{N}y_{i}: maximize cumulative task success over the task stream, where \pi is the overall online skill learning agent (action policy, skill induction and skill reuse rules), N the number of tasks g_i, and y_{i}\in\{0,1\} the ground-truth success of task g_i (used only for external benchmarking). Because y_i is unavailable during execution and library update, an evaluator model E gives a proxy \hat{y}_{i}=E(g_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i}) on trajectory \mathcal{T}_i, and the library is updated as \Delta\mathcal{S}_{i}=U(g_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}), \mathcal{S}_{i}=\mathcal{S}_{i-1}\cup\Delta\mathcal{S}_{i}, with new skills available only to later tasks. Here \mathcal{S}_{i} is the library after i tasks, \Delta\mathcal{S}_{i} is the newly induced skill set, and U is the skill-induction update function. Evaluation reports average success rate (SR) and the average number of steps to complete each task (# Steps); WebArena gives binary reward 1 for a correctly solved task and 0 otherwise. The local reranking objective is \operatorname{MMR}_{t}(s_{k})=\lambda\,\operatorname{score}_{t}(s_{k})-(1-\lambda)\,\max_{s_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\operatorname{sim}(d_{k},d_{k^{\prime}}), with \operatorname{score}_{t}(s_{k})=\alpha\,\cos\big(\phi(g), \phi(d_k)\big)+(1-\alpha)\,\cos\big(\phi(r_{t}), \phi(d_k)\big). Here t is the execution step; s_k is a candidate skill with description d_k; g is the task instruction; r_t is the LLM summary of the current webpage; \phi maps text to embeddings; cos is cosine similarity; \alpha balances task and state relevance; \mathcal{A}_{t} is the selected skill set; s_{k^{\prime}} and d_{k^{\prime}} denote a selected skill and its description; sim is cosine similarity of descriptions; and \lambda balances relevance and coverage. The overlap penalty is zero for an empty selected set, and selection greedily fills five slots from the top-M relevance candidates, where M is the coarse candidate budget (lines 205–221 and 315–334). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 164 of the saved text | 164 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Replace task-level one-shot skill reuse with step-level, state-conditioned retrieval: sliding-window extraction turns trajectories judged successful by an evaluator into intermediate-granularity sub-procedures stored as text-code pairs. Each induced skill is verified by substituting its call for the original action segment and retaining it only if the rewritten trajectory is still judged successful. At each decision step, skills are scored against both the task instruction and an LLM summary of the current webpage state, reranked with MMR, and injected only for that step. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On the single-domain WebArena tasks across five domains, SGDR achieves higher overall average success rate than Vanilla, AWM, ASI and CER: 37.5% with GPT-4.1 and 24.3% with Qwen3-4B, relative gains of 10.6% and 10.0% (3.6 and 2.2 points) over the strongest baseline CER. As a secondary result, SGDR uses 4.8 average steps with GPT-4.1 versus 6.0 (Vanilla), 5.2 (ASI) and 6.4 (CER). A skill step can execute multiple primitive browser actions; the reported step saving is not a measured latency or token reduction. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 90 of the saved text | 90 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Skill-augmented RL methods use strong LLMs to generate skills from trajectories and update a retrievable skill bank during online training, but rarely assess whether a newly generated skill is useful before it is stored and reused; generated skills (even from proprietary frontier LLMs) have highly mixed utility and can degrade performance. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Once a skill enters the bank its effect is hard to identify because rollout feedback is delayed and reflects the combined effect of multiple retrieved skills; measuring a skill's value by comparing rollouts with and without it would naively require extra counterfactual rollouts; and relying on proprietary frontier LLM APIs for skill generation is costly across repeated online RL updates. The paper states three challenges: estimating marginal utility without additional rollout cost, scoring a skill by its marginal contribution beyond the retrieved context, and reducing reliance on costly proprietary APIs without sacrificing skill quality. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 137 of the saved text | 137 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The collected base and skill-augmented rollouts optimize the agent policy with GRPO. Prompt-specific marginal utility is u(x_{i,j},\hat{s}_{i})=\frac{1}{/\mathcal{Y}_{i,j}^{\mathrm{skill}}/}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{i,j}^{\mathrm{skill}}}r(x_{i,j},y)-\frac{1}{/\mathcal{Y}_{i,j}^{\mathrm{base}}/}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{i,j}^{\mathrm{base}}}r(x_{i,j},y) (Eq. 4), and cross-prompt utility is U_{\hat{s}_{i}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}u(x_{i,j},\hat{s}_{i}). (Eq. 5). Here x_{i,j} is query j of induction unit \mathcal{X}_{i}, K is the number of queries in that unit, \hat{s}_{i} is its candidate skill, \mathcal{S}_{i,j} is the retrieved skill context, r(x,y) is the task reward for trajectory y, and \mathcal{Y}_{i,j}^{\mathrm{base}} and \mathcal{Y}_{i,j}^{\mathrm{skill}} are rollout sets conditioned respectively on that context and on the same context plus the candidate; vertical bars give each set size. The skill-generator objective is \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}}\left[\lambda[u(x_{i},\hat{s}_{i})]_{+}\,\ell_{\theta}(\hat{s}_{i};x_{i})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}}\left[[-u(x_{i},\hat{s}_{i})]_{+}\,\ell_{\theta}(\hat{s}_{i};x_{i})\right] (Eq. 7), with \ell_{\theta}(\hat{s}_{i};x_{i})=\log\pi_{\theta}(\hat{s}_{i}\mid x_{i},\mathcal{S}_{i},X_{\mathrm{skill}},\mathcal{Y}_{i}^{\mathrm{base}}). Here \pi_{\theta} is the policy with parameters \theta, x_i is the source query, \mathcal{S}_{i} its retrieved skills, X_{\mathrm{skill}} the skill-generation prompt, \mathcal{Y}_{i}^{\mathrm{base}} its base trajectories, and \ell_{\theta} the generated skill log-probability; [a]_{+}=\max(a,0) and \lambda\in[0,1] down-weights positive reinforcement. (Table 2), and validation success rate for training curves. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 284 of the saved text | 284 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Here \theta and \theta_{old} parameterize the current and old policies; Q is the task distribution; (q^{1},q^{2}) is a two-task chain from one scenario; G is the number of group rollouts; \tau_i is a Sequential Rollout trajectory; i indexes rollouts, k tasks in the chain and t generated output tokens; o_i^k is the output for task q^k, with environment observations masked; \epsilon is the clipping parameter. Responses that terminate without code receive a -1.0 penalty. Evaluation reports Task Goal Completion (TGC), the accuracy of completing individual tasks; Scenario Goal Completion (SGC), the proportion of scenarios with all three tasks completed; and average interaction steps (Avg. | 1 | framing_challenge | Existing UI-log approaches assume the log is already segmented into task traces, whereas a real recording is one unsegmented sequence mixing many routine instances with unrelated events; most existing approaches output frequent routines or control-flow models rather than executable specifications; and the same routine can be performed differently by different workers, yielding redundant routines. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The paper does not state one global scalar optimization objective. RQ1 asks whether candidate routines known to exist in a UI log are discovered; RQ2 asks whether known automatable routines are discovered. Candidate-routine quality uses the Jaccard Coefficient (JC), the ratio \frac{n}{m}, where n counts user interactions contained in both routines and m is the total number of user interactions present in the two routines. Each discovered routine receives its maximum JC over ground-truth routines; overall quality is the average. Evaluation also measures total coverage, average routine length and average ratio of automatable user interactions. Automatability quality is measured per user interaction: TP are correctly identified automatable interactions, TN correctly identified non-automatable interactions, FP interactions wrongly marked automatable and FN interactions wrongly marked non-automatable. The explicit formulas are Precision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}, Recall=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}, and F{\text{-}}score=2\cdot\frac{Precision\cdot Recall}{Precision+Recall}; these metrics are averaged across discovered routines in each log. Execution time (sec) is reported by pipeline step. Candidate patterns can be ranked by frequency, length, coverage or cohesion (pattern length minus the median number of gaps between elements); experiments use cohesion with minimum support 0.1 and minimum coverage 0.05. When aggregating equivalent routine specifications, the implementation selects by shortest length first and then frequency; duration is discussed as an alternative but potentially unreliable criterion. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1791 of the saved text | 1791 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A five-step pipeline: preprocess and normalize the UI log, split the unsegmented log into segments of frequently repeated step sequences, apply sequential pattern mining to find candidate routines, assess their automatability by discovering data transformations between action inputs and outputs and synthesize an executable specification for each automatable routine, then aggregate semantically equivalent routines into a non-redundant set. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Path extraction uses the finite-horizon episodic MDP \langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,R,H\rangle induced by the GUI graph \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{E}). Here \mathcal{S} contains unique GUI-page states, \mathcal{A} executable-action nodes, \mathcal{E} state-to-action and action-to-state edges, \mathcal{A}(s) available actions at state s, T the deterministic transition along graph edges, H the horizon, x the user instruction, s_{H} the terminal state, and R(s_{H},x) the binary reward (1 if that state satisfies x, otherwise 0). At step t, policy \pi(\cdot/s_{t},x) selects action a_{t}; the desired policy \pi^{*} identifies a successful path \tau^{*}. The Q-model also has explicit training objectives: Eq. (7), \mathcal{L}_{\text{init}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\tau_{t}^{+},\tau_{t}^{-})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{init}}}\left[\mathcal{R}(\tau_{t}^{+},\tau_{t}^{-})\right], with \mathcal{R}(\tau_{t}^{+},\tau_{t}^{-})=\log\sigma(Q_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t}^{+})-Q_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t}^{-})); and Eq. (9), \mathcal{L}_{\text{update}}(\theta)=-\underset{(s,a)\sim\mathcal{T}}{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\hat{Q}\log p_{\theta}+(1-\hat{Q})\log(1-p_{\theta})\Big]. Here Q_{\theta} is the trained Q-model with parameters \theta, \mathcal{D}_{\text{init}} the initialization dataset, and Eq. (7) denotes sampled preference pairs by (\tau_{t}^{+},\tau_{t}^{-}); the accompanying prose defines a_{t}^{+} as an expert action and a_{t}^{-} as a randomly sampled alternative available at s_{t}. In Eq. (9), \mathcal{T} contains state-action pairs from search trees, \hat{Q} is the soft target computed through bottom-up Bellman backup, and p_{\theta}=\sigma(Q_{\theta}(s,a)); the text uses \sigma as this output transform without separately defining it. The losses respectively initialize the model through pairwise ranking and refine it by binary classification with soft labels. | 0 | framing_problem | World models give long-horizon LLM agents foresight, but unreliable foresight can be ignored, misused or degrade decisions; under deployment-time distribution shift a frozen world model mispredicts future transitions, so a deployed world model must detect prediction-observation mismatches and adapt. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 74 of the saved text | 74 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Deployed agents face evolving environments and new task instances (a sim-to-real-like shift), so a frozen world model mispredicts; absorbing each mismatch through gradient-based parameter updates incurs high computation costs at LLM scale and risks over-editing or catastrophic forgetting; and since foresight conditions the next action, noisy foresight hurts action accuracy. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 81 of the saved text | 81 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Select and improve \hat{o}_{t+1}, the next predicted observation, through deployment-time continual evolution while keeping the agent policy \pi_{\theta} and world model W_{\theta} frozen. The textual interaction state is s_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}), the policy samples a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}), and the world model predicts (\hat{o}_{t+1},\ldots,\hat{o}_{t+K})\sim W_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}); o_{i} and a_{i} are observations and actions, t is the current step, K is the prediction horizon, and \theta denotes the fixed model parameters. The study focuses on one-step foresight. Prediction metrics are Exact Match (normalized string matching), Token F1 (tokenized lexical overlap, micro-averaged over examples), and Cosine Similarity (Qwen3-Embedding-8B embeddings). Agent planning uses Success Rate (task completion within the interaction budget), aggregated best-of-L, with L{=}5 trials and at most 30 steps per trial. Additional reported planning metrics are Progress Rate (maximum task progress across trials), Grounding (frequency of environment-accepted valid actions), and Success@1 (first-trial task success). Confidence evaluation uses ECE-F1-10 (sample-weighted absolute gap between mean confidence and mean Token F1 over ten bins) and C-index (frequency with which higher confidence corresponds to higher F1 across comparable pairs; 0.5 is random ranking and 1.0 perfect ranking). Cost reporting uses seconds per evaluated transition and total GPU hours, plus WM invocations/agent step, LLM calls/agent step, retrieval ms/call and peak prompt tokens/WM call. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 123 of the saved text | 123 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Instead of updating parameters, WorldEvolver evolves the evidence given to the frozen world model at inference time: Episodic Memory retrieves realized action transitions for retrieval-based simulation, Semantic Memory turns prediction-observation mismatches into persistent heuristic rules, and Selective Foresight filters low-confidence predictions before they reach the frozen agent. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 127 of the saved text | 127 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

(1): \phi_{1}\left(\mathcal{D},\hat{T},\hat{R}\right)=\quad\forall(s,a,r,s^{\prime},c,d)\in\mathcal{D}:(\hat{T},\hat{R})\vdash(s,a,r,s^{\prime},c,d). \text{where }(\hat{T},\hat{R})\vdash(s,a,r,s^{\prime},c,d)\text{ if }\hat{T}(s,a)=s^{\prime}\wedge\hat{R}(c)(s,a,s^{\prime})=(r,d). (2): \phi_{2}\left(s_{0},c,\hat{T},\hat{R}\right)=\quad\exists{a_{1},s_{1},a_{2},s_{2},...,a_{\ell},s_{\ell}}\qquad \qquad\forall i\in[\ell]:\hat{T}(s_{i-1},a_{i})=s_{i}\wedge\exists r>0:\hat{R}(c)(s_{\ell-1},a_{\ell},s_{\ell})=(r,1). | 1 | framing_challenge | Two failure modes motivate the design: path dependence, where single-lineage self-editors are biased by early edits and plateau, and cross-task interference, where an edit that fixes one task family regresses another and mixed-distribution evolution stagnates. Many edits win on a small subset but lose on the full benchmark. The paper contrasts its selection rule with DGM, which mutates one parent at a time and scores the child against that parent, leaving complementary lineages uncombined and a gain without an obligation to retain displaced capabilities. Noisy agent benchmarks also allow a single lucky rollout to masquerade as a capability gain. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 164 of the saved text | 164 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Fitness is the per-task solve rate \hat{p}_{t}(v) (avg@ k), where t is a task, v a harness variant, and k the number of rollouts per candidate per task; scoring uses the benchmark verifier without gold solutions. For child c and parent p, \Delta_{t}=\hat{p}_{t}(c)-\hat{p}_{t}(p), net gain g(c)=\sum_{t}\Delta_{t}, and bounded regression R(c)=\sum_{t}(-\Delta_{t})_{+}; the positive-part term sums decreases in solve rate. Admission requires g(c)>0 and R(c)\leq\delta, with \delta bounding allowed regression. The verifier agent f reads trial evidence \mathcal{E} and shared memory K_{g}, returning \mathrm{verdict}(c)=f(g,R,\mathcal{E},K_{g})\in\{\text{promote},\text{revert}\}; a promoted child must pass a higher-fidelity preservation probe before steering search. Lineage gain G(c)=G(p)+g(c) drives parent selection p^{*}\sim(1-\beta)\,\delta_{\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}}G(v)}+\beta\,\mathrm{Broaden}(\mathcal{P}): probability 1-\beta selects the highest-gain confirmed variant in steering set \mathcal{S}, while probability \beta broadens over population \mathcal{P}. For merged variants v_{1},\ldots,v_{n} with common ancestor H_{0}, H=H_{0}\oplus\Delta and \Delta=\Delta_{\text{code}}\oplus\Delta_{\text{skill}}\oplus\Delta_{\text{prompt}}\oplus\Delta_{\text{tool}} combine their additive code, skill, prompt, and tool edits. Acceptance requires S(\text{child})\supseteq\bigcup_{i}S(v_{i}), where S(v) is the set of tasks solved by v. Evaluation uses official avg@ 5 for Terminal-Bench 2.1, single-attempt pass@1 for held-out TerminalWorld, audit-clean pass@1 for WebArena-Infinity (invalid trajectories count as failures), and official pass@1 for SWE-bench Verified transfer. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 363 of the saved text | 363 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Self-evolving agents improve on the tasks they failed, but gains on failed tasks do not automatically preserve performance on previously successful tasks; the paper asks under what condition a self-evolved harness can be reliably adopted, i.e. improves expected reward over the full user-task distribution, and how validation can guarantee this. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 125 of the saved text | 125 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Modifications are generated from observed task failures, so an adopted agent may improve on failed tasks while performing worse on previously successful ones; adoption must be decided from finite, noisy validation-set estimates because outputs vary across runs; near the reward upper bound the remaining gains are small, so verification must separate small gains from degradation; and evolution can stall either because generation rarely produces qualified modifications or because validation lacks evidence to accept them. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 135 of the saved text | 135 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reliable adoption requires J_{\mathrm{user}}(A_{k}\oplus c)>J_{\mathrm{user}}(A_{k}), with V(A,t):=\mathbb{E}_{o\sim A(\cdot\mid t)}[r(t,o)] and J_{\mathrm{user}}(A):=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{user}}}[V(A,t)]. Here A_{k}=(M,C_{k}) is the current agent with fixed language model M and evolvable harness C_{k}, c is a modification, \oplus applies it, t and o are a task and output, r(t,o)\in[0,1] is fixed task reward, and \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{user}} is the user-task distribution. For candidate \widetilde{A}, \mathrm{Adv}_{A_{k}}(\widetilde{A},t):=V(\widetilde{A},t)-V(A_{k},t), L_{A_{k}}(\widetilde{A}):=Z_{k}\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{D}_{F,k}}[\mathrm{Adv}_{A_{k}}(\widetilde{A},t)], and D_{R}(\widetilde{A};A_{k}):=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{D}_{R,k}}/\mathrm{Adv}_{A_{k}}(\widetilde{A},t)/. Z_{k} is the current overall failure rate, and \mathcal{D}_{F,k} and \mathcal{D}_{R,k} are its induced failure-task and retained-task distributions. For L_{k}(c):=L_{A_{k}}(A_{k}\oplus c) and D_{k}(c):=D_{R}(A_{k}\oplus c;A_{k}), a qualified modification meets L_{k}(c)\geq\lambda and D_{k}(c)\leq\delta, where \lambda>0 is minimum failure-task contribution and \delta\geq 0 is maximum retained-task change; under the stated assumptions, \lambda>(1-Z_{k})\delta guarantees gain at least \lambda-(1-Z_{k})\delta>0. Two-Gate validates iff \widehat{L}_{k}\geq\tau, \widehat{D}_{R}\leq\delta, and \Delta_{k}:=\tau-\varepsilon_{L}-(1-\widehat{Z}_{k}+\varepsilon_{Z})(\delta+\varepsilon_{D})>0: hats denote validation estimates, \varepsilon_{L},\varepsilon_{D},\varepsilon_{Z} their error bounds, and \tau,\delta>0 the gate thresholds. The evaluation-cost metric N_{\mathrm{eval}} counts candidate agent runs returning one task reward each. Implicit world modeling minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\text{IWM}}=-\sum_{(s_{i},a_{i}^{j},s_{i}^{j})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{rollout}}}\log p_{\theta}(s_{i}^{j}\mid s_{i},a_{i}^{j}) (Eq. 3). Here K alternative actions a_{i}^{j}, j\in[K], are sampled from the initial policy at expert state s_{i}; executing each gives next state s_{i}^{j}, and their triples form \mathcal{D}_{\text{rollout}}. The language-model output distribution p_{\theta} shares parameters \theta with the policy. In practice, expert transitions (s_{i},a_{i},s_{i+1}) are also included, where s_{i+1} follows expert action a_{i}; IWM training precedes fine-tuning on \mathcal{D}_{\text{expert}} with \mathcal{L}_{\text{IL}}. Self-reflection minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\text{SR}}=-\sum_{(s_{i},a_{i}^{j},c_{i}^{j})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{refl}}}\log p_{\theta}(c_{i}^{j},a_{i}\mid s_{i}) (Eq. 4). The model-generated chain-of-thought c_{i}^{j} explains why expert action a_{i} is preferable to alternative a_{i}^{j}, based on their resulting states; \mathcal{D}_{\text{refl}} contains these triples. Training jointly predicts the concatenated reflection and expert action and mixes reflection data with \mathcal{D}_{\text{expert}}. (some but not all of the G returns are positive). State2State mid-training precedes RL on human-specified tasks. | 2 | framing_objective | The finite-horizon MDP is \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,H,\mu_{0}), where \mathcal{S} is the GUI state space (screenshots and parsed XML hierarchy), \mathcal{A} atomic GUI actions, P the Android/app transition mechanism, r the binary terminal reward, H the horizon, and \mu_{0} the distribution of initial states s_{0} and instructions c. The policy \pi_{\theta} has parameters \theta; an episode trajectory \tau ends at T\leq H with R(\tau)=r(s_{T},a_{T})\in\{0,1\}. Learning maximizes success probability (lines 175-187): \theta^{\star}=\arg\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{(s_{0},c)\sim\mu_{0},\;\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\bigl[R(\tau)\bigr]. The optimization also uses the empirical GRPO loss (Eq. 1, lines 208-221): \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=-\,\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\min\!\Bigl(\rho_{i,t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{i,t},\;\mathrm{clip}\!\bigl(\rho_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\bigr)\,\hat{A}_{i,t}\Bigr). A trajectory terminates on a terminate action or the maximum number of steps. For each task, G trajectories \{\tau^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G} receive binary rewards \{R^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G}. The multi-step GRPO action-sequence objective is (Eq. 3) \mathcal{J}^{(i)}_{t}(\theta)=\frac{1}{/a_{t}^{(i)}/}\sum_{k=1}^{/a_{t}^{(i)}/}\left(\min\left(r^{(i)}_{t,k}(\theta)\hat{A}^{(i)},\text{clip}\left(r^{(i)}_{t,k}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)\hat{A}^{(i)}\right)-\beta D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}//\pi_{\text{ref}})\right), with token probability ratio and group-normalized advantage (Eq. 4) r^{(i)}_{t,k}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}\left(a_{t,k}^{(i)}\big/I,s^{(i)}_{t},a_{t,<k}^{(i)}\right)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\left(a_{t,k}^{(i)}\big/I,s^{(i)}_{t},a_{t,<k}^{(i)}\right)},\ \ \ \ \hat{A}^{(i)}=\frac{R^{(i)}-\text{mean}\left(\{R^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G}\right)}{\text{std}\left(\{R^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G}\right)} Here i indexes trajectories, t the interaction step, k the output token, /a_{t}^{(i)}/ the action-sequence token count, a_{t,<k}^{(i)} the preceding action tokens, \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} the old policy, \pi_{\text{ref}} the reference policy, \epsilon the clipping bound, and \beta the KL-loss coefficient. The final objective averages over all action sequences (Eq. 5): \mathcal{J}(\theta)=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{G}T^{(i)}}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{T^{(i)}}\mathcal{J}^{(i)}_{t}(\theta), where T^{(i)} is trajectory i length in interaction steps. The KL term uses the per-token k2 estimator (Eq. 6): D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}//\pi_{\text{ref}})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\log\pi_{\theta}\left(a_{t,k}^{(i)}\big/I,s^{(i)}_{t},a_{t,<k}^{(i)}\right)-\log\pi_{\text{ref}}\left(a_{t,k}^{(i)}\big/I,s^{(i)}_{t},a_{t,<k}^{(i)}\right)\right)^{2} Rewards are estimated by Qwen2.5-VL-32B queried four times with unanimous agreement. OSWorld reports SR and (Eq. 7) \text{pass}@k\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim D}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c_{i}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right],\ \ \ \ \text{all-pass}@k\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim D}\left[\frac{\binom{c_{i}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right], where D is the evaluation task set, x_{i} a task, n the trials per task and c_{i} its correct samples; pass@k measures solving within k trials and all-pass@k success in all k trials. The paper sets n=8, k=4 and temperature 0.5 for these estimators. AndroidLab reports SR and sub-goal success rate (Sub-SR). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 197 of the saved text | 197 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | The RL goal is to maximize discounted cumulative rewards. The turn-level value is Q^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{h+t},a_{h+t})\right]. Here \pi is the policy, s_{h} and a_{h} are the state and action at turn h, r is the binary 0/1 task-completion reward judged by Gemini 1.5 Pro, and \gamma discounts future rewards; s_{t} combines tokenized interaction history and the current observation, and a_{t} is a token sequence executed as one turn. V^{\pi}(s_{h}) is Q^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h}) averaged over actions from \pi, and A^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})=Q^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})-V^{\pi}(s_{h}). Representation fine-tuning uses the binary cross-entropy objective J_{\mathcal{P}}(\theta_{\mathrm{VLM}})=-\mathbb{E}_{s_{t},a_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}}[y_{i}\log\mathcal{P}_{\theta_{\mathrm{VLM}}}(\mathrm{{}^{\prime}yes^{\prime}}/s_{t},a_{t})+(1-y_{i})\log\mathcal{P}_{\theta_{\mathrm{VLM}}}(\mathrm{{}^{\prime}no^{\prime}}/s_{t},a_{t})]. Here \mathcal{D} is the static transition dataset and \mathcal{P}_{\theta_{\mathrm{VLM}}} is the VLM next-token distribution. The label y_{t} is 0 when d(s_{t},s_{t+1})<\epsilon and 1 otherwise, where d is the \ell_{2} image distance and \epsilon the change threshold; Eq. (3) prints this label as y_{i}. With VLM features frozen, the critic objectives are J_{Q}(\theta_{\mathrm{MLP}})=\mathbb{E}_{s,a,r,s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}}[(Q_{\theta_{\mathrm{MLP}}}(f_{\theta_{\mathrm{VLM}}}(s,a))-r-\gamma\,V_{\bar{\psi}_{\mathrm{MLP}}}(f_{\bar{\psi}_{\mathrm{VLM}}}(s^{\prime})))^{2}], and J_{V}(\psi_{\mathrm{MLP}})=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot/s)}[\bigl(V_{\psi_{\mathrm{MLP}}}(f_{\psi_{\mathrm{VLM}}}(s))-Q_{\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLP}}}(f_{\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{VLM}}}(s,a^{\prime}))\bigr)^{2}]\Bigr]. Here s,a,r,s^{\prime} are state, action, reward and next state; Q and V are action- and state-value functions; \theta and \psi parameterize them, with VLM and MLP subscripts denoting backbone and head parameters; f denotes the backbone representations, barred parameters denote delayed targets, and \pi_{\phi} is the policy parameterized by \phi. Best-of-N policy extraction uses J_{\pi}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{t}\sim\mathcal{D},a_{i}\sim\pi_{\beta}(\cdot/s_{t})\end{subarray}}\!\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta(a_{i})\sum_{h=1}^{L}\log(a_{i}^{h}/s_{t},a_{i}^{1:h-1})\right], where \delta(a_{i})=\mathds{1}\{a_{i}=\arg\max_{i}Q(s_{t},a_{i})\text{\penalty\ and\penalty\ }Q(s_{t},a_{i})-V(s_{t})>0\}. Here \pi_{\beta} is behavior-cloned from the offline data, N=16 actions are sampled per state, L is the action-token length, h indexes tokens, and \delta selects the highest-Q action only when it has positive advantage over V. The implementation additionally uses A>1/H, with H=20 for Webshop and H=10 for General, as the actor-learning threshold (line 673). Evaluation reports AitW General and Web Shopping success rates using the autonomous evaluator on the first 96 instructions in the train and test sets; offline experiments are repeated three times with means and standard deviations. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 94 of the saved text | 94 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Train a Q-function with offline TD-learning on historical data using frozen intermediate-layer VLM representations first fine-tuned to predict whether an action substantially changes the screen. The Q-function scores candidate actions without rolling them out; Best-of-N policy extraction imitates the highest-valued sampled action when it has positive advantage, enabling policy improvement without additional environment interaction. Training a small value head reduces TD-learning compute. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 65 of the saved text | 65 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Evaluate judge reliability using binary accuracy, success recall (\mathrm{sRec}: the share of truly successful trajectories accepted), fail recall (\mathrm{fRec}: the share of truly failed trajectories caught), and balanced accuracy (\mathrm{BalAcc}: the mean of the two recalls). Low success recall means excessive strictness; low fail recall means excessive leniency. Accuracy uses all 1019 trajectories, treating rare unscored runs as errors, while recalls use only successfully scored trajectories. For the 440 successful OSReward-Multi trajectories, alignment and efficiency are scored by macro-recall (balanced accuracy of emitted levels) and AUC (pairwise ranking accuracy, with ties counting 0.5); Multi and its AUC are unweighted means across the two axes. The released efficiency labels are 0, 0.5 and 1.0; Appendix E.2 defines evaluation levels as {\leq}0.5 versus 1.0, while alignment uses 0.5 versus 1.0. A failed verdict on a human-positive trajectory forfeits the auxiliary axes. Dollar costs use official API list prices where available and May 2026 market rates for similar-size open models otherwise. The OS-Shepherd RL stage uses GRPO with rewards 1.0 for a correctly formatted correct verdict, 0.1 for a correctly formatted wrong verdict, and 0.0 for format violations; a token-level KL penalty to the SFT reference (coefficient 0.001, low-variance estimator) is added as a loss, not to the reward, with no entropy bonus. | 1 | framing_challenge | Evaluations are experiments, but the evaluation literature has largely ignored the experiment-analysis literature; eval scores are noisy because questions are a sample from an unseen super-population (variance of the conditional mean) and model answers are themselves random (conditional variance), and questions drawn in related groups violate the independence assumption so naive standard errors are inconsistent. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 44 of the saved text | 44 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Conduct inference on \mu=\mathbb{E}[s]=\mathbb{E}[x], the unobserved mean score of the question super-population, using \hat{\mu}=\bar{s} and \bar{s}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}s_{i}. Here s_{i}=x_{i}+\epsilon_{i} is question i's score, x_{i} its conditional mean, \epsilon_{i} its zero-mean random component, and \sigma_{i}^{2}=\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_{i}) its conditional variance; s,x are the unconditional score and conditional-mean variables, and n is the number of questions (assumed independent for unclustered formulas). The paper specifies \mathrm{SE}_{\rm C.L.T.}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(s)/n}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i}(s_{i}-\bar{s})^{2}\right)/n} (Eq. 1), \mathrm{SE}_{\rm Bernoulli}=\sqrt{\bar{s}(1-\bar{s})/n} for s_{i}\in\{0,1\} (Eq. 2), and \mathrm{CI}_{\ 95\%}=\bar{s}\pm 1.96\times\mathrm{SE}_{\rm C.L.T.} (Eq. 3). For independently drawn clusters, \mathrm{SE}_{\rm clustered}=\left(\mathrm{SE}_{\rm C.L.T.}^{2}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{c}\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}(s_{i,c}-\bar{s})(s_{j,c}-\bar{s})\right)^{1/2} (Eq. 4), where s_{i,c} is question i's score in cluster c and i,j index questions within c. Estimator variance is \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\mu})=\mathrm{Var}(s)/n=(\mathrm{Var}(x)+\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{i}^{2}])/n; answering each question K times and averaging gives \mathrm{Var}(s_{i})=\sigma_{i}^{2}/K. For models A and B, \hat{\mu}_{A-B}=\hat{\mu}_{A}-\hat{\mu}_{B}; the unpaired standard error is \mathrm{SE}_{A-B}=\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{A}^{2}+\mathrm{SE}_{B}^{2}}, with \mathrm{CI}_{A-B,95\%}=\hat{\mu}_{A-B}\pm 1.96\times\mathrm{SE}_{A-B} (Eq. 5) and z_{A-B}=\hat{\mu}_{A-B}/\mathrm{SE}_{A-B} (Eq. 6). On shared questions use \mathrm{SE}_{A-B,{\rm paired}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(s_{A-B})/n}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i}(s_{A-B,i}-\bar{s}_{A-B})^{2}\right)/n} (Eq. 7), where s_{A-B,i}=s_{A,i}-s_{B,i} and \bar{s}_{A-B}=\bar{s}_{A}-\bar{s}_{B}; for clustered shared questions use \mathrm{SE}_{A-B,{\rm paired},{\rm clustered}}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{c}\sum_{i}\sum_{j}(s_{A-B,i,c}-\bar{s}_{A-B})(s_{A-B,j,c}-\bar{s}_{A-B})\right)^{1/2} (Eq. 8), with s_{A-B,i,c} the within-cluster score difference, and substitute this standard error into the interval and z-score. For planning, n=(z_{\alpha/2}+z_{\beta})^{2}(\omega^{2}+\sigma_{A}^{2}/K_{A}+\sigma_{B}^{2}/K_{B})/\delta^{2} (Eq. 9), or \delta=(z_{\alpha/2}+z_{B})\sqrt{(\omega^{2}+\sigma_{A}^{2}/K_{A}+\sigma_{B}^{2}/K_{B})/n} (Eq. 10, retaining the printed z_{B}; the text defines z_{\beta} but does not separately define z_{B}). K_{A},K_{B} are the answer sample counts per question for models A,B; \alpha is the Type I error rate, \beta the Type II error rate (power 1-\beta), \delta the Minimum Detectable Effect (mean score difference under the alternative), and z_{p} the (1-p)th standard-normal percentile. The variance components are \omega^{2}=\mathrm{Var}(x_{A})+Var(x_{B})-2\mathrm{Cov}(x_{A},x_{B}), \sigma_{A}^{2}=\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{A,i}^{2}], and \sigma_{B}^{2}=\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{B,i}^{2}]. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 102 of the saved text | 102 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Treat eval questions as samples from an unseen super-population and apply experiment-design tools: CLT standard errors, clustered standard errors for related questions, variance reduction by averaging resampled answers or using next-token probabilities where suitable, paired question-level differences for model comparisons, and power analysis to choose eval size or resampling counts. The paper advises against changing sampling temperature solely to reduce variance, unless the purpose is to study the model at the new temperature. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 44 of the saved text | 44 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | The claims concern statistical precision and validity. In Table 4, clustered standard errors for Anthropic models exceed naive errors by over 3X on DROP (reported ratio 3.05); the paper separately attributes too-narrow Llama 3 intervals to unaccounted clustering and potentially too-wide intervals to applying the Bernoulli formula to fractional scores. In its hypothetical planning example with \sigma_{A}^{2}=\sigma_{B}^{2}=1/6, \omega^{2}=1/9, \mathrm{Corr}(x_{A},x_{B})=0.5, n=198, \alpha=0.05, and \beta=0.20, increasing K_{A}=K_{B} from 1 to 10 is reported to reduce the Minimum Detectable Effect from 13.2% to 7.5%. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 226 of the saved text | 226 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

B=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} is a batch of n tasks in environment E; A is the frozen target agent; R_{i}^{0} and R_{i}^{P} are its rewards before and after installing patch P, generated by engineer H_{\theta} from failure packet s_{B}. Every task in B is rerun, including initially successful ones, so this is a same-batch, transductive objective. Cold-start Eq. (2) minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}/y_{j}^{T}/}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{t=1}^{/y_{j}^{T}/}\log H_{\theta}\!\left(y_{j,t}^{T}\mid s_{j},y_{j,<t}^{T}\right): M is the number of retained teacher responses, s_j the failure packet, y_j^T the serialized teacher response, and t a response-token index. (4) maximizes \mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{T_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{k}}w_{k,t}g_{k,t}(\theta)\right], where g_{k,t}(\theta)=\min\!\Big\{\rho_{k,t}\widehat{A}_{k},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{k,t},1-\epsilon_{\ell},1+\epsilon_{h})\widehat{A}_{k}\Big\}. y_k is the engineer response parsed into P_k, T_k its length, \rho_{k,t}(\theta)=H_{\theta}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,<t})/H_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,<t}) the new/old policy token-probability ratio, and \epsilon_{\ell},\epsilon_h the clipping bounds. | 0 | framing_problem | Most web agents run a reactive execution loop (observe, reason about the next action, execute, repeat); this incurs latency and cost that grow with the number of actions and forces agents to repeatedly rediscover how the same web application works. The central question is whether web agents can replace step-by-step reactive reasoning with offline application knowledge and one-shot planning. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 62 of the saved text | 62 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Tasks within the same application share a stable structure (the same pages, controls, operations and navigation paths recur), but reactive agents do not exploit it: they rediscover how the application works and invoke the LLM throughout execution, so cost and latency grow with the number of actions and errors accumulate over long trajectories. Prior reuse via stored demonstrations/trajectories packages the decisions of one particular task, so a new task can reuse only some of its actions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Figure 4 additionally reports average input tokens, output tokens, LLM calls and estimated API cost per task; API cost uses $5/M input and $25/M output tokens, with caching discounts. Offline metrics include crawling time and cost and Break-even, the number of tasks needed to amortize crawling cost relative to Claude Code. The prefix-caching algorithm has the local load-balancing rule k^{*}\leftarrow\arg\min_{k}/\mathrm{ops}(C_{k})/: C_{k} is cluster/bucket k, /\mathrm{ops}(C_{k})/ counts its operations, and k^{*} is the selected smallest bucket, to which the next community P is assigned. | 3 | framing_solution | A Crawling Agent moves application discovery offline and constructs task-independent state-machine memory of interface states, operations and transitions. At runtime, a Planner generates a program sketch in one LLM call, and a deterministic compiler grounds it against the memory. The Executor runs the plan without further planning calls; generated programs may still call LLM helpers for runtime semantic reasoning, and large memories can require an additional state-filtering LLM call. A Patcher handles failures reactively and writes repairs to the memory. The paper describes one call per task as the common case, rather than a guarantee. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Four retained mechanisms form SoL-Pi: Action Fusion combines a mutation with its follow-up command; Online Context Compact uses projected savings and cache-rewrite cost to decide compaction; ObservationPack archives large outputs and replaces repeated full outputs with retrievable handles and excerpts; Evidence-Preserving Reducer uses a cheaper model to extract build/test-log evidence, with deterministic verification and fallback. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Harness evolution repeatedly proposes and selects edits using feedback from a finite evolve set (adaptive reuse), so overfitting arises through coupled behaviours: encoding benchmark-specific patterns, promoting candidates favoured by evaluation noise, and accumulating complexity that raises evolve-set scores without improving the underlying mechanism. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Eq. (1) measures S(H;\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim A(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,\tau)] and C(H;\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim A(\cdot\mid x)}[c(\tau)], where A=(\pi,H) has frozen backbone policy \pi and harness H, x is a task from task set \mathcal{D}, \tau its trajectory, r(x,\tau)\in[0,1] its verifier score, and c(\tau) the policy tokens consumed. With k trials per evolve task, Eq. (3) uses \hat{S}(H)=\frac{1}{k/\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}/}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}r(x,\tau_{x}^{(j)}) and \hat{C}(H)=\frac{1}{k/\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}/}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evolve}}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}c(\tau_{x}^{(j)}), with \tau_x^{(j)} the jth trajectory on x. RRSI retains the empirical-score objective but restricts admissible candidates: Eq. (8) selects H_{t+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}_{t}\cap\mathcal{A}_{t}}\hat{S}(H^{\prime}), retaining H_t if none is admissible, where t is the round, \mathcal{H}_t the proposed candidate set and \mathcal{A}_t the admissible set. After leakage screening, Eq. (5) requires \hat{S}(H^{\prime})\geq S^{\star}-\delta, with S^{\star} the best evolve score observed and \delta the empirical noise tolerance from repeated unchanged-base evaluations. Eq. (6) defines \Delta S=\hat{S}(H^{\prime})-\hat{S}(H_{t}) and \Delta C=\frac{\hat{C}(H^{\prime})-\hat{C}(H_{t})}{\hat{C}(H_{t})}. For \Delta S>\delta, Eq. (7) requires \Delta C\leq\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}\Delta S; \beta_0 is the cost increase tolerated for negligible gain and \beta_1 controls additional allowance as gain increases. For \Delta S\leq\delta, Eq. (17) instead requires w_{s}\Delta S-w_{c}\Delta C+w_{n}\nu_{t}(H^{\prime})>0, where nonnegative w_s,w_c,w_n weight score change, relative cost change and novelty, and \nu_t counts touched structural component types (client_tool, skill, memory, subagent) never present in a previously accepted edit. Coding sets w_s=0; the other two domains use positive w_s. Active domain guards must also pass: engineering design rejects a valid-output-rate drop above 0.03 or no-submission-rate rise above 0.02 relative to the incumbent. These are admissibility constraints around empirical-score maximization, not an L_p-penalized objective. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 121 of the saved text | 121 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Translate machine-learning regularization into harness search: on the proposal side an annealed edit budget (L0-style), evidence-aware credit assignment and structured exploration; on the selection side leakage screening by a critic, stability-aware acceptance against a noise band, complexity-aware acceptance that requires extra inference cost to be justified by measured gain (Ridge/L2-style), and structural pruning of unproductive components (Lasso/L1-style), so that reusable mechanisms rather than benchmark-specific ones survive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 135 of the saved text | 135 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Fully automated synthesis of compliance test cases faces three gaps: the Ambiguity Gap (regulations are unstructured natural language and typically lack the determinism needed for automated verification), the Validity Gap (naively using LLMs to generate traces often produces hallucinated API calls or invalid arguments), and the Inference Gap (simply stating safety rules in the instruction is trivial, so rigorous tests must require inferring implicit constraints). The introduction adds that existing benchmarks largely rely on static, manually curated or web-scraped test sets that are expensive to scale and primarily check functional correctness. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Given a toolset \mathcal{T} and regulatory policy \mathcal{P}, automatically synthesize a test case (I,\mathcal{S}^{*},\Phi_{\text{task}}), where I is the user instruction, \mathcal{S}^{*} the desired target states reachable by a generated valid ground-truth API trace, and \Phi_{\text{task}} the applicable regulatory constraints. The primary model-evaluation metric is Pass@1 (Safe Success Rate): a test case passes iff the LLM achieves the functional goal and satisfies every hidden LTL constraint. The Functional Oracle requires \mathcal{S}_{\text{mut}}\equiv\mathcal{S}^{*}, where \mathcal{S}_{\text{mut}} is the LLM's final state and \mathcal{S}^{*} is the state derived from the ground-truth trace. The Safety Oracle requires \forall\phi\in\Phi_{\text{task}},\tau_{\text{mut}}\models\phi, where \tau_{\text{mut}} is the LLM's execution trace and \phi is an applicable LTL constraint. Failures are Benign Failure (task failed safely), Unsafe Failure (safety violation and task failure), or Unsafe Success (task completion via rule violation). For generator diversity, Safety Critical API Coverage (S.C. Cov) measures the proportion of manually identified safety-critical APIs exercised across the 40 traces generated by each method. Adjacent Transition Coverage is \text{ATC}=\frac{/{(a_{i},a_{i+1})\mid 1\leq i<N}/}{/\mathcal{A}/^{2}}, where \tau=[a_{1},...,a_{N}] is an execution trace, a_i its ith action, N its number of actions, i indexes adjacent action pairs, and \mathcal{A} the set of unique APIs. Benchmark verification also reports an aggregate acceptance rate for candidate safety oracles (unanimous author agreement after three review rounds) and an acceptance rate for candidate instruction/masking outputs used to curate the benchmark. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 258 of the saved text | 258 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
